Since this is positive, the wide section has higher pressure and the narrow (faster) section has LOWER pressure — the student's intuition is the classic Bernoulli misconception. Correct answer A.
Distractor traps: B encodes the student's misconception itself (faster => higher pressure) and flips the sign. C forgets the factor of 1/2 in the kinetic-energy term, giving (1000)(32) = 32 kPa. D wrongly uses (1/2)ρ(v2 - v1)^2-type or only the speed difference reasoning, or applies (1/2)ρ(v2^2 - v1^2) with v2^2-v1^2 mistakenly taken as the area-scaled 6 kPa figure — it reflects an arithmetic path that under-computes the KE change. E is the common 'horizontal pipe means equal pressure' error, ignoring that speed (hence dynamic pressure) changes even at constant height.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Multi-step deduction: chaining conditionals via contrapositive and correctly interpreting "only if"
questions.stem:
A quality-assurance protocol for electronic components enforces exactly these three rules:

(1) If a component is certified, then it passed inspection.
(2) If a component passed inspection, then it was logged in the registry.
(3) A component is shipped only if it is certified.

During an audit, one component is found that was NOT logged in the registry. Assuming the three rules are the only constraints in force, which conclusion NECESSARILY follows?

options.B: The component was not certified, but it may still have been shipped.
options.C: The component passed inspection but was not certified.
options.D: Nothing can be concluded, because the rules only describe what happens to components that ARE certified or logged.
options.E: The component was neither inspected nor logged, yet it could have been certified through an alternate path.

questions.explanation:
Chain the contrapositives. "Not logged" applied to the contrapositive of (2) [not logged → not inspected] gives: the component did not pass inspection. Applying the contrapositive of (1) [not inspected → not certified] gives: it is not certified. Rule (3), "shipped only if certified," means shipped → certified; its contrapositive is not certified → not shipped. Therefore the component was not shipped — option A.

Distractor traps:
B) Correctly derives "not certified" but misreads (3) as "certified only if shipped" (certified → shipped), the converse of the real rule. Under that swap, "not certified" would leave shipping open — the classic "only if" direction error.
C) Result of applying the contrapositive to rule (1) but NOT to rule (2): the student stops the chain early and keeps "passed inspection" true, contradicting the fact that an unlogged component cannot have passed inspection (contrapositive of 2).
D) The converse/"one-way" fallacy — the belief that a conditional yields information only when its antecedent is affirmed, ignoring that every conditional is logically equivalent to its contrapositive.
E) Invents an exception outside the stated rules; the prompt fixes these as the only constraints, so no "alternate path" to certification exists.

questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Categorical syllogisms with mixed universal/existential premises
questions.skill: Chaining universal premises via contrapositive and correctly propagating an existential ("some") claim
questions.stem:
A research institute is described by three facts that are all true:

(1) Every researcher who has published in Nature is a member of the senior board.
(2) No member of the senior board teaches undergraduate courses.
(3) Some department heads teach undergraduate courses.

Which one of the following conclusions necessarily follows from these three facts?

options.A: Some department heads have not published in Nature.
options.B: No department head has published in Nature.
options.C: Some researchers who have published in Nature are department heads.
options.D: Every department head who teaches undergraduate courses is a member of the senior board.
options.E: No member of the senior board is a department head.

questions.explanation:
By (3) there exists at least one department head who teaches undergraduate courses. By (2) that person is not a member of the senior board. Taking the contrapositive of (1) — "anyone not on the senior board has not published in Nature" — that same department head has not published in Nature. So at least one department head has not published in Nature: option A necessarily follows.

Trap analysis of the distractors:
- B overgeneralizes the existential: the facts only place SOME department heads (those who teach undergrads) outside Nature-authorship; department heads who do NOT teach undergrads could still be senior-board members who published in Nature, so "no department head" is not forced.
- C is an unsupported existential conversion: nothing links Nature authors back to department heads; it invents an overlap the premises never assert.
- D reverses the inclusion in (1) and directly contradicts (2): a department head who teaches undergrads cannot be on the senior board, so this is not merely unproven but impossible.
- E asserts a disjointness that is never established: a department head who does not teach undergraduate courses may perfectly well sit on the senior board, so senior board and department heads can overlap.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Translating "only if"/"only" statements into implications and chaining several conditionals to classify a condition
questions.stem:
A hospital information system enforces three access rules:

Rule 1: A user can view patient records only if that user is logged in with two-factor authentication (2FA).
Rule 2: Any user who is both a licensed physician and logged in with 2FA can view patient records.
Rule 3: The 2FA credentials needed to log in are issued only to licensed physicians.

With respect to a user viewing patient records, being a licensed physician is:

options.E: sufficient, while its necessity cannot be determined.

questions.explanation:
Let P = licensed physician, T = logged in with 2FA, V = view records. The rules translate to: R1 V→T (2FA is necessary to view); R2 (P∧T)→V; R3 T→P (only physicians can obtain the 2FA credentials).

Necessity of P: anyone who views must satisfy V→T (R1), and T→P (R3), so by transitivity V→P. Every viewer is therefore a physician, making being a physician a necessary condition.

Sufficiency of P: being a physician does not by itself guarantee 2FA login (a physician may simply not be logged in), and R2 grants viewing only to someone who is BOTH a physician AND logged in with 2FA. So P alone does not guarantee V. Hence P is necessary but not sufficient — answer C.

Distractor traps:
- B misreads R2 as "physician ⇒ view," dropping the conjoined 2FA requirement; it treats one half of a jointly-sufficient pair as sufficient on its own, and also overlooks the V→T→P chain that makes P necessary.
- A likewise infers sufficiency from that misreading of R2, but correctly keeps necessity — the classic error of assuming a necessary condition is automatically also sufficient (affirming-the-converse).
- D fails to chain R1 with R3, so it never derives V→P and wrongly concludes physician status is unrelated to viewing.
- E spots a sufficiency-flavored claim in R2 but cannot resolve necessity; "necessity cannot be determined" ignores the explicit V→T→P chain that pins necessity down.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Negating a compound conditional using the equivalence ¬(P→C) ≡ P ∧ ¬C together with De Morgan's law on the consequent
questions.stem:
A control system obeys the following rule, printed in its manual:

"If the pump is running, then the pressure valve is open AND the coolant is flowing."

An engineer wants to state the exact condition under which this rule has been VIOLATED — that is, the logical negation of the printed rule. Which statement below is the correct negation?

options.A: The pump is running, and the pressure valve is not open or the coolant is not flowing.
options.B: The pump is running, and the pressure valve is not open and the coolant is not flowing.
options.C: If the pump is running, then the pressure valve is not open or the coolant is not flowing.
options.D: The pump is not running, and the pressure valve is open and the coolant is flowing.
options.E: If the pressure valve is not open or the coolant is not flowing, then the pump is not running.

questions.explanation:
Let P = "pump is running", Q = "valve is open", R = "coolant is flowing". The rule is P → (Q ∧ R). The negation of a conditional is ¬(P → C) ≡ P ∧ ¬C, so ¬[P → (Q ∧ R)] ≡ P ∧ ¬(Q ∧ R). Applying De Morgan to the consequent, ¬(Q ∧ R) ≡ ¬Q ∨ ¬R. Hence the violation is P ∧ (¬Q ∨ ¬R): the pump IS running, yet at least one of the two required conditions fails — exactly option A. A negation must be a flat (non-conditional) assertion that the antecedent holds while the consequent fails, which A alone expresses.

Trap in B (P ∧ ¬Q ∧ ¬R): a De Morgan error — the student distributes the negation as ¬(Q∧R) ≡ ¬Q∧¬R instead of ¬Q∨¬R, wrongly demanding BOTH conditions fail rather than at least one.

Trap in C (P → (¬Q ∨ ¬R)): the student negates only the consequent while leaving the "if…then" structure intact. A conditional is never the negation of a conditional, so this cannot be right regardless of the consequent.

Trap in D (¬P ∧ Q ∧ R): the student negates the antecedent and keeps the consequent — confusing "negation" with the inverse/opposite of the trigger condition.

Trap in E ((¬Q ∨ ¬R) → ¬P): this is the contrapositive of the original rule, which is logically EQUIVALENT to it, not its negation. Choosing it reflects confusing "equivalent transformation" with "negation".

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Area of triangles and lines in the plane
questions.skill: Combining area formula with a linear constraint to locate a point
questions.stem: In the coordinate plane, a triangle has vertices A(-2, 1), B(4, 1) and a third vertex P that lies on the line y = 2x. If the area of triangle ABP is exactly 15, what is the sum of the x-coordinates of ALL possible positions of P?

options.E: There is only one possible position, at x = 3

questions.explanation:
Base AB lies on the line y = 1 and has length |4 - (-2)| = 6. For area 15, we need (1/2)(6)(h) = 15, so the height h = |y_P - 1| = 5. Thus y_P - 1 = 5 or y_P - 1 = -5, giving y_P = 6 or y_P = -4. Since P is on y = 2x, x_P = y_P/2: the two solutions are x = 3 (from y = 6) and x = -2 (from y = -4). Their sum is 3 + (-2) = 1, answer B.

Trap A (-1): student takes y_P = -4 giving x = -2, but pairs it with a wrong second value or drops the first, or negates incorrectly.
Trap C (3): student finds only the y_P = 6 branch (height +5) and forgets the triangle can also lie below the base (height can be either sign), reporting the single x = 3.
Trap D (5): student computes the two y-values (6 and -4) and mistakenly sums the y-coordinates instead of the required x-coordinates: 6 + (-4) = ... or confuses base and height, landing on 5 through an off-by pairing.
Trap E: same 'only one solution' misconception as C but stated explicitly to catch students who never consider the reflected position below line AB.

verifyDefect.reason: Algebra correctly yields answer B (sum of x-coords = 1), but the figure's line labeled "y = 2x" is drawn with a negative slope (upper-left to lower-right through the origin) instead of the correct positive slope +2, so the graph contradicts its equation and would mislead a student relying on it.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Relating linear scale factor to area ratio in similar figures
questions.stem: In triangle ABC, point D lies on side AB and point E lies on side AC, with segment DE parallel to BC (see figure). The segment DE splits the triangle into the smaller triangle ADE, whose area is 9, and the trapezoid DBCE, whose area is 16. If DE = 6, what is the length of BC?
questions.explanation:
Because DE is parallel to BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC. The whole triangle ABC has area 9 + 16 = 25. For similar triangles the ratio of areas equals the SQUARE of the linear scale factor, so (BC/DE)^2 = area(ABC)/area(ADE) = 25/9. Thus BC/DE = sqrt(25/9) = 5/3, giving BC = 6 · 5/3 = 10 (option C).

Distractor traps:
A) 50/3 = 6 · 25/9: uses the correct whole-to-part area ratio 25/9 but forgets to take the square root, applying the area ratio directly as a length ratio.
B) 8 = 6 · 4/3: mistakes the trapezoid (area 16) for the whole triangle, forming 16/9, taking its square root 4/3, and scaling DE by that — confusing the part with the whole.
D) 32/3 = 6 · 16/9: uses the trapezoid-to-triangle ratio 16/9 AND forgets the square root, compounding both the part/whole confusion and the missing-square-root error.
E) 18/5 = 6 · 3/5: gets the scale factor 5/3 correct but inverts it, shrinking DE instead of enlarging it to reach the larger parallel side BC.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Circles — power of a point / chords
questions.skill: Combine the intersecting-chords (power of a point) relation with the perpendicular-diameter-bisects-chord property to solve for an unknown radius
questions.stem:
A water pipe has a circular cross-section. When partly full, the flat surface of the water forms a horizontal chord across the circle. Measured on the cross-section, the water surface is 16 cm wide, and the deepest point of the water (the bottom of the pipe) lies 4 cm below the level of that surface. What is the radius of the pipe?

(Hint: the vertical diameter of the circle is perpendicular to the water surface and cuts it into two equal halves.)
questions.explanation:
Let M be the point where the vertical diameter meets the water surface. Because a diameter perpendicular to a chord bisects it, M is the midpoint of the surface, so each half of the surface is 16/2 = 8 cm. The diameter is split by M into two pieces: the part below M (down to the bottom) = 4 cm, and the part above M = (2r − 4). By the intersecting-chords theorem (power of the point M), the product of the two half-surface pieces equals the product of the two diameter pieces: 8 · 8 = 4 · (2r − 4). So 64 = 8r − 16, giving 8r = 80 and r = 10 cm. (Check via the sagitta formula r = c²/(8h) + h/2 = 256/32 + 2 = 8 + 2 = 10.)

Distractor traps:
A) 8 cm — treats the water surface as if it were the full diameter (r = 16/2), ignoring that it is only a chord; equivalently, uses the truncated formula r = c²/(8h) and drops the +h/2 term.
C) 12 cm — uses the sagitta formula but adds the whole depth instead of half of it: c²/(8h) + h = 8 + 4.
D) 16 cm — solves 8·8 = 4·x correctly to get the upper diameter segment x = 16, then stops and reports that segment as the radius instead of using 2r − 4 = 16.
E) 34 cm — forgets to halve the chord and plugs the full width into the power-of-a-point relation: 16² = 4·(2r − 4) → 256 = 8r − 16 → r = 34.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Power dissipation in series–parallel resistor networks
questions.skill: Combining current division with P=I²R (series) and P=V²/R (parallel) to compare power in different resistors
questions.stem: In the circuit shown, R1 = 6 Ω and R2 = 3 Ω are in parallel, and this combination is in series with R3 = 4 Ω. An ideal 12 V battery (negligible internal resistance) drives the circuit. Rank the three resistors by the electrical power they dissipate, from greatest to least.
questions.explanation:
First reduce the network: R1||R2 = (6·3)/(6+3) = 2 Ω, so R_total = 2 + 4 = 6 Ω and the battery current is I = 12/6 = 2 A. This full 2 A flows through the series resistor R3, giving P3 = I²R3 = (2)²·4 = 16 W. The voltage across the parallel section is V = I·2 Ω = 4 V, shared by both branches, so use P = V²/R: P1 = 4²/6 = 2.67 W and P2 = 4²/3 = 5.33 W. (Check: 16 + 5.33 + 2.67 = 24 W = 12 V · 2 A.) Thus P3 > P2 > P1. The key insight is that R3 carries the FULL current (P=I²R rewards it), while inside the parallel section the branches share the SAME voltage, so the SMALLER resistor R2 dissipates MORE — the opposite of the series rule.
Trap B (P3>P1>P2): correctly spots R3 as largest but treats the two parallel branches as carrying equal current, applying P=I²R so the bigger R1 seems to win — the classic 'same current everywhere' error.
Trap C (P1>P3>P2): assumes one common current through the whole loop (pure series thinking), ranking power straight by resistance value 6>4>3.
Trap D (P2>P3>P1): assumes the SAME voltage across all three resistors and applies P=V²/R, ranking by 1/R (3<4<6) for every element — valid only within the parallel pair, not for R3.
Trap E (all equal): the naive belief that components in one circuit 'share the power equally,' ignoring both current division and unequal resistances.

verifyDefect.reason: R3 is drawn as a floating rectangle with no wire leads, so the figure shows R1||R2 directly across the battery with R3 disconnected, contradicting the stem's 'R1||R2 in series with R3' topology; the stored answer A is mathematically correct for the intended circuit but the figure is defective.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Modular arithmetic / simultaneous congruences (CRT with non-coprime moduli)
questions.skill: Recognizing a common residue to reduce three congruences to a single lcm-modulus, then counting solutions in a range
questions.explanation:
Each condition says N is one short of a full row: N ≡ 3 (mod 4), N ≡ 5 (mod 6), N ≡ 8 (mod 9) all mean N ≡ -1 in that modulus. So N+1 is divisible by 4, 6 AND 9, hence by their least common multiple lcm(4,6,9) = 2²·3² = 36 (NOT the product 4·6·9 = 216, since the moduli share factors). Thus N ≡ 35 (mod 36). The valid values below 1000 are 35, 71, 107, …, 971, i.e. 35 + 36k with 35 + 36k ≤ 999 ⇒ k ≤ 26.8 ⇒ k = 0,1,…,26, giving 27 values — answer B.
Distractor traps: (D) 4 comes from multiplying the moduli (216) instead of taking the lcm, giving period 216 → values 215, 431, 647, 863 under 1000. (E) 5 is that same product error plus an off-by-one that wrongly counts the out-of-range 1079. (A) 26 is an off-by-one that forgets the k = 0 term (N = 35). (C) 28 is the opposite off-by-one, over-counting by including a value at or beyond 1000.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Comparing states of a fixed quantity of ideal gas using T ∝ PV; interpreting a P–V diagram
questions.stem: A sealed rigid-walled apparatus contains a fixed quantity of an ideal gas that can be taken to different equilibrium states. The P–V diagram shows three such states, W, X and Y, which happen to lie on the same straight line. Using the diagram, which state is at the highest absolute temperature?

options.D: All three states are at the same temperature
options.E: It cannot be determined without knowing the number of moles of gas

questions.explanation: For a fixed quantity of ideal gas, PV = nRT with n constant, so absolute temperature is proportional to the product P·V. Read the coordinates: W = (1.0 L, 4.0×10^5 Pa) → PV = 4.0; X = (4.0 L, 1.0×10^5 Pa) → PV = 4.0; Y = (2.5 L, 2.5×10^5 Pa) → PV = 6.25 (units of 10^5 Pa·L). Y has the largest product, so it is hottest — this is the correct answer (C). The three points all lie on the line P + V = 5, and for a fixed sum the product is maximised at the midpoint, which is exactly Y.\n\nDistractor traps: (A) W is picked by students who equate the highest pressure with the highest temperature, ignoring volume. (B) X is picked by those who equate the largest volume with the highest temperature, ignoring pressure — note W and X actually have equal PV, so both these extremes are cooler than Y. (D) treats temperature as if it depended on the distance from the origin or on the sum P + V; because all three points share P + V = 5 they look 'equal', but T depends on the product, not the sum. (E) reflects the misconception that n is needed: since n is the same in every state, it cancels when comparing, so the number of moles is irrelevant to the ranking.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Deriving block constraints from adjacency/gap clues, enumerating all valid orderings, and distinguishing "must be true" from "could be true"
questions.stem:
Six students — Aylin, Berk, Cem, Deniz, Ela and Faruk — each give an oral presentation in one of six consecutive slots, numbered 1st through 6th, with exactly one student per slot. The schedule satisfies all of the following:
- Exactly one student presents in between Aylin and Berk, and Aylin presents before Berk.
- Ela presents immediately after Aylin.
- Cem presents at some point before Deniz.
- Faruk presents in the slot immediately before Cem.

Which one of the following MUST be true?

options.B: Deniz presents either third or last.
options.E: Ela presents in the slot immediately before Deniz.

questions.explanation:
Turn the clues into blocks. "Ela immediately after Aylin" gives Ela = Aylin+1; "exactly one student between Aylin and Berk, Aylin first" gives Berk = Aylin+2. So Aylin, Ela, Berk occupy three consecutive slots in that order (block [A-E-B]). "Faruk immediately before Cem" gives block [F-C], and Cem is before Deniz. The 3-slot block, the 2-slot block, and Deniz exactly tile the six slots. Ordering the three pieces so that Cem precedes Deniz leaves exactly three valid schedules: (1) A E B F C D, (2) F C A E B D, (3) F C D A E B. In (1) and (2) Deniz is 6th; in (3) Deniz is 3rd — so Deniz is always third or last, making B the only statement true in every case.
A (Aylin first) is true only in schedule (1): a "could be true," not "must be true" — the classic trap of promoting the first arrangement you find to a certainty. C (Cem before Berk) holds in (2) and (3) but fails in (1), where Cem is 5th and Berk 3rd — again only sometimes true. D (Faruk fourth) is true only in (1); in the other two Faruk is 1st — possible, not necessary. E is impossible: Ela is locked immediately before Berk (Ela = Aylin+1 = Berk−1), so she can never sit immediately before Deniz; it tempts solvers who blur the two adjacency clues together.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining slope of a line with the perpendicular-slope relationship to build a line equation and read its intercept
questions.stem: An engineer designs a bracket from two straight rigid bars that are welded together at the joint P(2, 5). The "load bar" runs from P down to the anchor point A(6, 3). For the bracket to be rigid, the second bar (the "support strut") must be welded PERPENDICULAR to the load bar at P. If the support strut is extended in a straight line, at what value of y does it cross the y-axis?
questions.explanation: Slope of the load bar P(2,5)→A(6,3): m = (3−5)/(6−2) = −2/4 = −1/2. The strut must be perpendicular, so its slope is the negative reciprocal: m⊥ = +2. Line through P(2,5) with slope 2: y − 5 = 2(x − 2) → y = 2x + 1, which crosses the y-axis at y = 1 (E). Distractor traps — B (6): used the load bar's OWN slope −1/2 instead of the perpendicular one (y = −x/2 + 6); this is exactly the "ignore perpendicularity" error. A (9): took the reciprocal but kept the negative sign, using slope −2 (y = −2x + 9). D (4): flipped the fraction to +1/2 without recognizing it must be the reciprocal-and-integer 2 (y = x/2 + 4). C (5): assumed the y-intercept equals the joint's height y = 5, confusing the weld point's y-coordinate with the intercept.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Absolute-value functions: reflection, translation and vertical stretch
questions.skill: Reconstruct the equation of a transformed absolute-value function from graphical features (axis of symmetry, vertex, intercepts)
questions.stem: A symmetric A-frame tent is drawn in a coordinate plane with all lengths in metres. Its outline is the graph of a single transformed absolute-value function y = a|x − h| + k. The graph is an inverted "V": the two base corners rest on the ground at the points (1, 0) and (5, 0), and the peak of the tent is at height 4 m. (See figure.) Which equation produces this graph?
questions.explanation: The axis of symmetry lies halfway between the two base corners: x = (1 + 5)/2 = 3, so h = 3 and the peak is at (3, 4), giving k = 4. Because the graph opens downward (an inverted V), a < 0. To find the magnitude of a, use a known point: at the corner (1, 0), 0 = a|1 − 3| + 4 = 2a + 4, so a = −2. Thus y = −2|x − 3| + 4 (correct, A). Distractor B (y = −|x−3|+4) reflects and shifts correctly but assumes the default slope ±1, ignoring the vertical stretch needed to reach the corners — its corners would be at (−1,0) and (7,0), not (1,0) and (5,0). Distractor C uses |x + 3|, moving the axis of symmetry to x = −3 (shifting the vertex the wrong direction). Distractor D (y = 2|x−3|+4) has the right vertex and stretch but positive a, so it opens upward — it fails to read the inverted shape. Distractor E puts k = −4, dropping the vertex to (3, −4) below the ground instead of at the peak height +4 (vertical-shift sign error).

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Composite plane figures — area and perimeter
questions.skill: Decomposing composite figures and reasoning about how a corner cut affects area versus perimeter
questions.stem:
A landscaper builds an L-shaped lawn by cutting a rectangular corner out of a plain rectangular plot. The original plot is 12 m wide and 9 m tall, and the removed corner rectangle measures 7 m (horizontal) by 5 m (vertical), taken from the top-right corner. To finish the job he must (i) run a fence around the entire boundary of the L-shaped lawn and (ii) lay rolled sod over its whole surface. Which pair gives the correct fencing length and sod area?

Fencing = total perimeter of the L-shape; Sod = total area of the L-shape.
questions.explanation: Area: start from the full rectangle 12×9 = 108 m² and subtract the removed corner 7×5 = 35 m², giving 108 − 35 = 73 m² (equivalently, bottom strip 12×4 = 48 plus left column 5×5 = 25). Perimeter: tracing the L-boundary gives 12 + 4 + 7 + 5 + 5 + 9 = 42 m. The key insight is that cutting a rectangular notch out of a CORNER leaves the perimeter unchanged: the 7 m and 5 m you "lose" from the outer top and right edges are exactly replaced by the 7 m and 5 m inner edges of the notch. So fencing = 42 m (same as the original rectangle) and sod = 73 m². Distractor traps: B keeps the correct perimeter but uses the full-rectangle area 108 m², forgetting to subtract the removed corner. C has the right area but wrongly shortens the perimeter to 42 − (7+5) = 30 m, removing the outer edge lengths without adding back the notch's inner edges. D has the right area but adds the two inner edges (7+5) on top of the full rectangle's 42 m to get 54 m, double-counting the boundary. E combines two errors: it reduces the perimeter to 30 m and reports the removed corner's area (7×5 = 35 m²) instead of the L-shape's area.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Solids of revolution — cones and their nets
questions.skill: Relating a cone's 3-D dimensions to the flat sector of its lateral surface
questions.stem: A sheet-metal worker makes a cone-shaped funnel with no top and no base by rolling up a single flat piece of metal. The finished funnel is to have a base radius of 9 cm and a vertical height of 12 cm. Before rolling, the flat piece is a sector cut from a circular disc, and the two straight edges of the sector are joined to form the cone. Through what central angle must this flat sector be cut?
questions.explanation: First find the slant height, which becomes the radius of the flat sector: l = √(9² + 12²) = √225 = 15 cm. When the lateral surface is unrolled it is a sector of radius l = 15 whose arc length equals the base circumference 2π(9) = 18π. The central angle is (arc ÷ full circumference of a radius-15 circle) × 360° = (18π ÷ 30π) × 360° = (r/l)×360° = (9/15)×360° = 216°. Distractor traps — B 270°: used the vertical height 12 as the sector radius instead of the slant, (18/24)×360°. C 288°: plugged the height into the correct formula, (h/l)×360° = (12/15)×360°, confusing height with base radius. D 360°: assumed the base circle unrolls into a full circle, forgetting the net is only a partial sector. E 144°: computed the wedge that is removed rather than the sector that remains, (l−r)/l ×360° = (6/15)×360°.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Volume of prisms and cylinders with optimization under geometric constraints
questions.skill: Multi-step spatial reasoning: identifying constrained radius and drilling depth per orientation, then optimizing
questions.stem:
A machinist must lighten a solid aluminium block measuring 10 cm × 6 cm × 4 cm by drilling ONE cylindrical hole straight through it. The hole must be perpendicular to a face and pass completely through the block (so its depth equals the block dimension perpendicular to the entry face). To fit inside the entry face, the drill's radius can be at most half of the SHORTER side of that face. The machinist chooses the orientation that removes the greatest possible volume of metal. What is the volume (in cm³) of the remaining solid?

Total block volume = 10 × 6 × 4 = 240 cm³.
questions.explanation:
There are three drilling orientations. For each, the max radius is half the shorter side of the entry face, and the hole depth is the remaining (perpendicular) dimension. Removed volume = π·r²·depth.
• Enter the 6×4 face (shorter side 4 → r=2), depth = 10: removed = π·2²·10 = 40π.
• Enter the 10×4 face (shorter side 4 → r=2), depth = 6: removed = π·2²·6 = 24π.
• Enter the 10×6 face (shorter side 6 → r=3), depth = 4: removed = π·3²·4 = 36π.
The maximum removed volume is 40π, so remaining = 240 − 40π ✓ (A). The key insight is that a bigger radius does not automatically remove more metal, because a wider entry face forces a shorter drilling depth — you must evaluate all three orientations.
Distractor traps:
B) 240 − 90π: "greedy" error — combines the largest radius (r=3) with the largest depth (10) as if they were independent (π·9·10), ignoring that r=3 is only available on the 6-cm side, which forces depth 4.
C) 240 − 36π: picks the largest-radius orientation (r=3, depth 4), assuming a wider hole always removes the most metal.
D) 240 − 24π: correctly limits r=2 but drills through the 10×4 face (depth 6) instead of choosing the deepest 10-cm path.
E) 240 − 16π: uses the "default" r=2 but the shortest depth of 4 (the original easy setup), failing to optimize orientation at all.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: Multi-step unit conversion combining bit depth, bit-packing, and binary storage prefixes
questions.stem: A data logger samples a sensor at 2000 samples per second. Each sample is stored using a 12-bit value, and the samples are bit-packed contiguously with no padding between them. The device must retain exactly 1 minute of continuous data. Using the binary convention 1 KiB = 1024 bytes and 1 byte = 8 bits, approximately how much storage does this recording require?
questions.explanation:
Correct path (B): total samples = 2000 samples/s x 60 s = 120,000 samples. At 12 bits each, that is 120,000 x 12 = 1,440,000 bits. Convert to bytes: 1,440,000 / 8 = 180,000 bytes. Convert to KiB with the binary prefix: 180,000 / 1024 = 175.8 KiB, which rounds to 176 KiB.

Distractor traps:
A) 117 KiB — assumes 1 byte (8 bits) per sample, ignoring the stated 12-bit depth: 120,000 bytes / 1024 = 117 KiB. Trap: dropping the bit-depth factor.
C) 180 KiB — does everything correctly but converts the final 180,000 bytes using the decimal 1 KiB = 1000 bytes instead of 1024. Trap: binary-vs-decimal prefix confusion (KiB vs kB) — the classic near-miss.
D) 234 KiB — pads each 12-bit sample up to a whole 2 bytes (16 bits) instead of bit-packing: 120,000 x 2 = 240,000 bytes / 1024 = 234 KiB. Trap: assuming byte-aligned storage when the problem explicitly states no padding.
E) 1406 KiB — computes the 1,440,000 bits correctly but forgets to divide by 8, treating bits as bytes: 1,440,000 / 1024 = 1406 KiB. Trap: bit-vs-byte confusion (off by a factor of 8).

questions.subject: reading
questions.skill: Identifying how a passage revises or overturns a prior explanation (cause-effect inference)
questions.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question below.

"For decades the Arctic tern's astonishing migration was explained almost entirely by its pursuit of endless summer: by shuttling between the two polar regions, the bird supposedly enjoyed more daylight than any other creature and therefore more hours in which to feed. Recent tracking studies complicate that tidy story. Tagged terns do not follow the direct meridian route that a daylight-maximising bird would choose; instead they trace a great looping detour, swinging far out over the open ocean before turning south. This detour adds thousands of kilometres to the journey, yet the birds that take it arrive in better condition than the few that fly straighter. The looping path, it turns out, keeps the terns inside broad belts of prevailing wind, so that although they travel a longer distance, they expend markedly less energy doing so. Daylight, the researchers now suggest, is a by-product of the route rather than its purpose."

Which statement best captures the passage's central revision of the older explanation?

options.A: The tern's route is shaped mainly by energy efficiency, not by a drive to maximise feeding daylight, even though the longer path covers more distance
options.B: The tern flies farther than necessary because chasing continuous daylight forces it away from the direct meridian route
options.C: The tracking studies show that terns taking the straighter route are healthier because they save distance and therefore energy
options.D: The looping detour proves that the tern gains no benefit from daylight and feeds no more than other migratory birds
options.E: The older explanation was correct that daylight drives the route, and the new studies simply add wind as a second motive

questions.explanation:
The passage overturns the "endless summer / more daylight" account: the looping detour is longer yet leaves birds in better condition because it keeps them inside prevailing wind belts, saving energy; daylight is recast as a by-product "rather than its purpose." So the central revision is that energy efficiency, not daylight-maximising, shapes the route (A).

B repeats the OLD explanation the passage rejects — it says daylight-chasing causes the extra distance, but the text explicitly says a daylight-maximising bird would take the DIRECT meridian route, so daylight cannot be what pushes the tern onto the longer path.

C inverts the evidence: the passage says birds on the LONGER looping route arrive in better condition, not the straighter-flying ones; it also wrongly equates "shorter distance" with "less energy," the very link the passage dismantles.

D over-generalises: the passage demotes daylight to a by-product but never claims the tern gains NO benefit from it or that it feeds no more than other birds — an unsupported absolute.

E misreads the revision as an addition rather than a replacement: the passage does not keep daylight as the driver and merely append wind; it reassigns cause and effect, making energy/wind primary and daylight incidental.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining conditional probability with the complement rule in a multi-step setup
questions.stem:
A quality-control machine tests components one at a time. Each component independently passes with probability 2/3 and fails with probability 1/3. The machine stops as soon as it records the FIRST failure, or after it has tested three components, whichever comes first. Given that the machine tested exactly three components in total, what is the probability that all three of those components passed?

(Note: the machine stops early only when a failure occurs, so testing three components means either the third one was the first failure, or none of the three failed.)
questions.explanation:
The machine tests a third component only if the first two components both passed (otherwise it would have stopped at the first failure). So the event "tested exactly three components" = {first two pass}, which has probability (2/3)(2/3) = 4/9. Within that, the third component may pass or fail, and testing stops after the third regardless. The event "all three passed" is {pass, pass, pass} with probability (2/3)^3 = 8/27. The conditional probability is therefore P(all three pass | tested three) = (8/27) / (4/9) = (8/27)(9/4) = 8/12 = 2/3... let me instead compute directly: given the first two passed (a certainty in the conditioning event), the answer is just P(third passes) = 2/3. Correct answer: the conditioning event is exactly "first two passed," and conditional on that the third pass probability is 2/3. Wait — reconcile: (8/27)/(4/9) = 2/3. So the correct value is 2/3, option D.

CORRECTION — the intended correct option is D (2/3). Reasoning: reaching a third test requires the first two to pass; conditional on that, all-three-passed happens exactly when the third also passes, probability 2/3.

Distractor traps: A) 4/5 comes from mis-forming the conditional as favorable/(favorable+one-other-path), e.g. (8/27)/(8/27 + 2/27) using only the "third is first failure" path incorrectly weighted. B) 8/27 is the unconditional P(all three pass), forgetting to condition on the stopping event. C) 8/9 = 1 − (1/3)(1/3) mixes up 'at least one passes in two trials' style complement. E) 4/9 is P(tested three components), the conditioning event's probability, mistaken for the answer.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Analyzing solution structure of absolute-value equations with a parameter
questions.stem: Consider the equation |2x − 3| = |x + k|, where k is a real parameter. For how many values of k does the equation have exactly one real solution?
questions.explanation:
The equation |2x − 3| = |x + k| holds exactly when 2x − 3 = x + k OR 2x − 3 = −(x + k). Solving each: (1) 2x − 3 = x + k gives x = k + 3. (2) 2x − 3 = −x − k gives 3x = 3 − k, so x = (3 − k)/3 = 1 − k/3. These two candidate roots coincide (giving a single solution) exactly when k + 3 = 1 − k/3, i.e. (4/3)k = −2, so k = −3/2. For every other k the two roots are distinct, so the equation has two solutions; there are no k giving zero solutions (each linear branch always yields a root). Hence exactly ONE value of k, namely k = −3/2, gives a single solution → answer B.

Distractor traps:
A) 0 — student believes an absolute-value equation of this form can never collapse to one root, or thinks the two branches always give distinct values.
C) 2 — student sets the two roots' expressions equal but mishandles signs (e.g. also equates k + 3 = −(1 − k/3)) and finds a spurious second value of k, or double-counts.
D) 3 — student conflates 'number of solutions' with 'number of k values' or adds an extra case from the |x + k| = 0 boundary, over-counting.
E) infinitely many — student reasons that whenever the two branches' slopes differ the graphs always meet once, mistaking the generic two-intersection picture, or thinks any k where one root is extraneous works.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Areas of circles and polygons (inscribed figures)
questions.skill: Combining multiple area relations and recognizing algebraic cancellation
questions.stem: A square tile has side 12. A circle is inscribed in the square, touching all four sides. A second, smaller square is then inscribed in that circle, with its four vertices lying on the circle. The tile is decorated so that two zones are shaded: (1) the four corner pieces of the large square that lie OUTSIDE the circle, and (2) the region that lies INSIDE the circle but OUTSIDE the smaller inscribed square. What is the total shaded area?
questions.explanation: Compute the three areas. Large square: 12² = 144. Inscribed circle: radius = 12/2 = 6, area = 36π. The corner pieces (zone 1) = 144 − 36π. The smaller square is inscribed in the circle, so its diagonal equals the circle's diameter = 12; a square with diagonal d has area d²/2 = 144/2 = 72. The region inside the circle but outside this square (zone 2) = 36π − 72. Total shaded = (144 − 36π) + (36π − 72) = 72. The π terms cancel: the shaded region is exactly the large square minus the inner square, so the answer is independent of π. Correct: A (72). Distractor B (144 − 36π) counts only zone 1 (the corner pieces) and forgets zone 2. Distractor D (36π − 72) counts only zone 2 and forgets the corners. Distractor C (108) comes from taking the inner square's side equal to the radius 6 (area 36) instead of using the diagonal = diameter, giving (144 − 36π) + (36π − 36) = 108. Distractor E (216 − 72π) results from subtracting the two zones instead of adding them: (144 − 36π) − (36π − 72) = 216 − 72π, a sign/combination error.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Inscribed and circumscribed figures; area ratios
questions.skill: Chaining inscription relationships (side = diameter, diagonal = diameter) and forming a scale-invariant area ratio
questions.stem: A designer produces a square floor tile. Inside the tile a circular disc is inscribed so that it touches all four edges of the tile. Inside that disc a second square is inscribed so that all four of its corners lie on the circle (this inner square is rotated 45° relative to the tile). The disc is coloured, except for the inner square, which is left blank — so the coloured part is the ring-like region that lies inside the circle but outside the inner square (shaded in the figure).\n\nWhatever the size of the tile, what fraction of the ENTIRE tile's area is coloured?
questions.explanation:
Let the circle have radius r. The circle is inscribed in the tile, so the tile's side equals the diameter 2r, giving tile area = (2r)² = 4r². The inner square is inscribed in the circle, so its DIAGONAL equals the diameter 2r; a square with diagonal d has area d²/2, so the inner square's area = (2r)²/2 = 2r². The coloured region = circle − inner square = πr² − 2r². Dividing by the tile area: (πr² − 2r²)/(4r²) = (π − 2)/4. The r² cancels, so the answer is independent of tile size (≈ 0.285). 

Trap B (π − 2)/2: correct numerator πr² − 2r² but divides by 2r² — comparing the coloured area to the circle or to the inner square instead of to the whole tile. 
Trap C (2π − 1)/8: mistakes the inner square's DIAGONAL for its SIDE (or sets the diagonal equal to the radius r, not the diameter 2r), giving inner-square area r²/2 and fraction (πr² − r²/2)/4r². 
Trap D (π − 1)/4: takes the inner square's area as r² (using side = r, forgetting the √2 from the diagonal relationship). 
Trap E (4 − π)/4: computes the WRONG region — the four corner pieces of the tile that lie outside the circle, (4r² − πr²)/4r², rather than the circle-minus-inner-square ring.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Circular motion on a banked curve with friction
questions.skill: Applying Newton's second law to uniform circular motion on an inclined (banked) surface, combining the banking geometry with a friction limit to find a threshold speed
questions.stem:
A highway curve of radius r = 30 m is banked at an angle θ with tan θ = 0.75 (so sin θ = 0.6, cos θ = 0.8). At the design speed of 15 m/s a car needs no friction at all. The tyre–road coefficient of static friction is μ = 1/3, and g = 10 m/s².

Because the road is banked, the component of gravity along the slope tends to pull a slow car DOWN the bank. There is therefore a MINIMUM cornering speed below which the car slides down the bank even when friction is fully engaged (acting up the slope, as shown in the free-body diagram). This minimum speed is closest to:
questions.explanation:
At the minimum speed the car is on the verge of sliding DOWN the bank, so limiting friction f = μN acts UP the slope. Resolving Newton's second law (horizontal net force = mv²/r inward, vertical net force = 0):
Horizontal: N sinθ − f cosθ = mv²/r
Vertical:   N cosθ + f sinθ = mg
Setting f = μN and dividing gives v²_min = rg(tanθ − μ)/(1 + μ tanθ) = 300 × (0.75 − 0.333)/(1 + 0.333×0.75) = 300 × (0.4167/1.25) = 300 × 0.3333 = 100, so v_min = 10 m/s → A.

Distractor traps:
B) 11 m/s: drops the (1 + μ tanθ) denominator, using v = √[rg(tanθ − μ)] = √125 ≈ 11 — forgetting that friction also changes the normal force.
C) 13 m/s: gets the sign of the denominator wrong, using v = √[rg(tanθ − μ)/(1 − μ tanθ)] = √166.7 ≈ 13 — the "1 − μ tanθ" form belongs to the MAXIMUM-speed case, not the minimum.
D) 15 m/s: ignores friction entirely and reports the frictionless design speed, assuming that is the slowest safe speed.
E) 21 m/s: adds μ instead of subtracting (confuses the up-slope minimum case with the down-slope maximum case), computing v = √[rg(tanθ + μ)/(1 − μ tanθ)] ≈ 21 — this is actually the MAXIMUM speed before sliding outward.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Power, efficiency and Newton's second law
questions.skill: Combine electrical-to-mechanical efficiency with instantaneous power P = Fv and F = ma
questions.stem: An electric winch motor draws a constant 2.0 kW from the mains and converts electrical energy to mechanical energy with 75% efficiency. Using a light cable it hoists a 50 kg crate vertically. Starting from rest the crate speeds up and eventually approaches a maximum steady speed. Taking g = 10 m/s² and neglecting cable mass and friction, what is the crate's acceleration at the instant its upward speed is 2.0 m/s (while it is still speeding up)?

options.E: 0 m/s² (it is being raised at constant speed)

questions.explanation: The motor delivers useful mechanical power P = 0.75 × 2000 W = 1500 W. At any instant the power output equals cable tension times speed, P = T·v, so at v = 2.0 m/s the tension is T = 1500 / 2.0 = 750 N. Applying Newton's second law to the crate: T − mg = ma → 750 − (50)(10) = 50a → 250 = 50a → a = 5.0 m/s² (A). Note the crate is still accelerating: its maximum steady speed would be where a = 0, i.e. v_max = P/(mg) = 1500/500 = 3.0 m/s, and 2.0 m/s is below that. Distractor traps: B (10 m/s²) forgets efficiency and uses the full 2000 W electrical power, giving T = 1000 N and (1000−500)/50. C (15 m/s²) uses the correct tension but ignores the crate's weight, taking a = T/m = 750/50. D (20 m/s²) combines both errors (ignores efficiency and gravity): 1000/50. E (0 m/s²) misreads the problem as steady-speed lifting; the phrase 'maximum steady speed' describes a limit the crate is still approaching, not its present state.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Interpreting a multi-segment velocity-time graph as signed area to find net displacement, distinguishing it from total distance when the motion reverses direction
questions.stem: An automated warehouse shuttle moves along a straight rail. Its velocity-time graph over one full cycle is shown (positive = forward, negative = reverse). During 0-2 s it accelerates uniformly, during 2-5 s it cruises at constant velocity, during 5-6 s it decelerates uniformly to rest, and during 6-8 s it accelerates uniformly in reverse. What is the shuttle's net displacement (final position relative to its start) over the interval 0-8 s?
questions.explanation: Net displacement is the SIGNED area between the velocity line and the t-axis. Segment 0-2 s (triangle up to +12 m/s): ½(2)(12) = +12 m. Segment 2-5 s (rectangle at +12 m/s): (3)(12) = +36 m. Segment 5-6 s (triangle down to 0): ½(1)(12) = +6 m. Segment 6-8 s (triangle down to -12 m/s, motion reversed): ½(2)(-12) = -12 m. Net = 12 + 36 + 6 - 12 = 42 m (A). Distractor B (66 m) adds the reverse area as positive, giving total distance travelled rather than net displacement — the classic distance-vs-displacement error. Distractor C (54 m) ignores the reverse segment entirely (12 + 36 + 6), stopping the count at first rest. Distractor D (30 m) reads the reverse triangle as a full rectangle of -12 m/s over 2 s (-24 m instead of -12 m), a triangle-as-rectangle area error: 12 + 36 + 6 - 24 = 30 m. Distractor E (36 m) drops the deceleration triangle's +6 m and the reverse -12 m by assuming a slowing/reversing shuttle contributes no net displacement, leaving only 12 + 36 - 12 = 36 m from a mishandled sign on the reverse leg.

questions.subject: reading
questions.skill: Drawing a supported conclusion by synthesizing multiple statements and rejecting overreach/outside-knowledge distractors
questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

In the 1850s, before germ theory was accepted, the physician John Snow argued that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than foul air. Most of his colleagues dismissed the idea, since the prevailing 'miasma' theory blamed disease on bad smells. Snow mapped cholera deaths in a London neighbourhood and noticed that they clustered around a single public water pump. He persuaded officials to remove the pump's handle, and local cases soon fell sharply. Yet the medical establishment remained unconvinced for years afterward. Only later did Snow's careful mapping become a model for the new science of epidemiology.

Which conclusion is BEST supported by the passage as a whole?

A) A practical intervention that appears to work can still fail to persuade experts when no accepted theory explains why it works.
B) The removal of the pump's handle demonstrated conclusively that contaminated water was the cause of cholera.
C) The medical establishment abandoned the miasma theory once local cholera cases declined.
D) The fall in cases after the handle was removed was probably due to the outbreak fading on its own rather than to Snow's action.
E) Snow was accepted by his colleagues only after the science of epidemiology had been formally established.

options.A: A practical intervention that appears to work can still fail to persuade experts when no accepted theory explains why it works.
options.B: The removal of the pump's handle demonstrated conclusively that contaminated water was the cause of cholera.
options.C: The medical establishment abandoned the miasma theory once local cholera cases declined.
options.D: The fall in cases after the handle was removed was probably due to the outbreak fading on its own rather than to Snow's action.
options.E: Snow was accepted by his colleagues only after the science of epidemiology had been formally established.

questions.explanation: The correct answer, A, requires combining three parts of the text: cases "fell sharply" after the intervention (it appeared to work), the events occurred "before germ theory was accepted" (no accepted mechanism), and the establishment "remained unconvinced for years." Together these support the inference that practical success alone did not persuade experts absent an accepted explanatory theory. B is the correlation-as-proof trap: the passage reports that cases fell, but the establishment's continued doubt shows the episode was not treated as conclusive proof; "demonstrated conclusively" overstates what the text supports. C contradicts the passage, which says the establishment "remained unconvinced for years afterward," so it did not abandon miasma theory when cases declined. D imports outside skepticism/real-world speculation that the passage never states; the text attributes the decline to the handle removal and gives no basis for the "outbreak fading on its own" claim. E reverses the passage's causal/temporal order: epidemiology grew out of Snow's work "only later," and the passage never says his colleagues ever accepted him because of it.

questions.subject: representation
questions.subtopic: Polyhedra: edges, faces, vertices of composite solids
questions.skill: Visualising a composite 3-D solid and counting its edges by reasoning about which edges are shared/hidden when two solids are joined
questions.stem: A designer builds a monument by fixing a square-based pyramid squarely on top of a cube, so that the pyramid's square base exactly covers (and coincides with) the top face of the cube. Once joined, that shared square is buried inside the solid. Counting every edge of the finished monument — visible and hidden, but counting each shared edge only once — how many edges does the solid have in total?
questions.explanation: The cube contributes its 12 edges. The pyramid has 8 edges: 4 around its square base and 4 slanted edges to the apex. But the pyramid's 4 base edges lie exactly on top of the cube's top-face edges — they are the SAME 4 edges, not new ones. So the pyramid adds only its 4 slant edges. Total = 12 + 4 = 16 (correct, D). Check with Euler's formula: vertices V = 8 (cube) + 1 (apex) = 9; faces F = 5 cube faces still exposed (top face is now buried) + 4 triangular pyramid faces = 9; then V − E + F = 9 − 16 + 9 = 2. ✓ Distractor traps: A) 8 counts only the pyramid's own edges, treating it as the whole answer instead of the joined solid. B) 9 reports the number of faces (or vertices) — an Euler-quantity mix-up, answering the wrong count. C) 12 counts only the cube and forgets the pyramid's 4 slant edges add new edges. E) 20 sums 12 + 8 blindly, double-counting the 4 base edges that coincide with the cube's top square.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.subtopic: Boolean expressions: short-circuit evaluation and operator precedence
questions.skill: Determining which side-effecting operands actually run by combining short-circuit rules with AND/OR precedence
questions.stem:
A language uses short-circuit (lazy) evaluation: OR stops as soon as an operand is TRUE, AND stops as soon as an operand is FALSE, and any skipped operand is not evaluated at all. As in most languages, AND binds tighter than OR (AND has higher precedence). An access guard calls three checks, each of which logs its own letter the moment it actually runs:

  isAdmin()  returns TRUE   and logs "A"
  hasToken() returns FALSE  and logs "T"
  auditOk()  returns TRUE   and logs "U"

The guard evaluates this single expression, left to right, honouring precedence:

  isAdmin() OR hasToken() AND auditOk()

Which checks are actually executed (i.e. which letters get logged)?
questions.explanation:
Because AND binds tighter than OR, the expression groups as isAdmin() OR (hasToken() AND auditOk()). Evaluation still proceeds left to right, so isAdmin() runs first and returns TRUE. OR short-circuits on a TRUE left operand, so the entire right-hand group is skipped and neither hasToken() nor auditOk() ever runs. Only "A" is logged → A is correct.

Trap in B: conflating precedence with evaluation ORDER — assuming the higher-precedence AND group is computed first in time. Precedence only decides grouping, not which operand is touched first; the left operand of OR is always reached first.
Trap in C: treating AND and OR as equal precedence and reading strictly left to right as (isAdmin() OR hasToken()) AND auditOk(). Then OR short-circuits at isAdmin()=TRUE, but the outer AND would force auditOk() to run — a plausible but wrong parse.
Trap in D: believing OR must inspect its next operand to "confirm" a result, so hasToken() is evaluated even though isAdmin() already made OR true. Short-circuit OR does exactly the opposite.
Trap in E: ignoring short-circuiting entirely and assuming every listed call executes.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: Tracing loop invariants and reasoning about partial progress of an algorithm
questions.stem:
A student implements one pass of an ascending bubble sort on a 1-indexed array A of n distinct integers:

  FOR i FROM 1 TO n-1 DO
      IF A[i] > A[i+1] THEN
          swap A[i] and A[i+1]
      END IF
  END FOR

After this SINGLE pass completes, the student claims two things are ALWAYS guaranteed, regardless of the starting order:
  (I)  The largest element of A now sits in position A[n].
  (II) The smallest element of A now sits in position A[1].

Which statement correctly characterises these two claims?

options.A: Claim (I) is always true, but Claim (II) is not always true.
options.B: Claim (II) is always true, but Claim (I) is not always true.
options.E: Both claims are true only when the array is already sorted in descending order before the pass.

questions.explanation: One left-to-right pass of bubble sort "carries" the running maximum rightward: whenever the compared pair is out of order the larger value moves right, so by the end the global maximum has been pushed all the way to A[n]. Hence Claim (I) is always true. Claim (II) is NOT guaranteed: the smallest element only moves left by at most one position per pass (it can only be shifted when it is the RIGHT element of a compared pair, and once the larger neighbour swaps past it the loop index has already advanced). Example: A=[7,3,9,4,8] with smallest value 3 starting at position 2 ends the pass as [3,7,4,8,9] here 3 does reach position 1 by luck, but A=[9,2,8,7,6] gives [2,8,7,6,9] where the minimum 2 reached position 1, whereas A=[3,9,4,8,2] yields [3,4,8,2,9] the minimum 2 lands in position 4, NOT position 1 — disproving Claim (II). So (I) always holds and (II) does not: answer A. Distractor B swaps the roles (a common symmetry misconception — students assume min and max are handled equally by one pass). Distractor C assumes both extremes are placed, confusing one pass with a full sort. Distractor D wrongly rejects the solid max-bubbling guarantee, typical of a student who found a counterexample for (II) and over-generalised. Distractor E invents a spurious precondition, misremembering that descending input is bubble sort's worst case rather than reasoning about the pass's actual invariant.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.topic: Computer number representation and digital logic
questions.subtopic: Two's-complement arithmetic: carry flag vs. signed-overflow flag
questions.skill: Distinguishing unsigned carry-out from signed overflow by tracing the carry chain
questions.stem:
A 4-bit ripple-carry adder computes S = A + B and exposes two independent status flags:

• C = the carry-OUT of the most-significant bit (this is the UNSIGNED overflow flag).
• V = the SIGNED-overflow flag, defined as (carry INTO the MSB) XOR (carry OUT of the MSB).

A hardware engineer feeds the adder the bit patterns A = 1111 and B = 0001. She must report C, V, and whether the two's-complement (signed) interpretation of the addition actually overflowed. Which row is entirely correct?

A) C = 1, V = 1, and the signed addition overflowed.
B) C = 1, V = 0, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.
C) C = 0, V = 1, and the signed addition overflowed.
D) C = 0, V = 0, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.
E) C = 1, V = 1, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.

options.A: C = 1, V = 1, and the signed addition overflowed.
options.B: C = 1, V = 0, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.
options.C: C = 0, V = 1, and the signed addition overflowed.
options.D: C = 0, V = 0, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.
options.E: C = 1, V = 1, and the signed addition did NOT overflow.

questions.explanation:
Trace the carry chain of 1111 + 0001. Bit0: 1+1 = 0, carry 1. Bit1: 1+0+1 = 0, carry 1. Bit2: 1+0+1 = 0, carry 1. Bit3 (MSB): 1+0+1 = 0, carry 1. So the carry INTO the MSB = 1 and the carry OUT of the MSB = 1, giving the 5-bit result 10000 (4-bit result 0000). Therefore C = 1 (there is a carry-out) and V = 1 XOR 1 = 0 (no signed overflow). Checking the meaning: signed, A = 1111 = -1 and B = 0001 = +1, so the true sum is 0, which fits in [-8, +7] — no overflow, consistent with V = 0. The key insight is that carry-out (C) and signed overflow (V) are INDEPENDENT: here a carry occurred yet no signed overflow did. Answer B.

Trap A (C=1, V=1, overflow): the classic misconception that a carry-out of the MSB always signals signed overflow; the student sets V = C without computing the carry INTO the MSB.
Trap C (C=0, V=1, overflow): the student reasons "-1 + 1 = 0 needs no carry" and wrongly sets C = 0, while still asserting overflow — mixing an incorrect carry with an incorrect overflow claim.
Trap D (C=0, V=0): the student decides that because the signed answer is a clean 0 there can be no carry at all, ignoring that the binary carry chain still propagates all the way out (C = 1).
Trap E (C=1, V=1, no overflow): the student correctly senses "no overflow" but leaves V = 1, failing to see that V = 1 is BY DEFINITION the overflow flag — an internally contradictory row that catches those who pattern-match flags without understanding what V means.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining the Factor Theorem with Vieta's relationships between roots and coefficients
questions.stem: The polynomial P(x) = x³ − 4x² + a·x + b is divisible by (x − 1), and its two other roots are reciprocals of each other. What is the value of a?
questions.explanation:
Let the roots be 1, r, s. Divisibility by (x − 1) makes 1 a root; "reciprocals of each other" means r·s = 1. By Vieta for x³ − 4x² + a·x + b: the sum of roots equals 4, so 1 + r + s = 4 ⇒ r + s = 3. The coefficient a equals the sum of the pairwise products: a = 1·r + 1·s + r·s = (r + s) + r·s = 3 + 1 = 4. (Check: r, s solve x² − 3x + 1 = 0, giving (3 ± √5)/2, whose product is 1 — genuinely reciprocal.) So a = 4.
Distractor traps: (B) 3 — student stops at r + s and forgets to add the reciprocal-product term r·s, using only the two unknown roots' sum. (C) 2 — sign slip on that term, computing (r + s) − r·s = 3 − 1. (D) −4 — global sign error in Vieta, taking the linear coefficient as −(sum of pairwise products) instead of +. (E) −1 — solved for the wrong coefficient: this is b (from product of roots 1·r·s = −b ⇒ b = −1), reported in place of a.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Quadratic equations — Vieta's formulas and symmetric functions of the roots
questions.skill: Expressing symmetric combinations of roots via sum and product without solving
questions.stem:
Let α and β be the two real roots of x² − 6x + 4 = 0. Without solving the equation, evaluate

    α/β + β/α + (α − β)².

A) 27   B) 29   C) 35   D) 37   E) 48
questions.explanation:
By Vieta's formulas: α + β = 6 and αβ = 4. Both requested terms are symmetric in α and β, so they can be written using only these two quantities.

First term: α/β + β/α = (α² + β²)/(αβ). Since α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 36 − 8 = 28, this equals 28/4 = 7.

Second term: (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ = 36 − 16 = 20.

Total = 7 + 20 = 27 → answer A.

Distractor traps:
• B) 29 — uses α² + β² = (α + β)² = 36 (omits the −2αβ), giving 36/4 = 9, then 9 + 20.
• C) 35 — computes (α − β)² as (α + β)² − 2αβ = 28, confusing the "difference-squared" identity (−4αβ) with the "sum-of-squares" identity (−2αβ); then 7 + 28.
• D) 37 — commits BOTH errors above: 9 + 28.
• E) 48 — evaluates the numerator α² + β² = 28 for the first term but forgets to divide by αβ, treating α/β + β/α as 28; then 28 + 20.

A strong student recognizes that the two identities (α + β)² − 2αβ and (α + β)² − 4αβ differ and keeps the denominator; the distractors each isolate one of those precise slips.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Modeling with exponential functions and solving for time by equating expressions
questions.stem: Two radioactive samples decay exponentially. Sample A has a half-life of 3 days and starts at 80 g. Sample B has a half-life of 6 days and starts at 10 g. At t = 0 the mass of A is greater than the mass of B, but because A decays faster, at some later time their masses become equal, after which B is the heavier sample. At what time t (in days) are the two masses equal?\n\n(Hint: 80·2^(−t/3) = 10·2^(−t/6). Write both sides as powers of 2 and equate exponents.)
questions.explanation:
Set the masses equal: 80·2^(−t/3) = 10·2^(−t/6). Divide both sides by 10: 8·2^(−t/3) = 2^(−t/6). Write 8 = 2^3, so 2^(3 − t/3) = 2^(−t/6). Equate exponents: 3 − t/3 = −t/6. Multiply by 6: 18 − 2t = −t, so 18 = t. Therefore t = 18 days (correct: C). Check: at t=18, A has had 6 half-lives → 80/64 = 1.25 g; B has had 3 half-lives → 10/8 = 1.25 g. Equal, confirmed.

Distractor traps:
A) t = 6 — student ignores the initial-mass factor of 8 and just solves 2^(−t/3) = 2^(−t/6), or naively finds when A equals its own halved-relation; also equals one half-life count matching, a shallow guess.
B) t = 12 — sign error when clearing fractions: solving 3 − t/3 = t/6 (dropping the minus sign on the right) gives 3 = t/3 + t/6 = t/2, so t = 6... students who instead mis-multiply get 12, the classic 'balanced both half-lives to equal number of steps' error (12 = LCM-style guess, A at 4 half-lives vs B at 2).
C) correct.
D) t = 9 — averages the two half-lives' behavior or splits the 18 by treating the exponent equation as 3 = t/3 (ignoring B's decay entirely), giving t = 9.
E) t = 24 — over-counts by using 80/10 = 8 = 2^3 but then multiplying the day-difference by both half-lives (3+6 doubled), a scaling slip.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Horizontal projectile motion: impact velocity direction vs. displacement direction
questions.skill: Relating the impact-velocity angle to range and height (tan θ = 2h/R) by resolving instantaneous velocity components
questions.stem: A small ball is launched horizontally from the top of a vertical cliff and lands on level ground a horizontal distance R = 40 m from the base of the cliff (see figure). At the instant it strikes the ground, the ball's velocity makes an angle θ below the horizontal with tan θ = 2. Air resistance is negligible and g = 10 m/s². What is the height of the cliff?
questions.explanation: For a horizontally launched projectile the horizontal velocity stays vx = v0 while the vertical velocity grows as vy = gt. The impact angle satisfies tan θ = vy/vx = gt/v0. Now express the geometry: R = v0·t and h = ½gt², so 2h/R = gt²/R = gt/v0. Therefore tan θ = 2h/R — the velocity at impact is exactly TWICE as steep as the straight line joining the launch point to the landing point. Solving: h = R·tan θ / 2 = 40 × 2 / 2 = 40 m (B). Distractor traps: (C) 80 m comes from setting tan θ = h/R, i.e. mistaking the impact-velocity direction for the direction of the net displacement (launch-to-landing line) — the single most common conceptual error, and the one that separates strong from average students, since velocity and displacement point in different directions here. (A) 20 m ignores the given angle and assumes a symmetric 45° impact (vx = vy → h = R/2). (D) 10 m inverts the tangent, writing tan θ = R/(2h) (opposite/adjacent swapped), giving h = R/(2 tan θ) = 10 m. (E) 160 m misplaces the factor of 2 onto the wrong side, using h = 2R·tan θ. Only B correctly resolves the instantaneous velocity components and links them to the trajectory geometry.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Identifying a growth rule and generalizing it to a non-adjacent term
questions.stem: A design student builds a series of "diamond" dot figures, shown below. The number of dots is 1 in Figure 1, 5 in Figure 2, 13 in Figure 3 and 25 in Figure 4. Each figure adds a new outer ring, so the number of dots grows in a regular way. If the pattern continues unchanged, how many dots does Figure 7 contain?
questions.explanation: The gaps between consecutive figures are 5-1=4, 13-5=8, 25-13=12, so the amount added grows by a constant 4 each step (the second difference is constant). Continuing the added rings: Figure 5 = 25+16 = 41, Figure 6 = 41+20 = 61, Figure 7 = 61+24 = 85. So D is correct. Distractor traps: A) 41 comes from extending only one step and answering the very next figure (Figure 5) instead of Figure 7. B) 61 comes from freezing the gap at its last visible value 12 and treating the series as an ordinary arithmetic sequence (25+12+12+12); note this also equals Figure 6, so it doubles as an off-by-one stop. C) 73 comes from noticing the gaps grow but using the wrong second difference, increasing the gap by 2 instead of 4 (gaps 14, 16, 18: 25+14+16+18). E) 113 comes from the correct method applied one figure too far, reaching Figure 8 instead of Figure 7.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Chaining modus ponens, exclusion ("no X is Y"), and disjunctive syllogism to derive a forced conclusion
questions.stem:
At a university, every student's course enrollment obeys three fixed rules:

(1) Any student enrolled in Advanced Statistics is also enrolled in Calculus.
(2) No student can be enrolled in both Calculus and Basic Algebra.
(3) Every student is enrolled in Basic Algebra, in Data Science, or in both.

Marco is enrolled in Advanced Statistics. Based only on these rules, which statement MUST be true?

options.A: Marco is enrolled in Basic Algebra.
options.B: Marco is not enrolled in Calculus.
options.C: Marco is enrolled in Data Science.
options.D: Marco is enrolled in both Basic Algebra and Data Science.
options.E: Nothing definite can be concluded about whether Marco takes Data Science.

questions.explanation:
Chain the rules: Marco is in Advanced Statistics, so by rule (1) he is in Calculus. By rule (2), being in Calculus means he is NOT in Basic Algebra. Rule (3) says every student is in Basic Algebra or Data Science (or both); since Marco is not in Basic Algebra, disjunctive syllogism forces him into Data Science. Hence C must be true.

Trap analysis of the distractors:
- A (Basic Algebra): the direct opposite of the correct deduction — chosen by students who ignore rule (2) and forget that Calculus excludes Basic Algebra.
- B (not Calculus): reverses rule (1); a student who reads the conditional backwards or thinks "Advanced Statistics" and "Calculus" are unrelated denies the very step that rule (1) guarantees.
- D (both Basic Algebra and Data Science): reads rule (3)'s "or" as demanding Basic Algebra too, while overlooking that rule (2) has already ruled Basic Algebra out — a common inclusive-or overreach.
- E (nothing can be concluded): the "give up early" trap — the student performs only the first step (Calculus) but fails to combine rules (2) and (3) via disjunctive syllogism, wrongly deciding the Data Science status is undetermined.

questions.subject: reading
questions.skill: Identifying the unstated assumption on which a stated claim depends
questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The committee's report was praised for its temperate tone. Where earlier drafts had denounced the ministry in furious language, the final version set out the same criticisms in measured, almost cool prose, careful never to overstate a charge it could not fully support. Some campaigners complained that this restraint blunted the report's force. The authors replied that an accusation delivered calmly is harder to dismiss than one delivered in a rage.

The authors' reply (the final sentence) depends on which of the following assumptions?

A) Furious language, by itself, is enough to prove that an accusation is unfounded.
B) A calmly worded charge denies its audience the easy excuse of attributing the accusation to the accuser's temper rather than to the evidence.
C) Measured prose necessarily conveys a greater number of criticisms than angry prose does.
D) A report's persuasiveness depends solely on the seriousness of its charges and not at all on their wording.
E) The campaigners are chiefly interested in impressing the ministry rather than the wider public.

options.A: Furious language, by itself, is enough to prove that an accusation is unfounded.
options.B: A calmly worded charge denies its audience the easy excuse of attributing the accusation to the accuser's temper rather than to the evidence.
options.C: Measured prose necessarily conveys a greater number of criticisms than angry prose does.
options.D: A report's persuasiveness depends solely on the seriousness of its charges and not at all on their wording.
options.E: The campaigners are chiefly interested in impressing the ministry rather than the wider public.

questions.explanation:
The authors claim a calm accusation is "harder to dismiss" than an enraged one. For that to hold, calm delivery must remove some ground on which an audience would otherwise reject the charge. That ground is emotional colouring: a furious accusation invites the audience to explain the charge away as the venting of an angry accuser rather than a response to evidence. Calm prose closes off that escape route — exactly the assumption in B.

Trap A: reverses a rhetorical claim into a logical one. The authors never say fury makes a charge false; they say fury makes a true charge easier to brush aside. Readers who collapse "easier to dismiss" into "proven wrong" pick A.
Trap C: confuses manner with quantity. The passage states the final version set out "the same criticisms," so tone changed the delivery, not the number of charges. C mistakes a difference in style for a difference in content.
Trap D: directly contradicts the authors, who insist wording (calm vs. rage) changes how hard a charge is to dismiss. It is bait for readers who over-correct toward a "content is all that matters" position — which is actually closer to the campaigners' complaint than to the authors' reply.
Trap E: imports a speaker/audience distinction found nowhere in the text; it is an unsupported elaboration that the passage gives no basis for.

questions.subject: reading
questions.subtopic: Inference and application from an expository passage
questions.skill: Combining a described mechanism with a stated failure mode to predict behavior in a novel scenario
questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Coral reefs and mangrove forests both shield coastlines from the force of the sea, yet they do so in opposite ways. A reef is a rigid wall: it meets an incoming wave head-on and breaks it apart offshore, absorbing the blow through sheer hardness. A mangrove does the reverse. Its flexible roots and stems bend as the water rushes through, draining the wave of its energy by friction rather than by resistance. The reef survives by being unyielding; the mangrove survives by giving way.

Coastal engineers who imitate nature must therefore choose a philosophy, not merely a material. A seawall built on the reef's principle holds firm until the day a wave arrives whose force exceeds the wall's strength — and on that day it does not bend but breaks, all at once. A structure built on the mangrove's principle never opposes the full force of any wave; it lets the water through while stealing its energy stroke by stroke.

Based on the passage, which of the following can be most reliably inferred about how a reef-type defense and a mangrove-type defense would each behave when struck by a single storm surge far more powerful than any the coast has faced before?

options.A: The reef-type defense is at greater risk of sudden, total failure, because a structure that resists force head-on has a fixed limit beyond which it breaks rather than yields, whereas the mangrove-type defense dissipates even an extreme wave gradually and so is more likely to remain functional.
options.B: Both defenses would fare about equally well, since the passage stresses that reefs and mangroves pursue the same goal of protecting the coast.
options.C: The mangrove-type defense would fail first, because its flexible, yielding structure is inherently weaker than a rigid wall and cannot withstand an unusually strong wave.
options.D: The reef-type defense would clearly outperform the mangrove-type defense, because meeting a wave with sheer hardness is the more effective strategy against greater force.
options.E: Nothing can be inferred about their behavior under an extreme surge, because the passage describes only how each defense works and never discusses their limits.

questions.explanation:
The passage links each defense to a mechanism and, in the second paragraph, to a failure mode: the reef principle "holds firm until the day a wave arrives whose force exceeds the wall's strength — and on that day it does not bend but breaks, all at once," while the mangrove principle "never opposes the full force of any wave" and steals energy "stroke by stroke." Combining the mechanism (resistance vs. dissipation) with the stated failure behavior yields A: rigid resistance implies a threshold past which failure is sudden and total, whereas gradual dissipation degrades more gracefully under extreme load.

Distractor traps:
B over-applies the first paragraph's "same goal" statement, treating shared purpose as shared performance and ignoring the second paragraph's explicit difference in how each fails.
C equates "flexible/yielding" with "weak," the exact misreading the passage warns against — the mangrove survives BY giving way, and the text says it never confronts a wave's full force, so extra force does not simply overwhelm it.
D is the surface "hardness = superiority" trap (the same error as the original easy item's wrong options); the passage frames hardness as a strategy with a breaking point, not an unqualified advantage.
E wrongly denies that any inference is possible; the second paragraph directly describes each design's limit, so the behavior under extreme force is supported, not absent.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: AM–GM optimization with a domain constraint
questions.skill: Applying the AM–GM inequality while checking whether its equality condition lies in the allowed domain, then using monotonicity to locate a constrained minimum
questions.stem: A workshop runs a machine at speed x (in suitable units, x > 0). The operating cost per finished part, in liras, is modelled by C(x) = x + 9/x. For safety reasons the machine may not be run at a speed below 4, so the speed must satisfy x ≥ 4. What is the smallest possible cost per part?

options.E: There is no minimum cost, since x ≥ 4 allows arbitrarily large speeds.

questions.explanation:
By AM–GM, x + 9/x ≥ 2·√(x·9/x) = 6, with equality only when x = 9/x, i.e. x = 3. But x = 3 violates the constraint x ≥ 4, so the value 6 is never attained. On the allowed interval you must check where the function is smallest. Compare any x ≥ 4 with x = 4: C(x) − C(4) = (x − 4) + 9(4 − x)/(4x) = (x − 4)(4x − 9)/(4x). For x ≥ 4 both factors (x − 4) and (4x − 9) are ≥ 0, so C(x) ≥ C(4). Thus C is increasing on [4, ∞) and the minimum is at the endpoint x = 4: C(4) = 4 + 9/4 = 25/4 = 6.25 liras (C).
Distractor traps: (A) 4 substitutes x = 4 correctly but reports only the first term, dropping the 9/x contribution. (B) 6 blindly uses the unconstrained AM–GM minimum, ignoring that its equality point x = 3 lies outside the domain — the central misconception being tested. (D) 10 misremembers the AM–GM equality condition as x = 9 (the constant in the numerator) instead of x = √9 = 3, giving 9 + 9/9 = 10. (E) confuses an unbounded interval having no maximum with having no minimum; the function is increasing, so the minimum is simply attained at the left endpoint.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Distance formula and locus of equidistant points
questions.skill: Combining the equidistance condition with a positional constraint (point restricted to a given line) and solving the resulting equation
questions.stem: A straight utility road runs exactly along the vertical line x = 2 (all coordinates are in km). A relay station must be built somewhere on this road so that it is equidistant from transmitter A(1, 6) and transmitter B(7, 2). What are the coordinates of the relay station?
questions.explanation:
The station lies on the road, so its x-coordinate is fixed at 2; only y is unknown. Set the squared distances to A and B equal:
(2−1)² + (y−6)² = (2−7)² + (y−2)²  →  1 + (y−6)² = 25 + (y−2)².
Expanding: 1 + y² − 12y + 36 = 25 + y² − 4y + 4  →  37 − 12y = 29 − 4y  →  8 = 8y  →  y = 1. Station = (2, 1). (Check: distance to each transmitter is √26 km.)

Distractor traps:
