B) (2, 4): equates only the vertical parts (y−6)² = (y−2)², dropping the different horizontal offsets (the 1 and 25) — i.e. ignoring that A and B are at different distances from the road.
C) (4, 4): simply reports the midpoint of A and B, forgetting the station is constrained to lie on the road x = 2.
D) (2, 7): reverses the subtraction of the horizontal-offset squares (uses 1 − 25 instead of 25 − 1), a sign error that gives 37 − 12y = 29 − 4y with the constant flipped, yielding y = 7.
E) (2, 2): uses horizontal-plus-vertical (Manhattan) distance instead of the straight-line Pythagorean distance: |2−1|+|y−6| = |2−7|+|y−2| gives y = 2.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Simple harmonic motion of a vertical spring
questions.skill: Combining Hooke's law equilibrium with the SHM period formula
questions.stem: A block is hung from a light vertical spring and, at rest, stretches it by x = 0.080 m from its natural length (see figure). The block is then pulled down a little and released, so it oscillates vertically in simple harmonic motion about the equilibrium position. The mass of the block is NOT given. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the period of the oscillation? (Neglect air resistance and the spring's mass.)

options.E: It cannot be determined unless the mass of the block is known

questions.explanation:
Key insight: the period is independent of the mass. At equilibrium Hooke's law gives mg = kx, so m/k = x/g. The SHM period is T = 2π√(m/k) = 2π√(x/g) = 2π√(0.080/10) = 2π√(0.008) = 2π(0.0894) ≈ 0.56 s. The static stretch alone fixes the period — this is why C is correct.
Distractor traps:
E encodes the most common misconception: students believe m and k are both needed, missing that their ratio is pinned by the static stretch, so they declare it indeterminate.
A (0.050 s) comes from dropping the square root: computing 2π(x/g) = 2π(0.008) instead of 2π√(x/g).
B (0.089 s) comes from forgetting the 2π factor: just evaluating √(x/g) = 0.0894.
D (70 s) comes from inverting the ratio inside the root, using T = 2π√(g/x) = 2π√(10/0.080) = 2π√125 ≈ 70 s — confusing which quantity goes on top.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Triangles: isosceles triangles and the exterior-angle theorem
questions.skill: Multi-step angle chasing (repeated isosceles + exterior-angle relations)
questions.stem: In triangle ABC the sides AB and AC are equal. A point D is taken on side AC so that the three segments AD, BD and BC are all equal to one another (shown by the single tick marks in the figure; the double tick marks show AB = AC). What is the measure of the apex angle BAC?
questions.explanation: Let angle BAC = x. In triangle ABD, AD = BD, so it is isosceles with base angles at A and B equal: angle ABD = angle DAB = x. The angle BDC is the exterior angle of triangle ABD at D, so angle BDC = x + x = 2x. In triangle BDC, BD = BC, so angle BCD = angle BDC = 2x; since D lies on AC this means angle ACB = 2x. Finally AB = AC gives angle ABC = angle ACB = 2x. The angle sum of triangle ABC is x + 2x + 2x = 5x = 180°, so x = 36°. Distractor traps: (B) 72° is the base angle 2x — the student solves correctly but reports angle ACB/ABC instead of the requested apex. (C) 108° = 180° − 72°, taking the supplement of the base angle (or confusing this with the obtuse-apex golden triangle). (D) 60° comes from wrongly assuming the many equal segments force an equilateral triangle (equivalently, from dropping the exterior-angle doubling so every angle looks equal). (E) 45° comes from conflating angle ABC with its part angle ABD = x — forgetting the extra sub-angle DBC — which gives the wrong sum x + x + 2x = 4x = 180°.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Circular sectors and solids of revolution (cones)
questions.skill: Multi-step mensuration: linking a sector's radius/arc to a cone's slant height and base circumference, then applying Pythagoras and the cone-volume formula
questions.stem: A flat sheet-metal circular sector has radius 15 cm and arc length 18π cm (see figure, left). A worker joins the two straight edges of the sector to form the lateral surface of a cone (see figure, right), with no overlap. What is the volume of the resulting cone?
questions.explanation:
When the sector is rolled into a cone, its radius becomes the slant height (l = 15) and its arc becomes the base circumference. So 2πr = 18π → r = 9. The height comes from Pythagoras: h = √(l² − r²) = √(225 − 81) = √144 = 12. Volume = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π·81·12 = 324π cm³ → B.
Distractor traps: A (135π) stops at the flat sector's area, ½·l·arc = ½·15·18π, never forming the cone. C (405π) uses the slant height 15 as the cone's vertical height, skipping Pythagoras: (1/3)π·81·15. D (486π) carries the ½ from the sector-area formula into the volume instead of the correct ⅓: (1/2)π·81·12. E (972π) uses the cylinder formula πr²h, forgetting the ⅓ factor for a cone.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: Reasoning about the structure (not just the return value) of a recursive computation
questions.explanation: The base-case calls are exactly the leaves of the recursion tree. Let L(n) be the number of leaf (base-case) calls made by f(n). A base case is a leaf, so L(0)=1 and L(1)=1; otherwise the two subcalls give L(n)=L(n-1)+L(n-2). This yields L(2)=2, L(3)=3, L(4)=5, L(5)=8. So f(5) reaches the base case 8 times — answer D. Note L(n) equals a Fibonacci number, and the total returned value f(5)=fib(5)=5. Trap A (5): reporting the value f(5) returns instead of the number of base-case calls — confusing the result with the structure. Trap B (6): assuming the count grows linearly, roughly n+1. Trap C (7): counting the internal (non-base) calls — the nodes that perform an addition. There are 8 leaves and 7 internal nodes, so this is an off-by-one that miscategorizes the internal calls as the answer. Trap E (15): counting every call in the tree (all nodes = leaves + internal = 8 + 7 = 15), not only the ones that hit the base case.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.subtopic: Character encoding and modular-arithmetic shift ciphers
questions.skill: Reasoning about composition of modular shifts and self-inverse (involution) conditions
questions.stem:
A developer obfuscates uppercase-only tags (letters 'A'..'Z', codes 65..90) with the function

    encode(c) = ( (code(c) - 65 + k) mod 26 ) + 65

for some fixed integer shift k with 0 <= k < 26. To avoid shipping a separate decoder, the developer wants ONE function that acts as both encoder and decoder: passing any text through encode twice must reproduce the original for every uppercase letter. Among all shifts that satisfy this, they want the one that actually alters the letters (i.e. not the identity mapping). Which value of k meets both requirements?
questions.explanation: Applying encode twice composes the two shifts: a letter at offset x maps to x + k then to x + 2k, all taken mod 26. For the double application to return the original letter for EVERY input, we need 2k ≡ 0 (mod 26), i.e. k ≡ 0 (mod 13). Within 0 <= k < 26 the solutions are k = 0 and k = 13. The requirement that the letters actually change rules out k = 0, leaving k = 13 (this is exactly why ROT13 is its own inverse). Correct: A) 13. Trap B) 26 — confuses k with 2k: the student sees that two shifts of 13 total 26 ('a full circle') and reports that sum as the answer, and 26 is also out of the allowed range. Trap C) 25 — ignores the self-inverse constraint entirely and just picks the largest shift under 26 that 'changes the letters.' Trap D) 0 — correctly derives k ∈ {0, 13} but forgets the clause requiring the letters to change, choosing the trivial identity shift. Trap E) 12 — sets up 2k ≡ 0 (mod 26) but solves it as 2k = 24 (the largest even value below 26), giving k = 12, an off-by-one arithmetic slip that fails: two shifts of 12 total 24, not a multiple of 26.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.subtopic: Combinational logic, De Morgan's laws, circuit equivalence
questions.skill: Evaluate two Boolean functions of the same inputs and count the combinations where they disagree, applying De Morgan correctly
questions.stem: A machine has a safety-enable output E. The intended design is: E = 1 only when the guard is closed (G = 1) AND no emergency-stop button is pressed, where there are two stop buttons S1 and S2. So the intended circuit computes E = G AND NOT(S1 OR S2). A technician instead wires the circuit shown as "Circuit 2 (as built)", which computes E' = G AND (NOT S1 OR NOT S2). Each of G, S1, S2 is a single bit, giving 8 possible input combinations. For how many of these 8 combinations do the intended output E and the as-built output E' DIFFER?
questions.explanation: Intended: E = G AND NOT(S1 OR S2) = G AND NOT S1 AND NOT S2, which is 1 only for (G,S1,S2) = (1,0,0) — exactly one combination. As-built: E' = G AND (NOT S1 OR NOT S2); since NOT S1 OR NOT S2 = NOT(S1 AND S2) is true unless S1=S2=1, E' = 1 for G=1 with (S1,S2) ∈ {00,01,10} — three combinations. All G=0 rows give E=E'=0 (agree). Among G=1 rows: 00 → both 1 (agree); 11 → both 0 (agree); 01 and 10 → E=0 but E'=1 (differ). So they differ in exactly 2 combinations → C. Trap A (0): the classic false De Morgan NOT(S1 OR S2) = NOT S1 OR NOT S2, which would make E ≡ E' and never differ — but the correct De Morgan gives AND, not OR. Trap B (1): counts where the intended E = 1 (the single safe state) instead of where the two outputs disagree. Trap D (3): counts the combinations where the faulty E' = 1, not where E and E' actually differ. Trap E (4): assumes the two circuits disagree on every G=1 row, over-counting by including the 00 and 11 rows where they in fact agree.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.subtopic: Binary fractional representation and terminating expansions
questions.skill: Reasoning about which decimal fractions have a finite (exact) binary representation
questions.stem: A microcontroller stores non-integer values in a fixed-point binary format: a whole part followed by a binary point and a FINITE number of fractional bits (for example, 101.011₂ = 5.375). A value can be stored EXACTLY only if it can be written as such a finite binary fraction. A technician needs to store the following four decimal values exactly: 0.1, 0.25, 0.375, and 0.6. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Only 0.25 and 0.375 can be stored exactly; 0.1 and 0.6 cannot.
options.B: All four values can be stored exactly, since each has a finite number of decimal digits.
options.C: Only 0.25 can be stored exactly; the other three require infinitely many fractional bits.
options.D: Only 0.1 and 0.6 cannot be stored exactly because they are the only values that are not already sums of distinct fractions.
options.E: None of the four can be stored exactly, because every decimal fraction repeats forever in binary.

questions.explanation:
A decimal fraction has a FINITE (terminating) binary representation if and only if, when written in lowest terms, its denominator is a power of 2. Check each: 0.25 = 1/4 → denominator 4 = 2² → finite (0.01₂). 0.375 = 3/8 → denominator 8 = 2³ → finite (0.011₂). 0.1 = 1/10 = 1/(2·5) → the factor 5 in the denominator means it is NOT a power of 2 → infinite/repeating in binary. 0.6 = 3/5 → denominator 5 → NOT a power of 2 → infinite in binary. So exactly 0.25 and 0.375 store exactly, giving A.

Distractor traps:
B — the misconception that 'finite in decimal ⇒ finite in binary.' Termination is base-dependent; a finite decimal is not necessarily a finite binary fraction. This is the single most common error.
C — over-restrictive: the student remembers only the cleanest power-of-two case (1/4) and wrongly assumes 3/8 also fails, forgetting that any k/2ⁿ terminates regardless of the odd numerator.
D — invents a false rule (about being 'sums of distinct fractions') and, by coincidence of wording, still splits the set wrongly; it rewards pattern-matching the answer without the real criterion. It also mislabels WHY 0.1 and 0.6 fail.
E — the over-generalization of the 0.1 example ('binary can't represent decimals') into the false claim that NO decimal fraction terminates in binary, ignoring the exact powers of two.

questions.subject: representation
questions.subtopic: 3D solids from unit cubes / painted-cube surface counting
questions.skill: Isometric visualization combined with surface-area / exposed-face reasoning
questions.stem: The figure shows a solid built from 6 identical unit cubes, drawn in isometric projection. The solid is exactly one cube deep, so nothing is hidden behind. The whole solid is fully immersed in paint, so that EVERY exposed face is coated; after the paint dries, the cubes are separated. Counting over all six cubes together, how many unit-square faces are painted in total?
questions.explanation:
Because the solid is only one cube deep, the front face AND the back face of every cube are exposed: that is 2 x 6 = 12 painted faces before looking at any edges. The remaining painted faces are the lateral faces lying along the outline of the flat staircase. The staircase is a monotone step-shape sitting in a 3x3 bounding region, so its outline (perimeter) is the same length as the bounding box, 2 x (3 + 3) = 12 unit edges; each corresponds to one exposed lateral face. Total = 12 (front+back) + 12 (outline) = 24. Equivalently, since separated cubes keep paint only where the solid's exterior was, the answer just equals the solid's total surface area: front 6 + back 6 + outline 12 = 24.
Distractor traps: D) 12 counts only ONE of the two contributions — either the front+back pair alone (12) or the outline alone (12) — forgetting the other set. A) 18 correctly keeps front+back (12) but, for the sides, paints only the top and right faces that are visible in the drawing (6), missing the hidden left-side and bottom faces (another 6). C) 36 paints all 6 faces of all 6 separated cubes (6 x 6), ignoring that the 6 interior contact faces where cubes touch were never exposed to paint (this over-counts by 12). E) 21 reaches 24 but then assumes the solid rests on a table so its 3 base faces stay unpainted (24 - 3); the problem states full immersion, so the base is painted too.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining logarithm laws with the range/maximum of a quadratic to analyze existence of solutions under a parameter and domain constraint
questions.stem: The equation log(x) + log(10 − x) = k is given, where log denotes the base-10 logarithm and k is a real parameter. For k = 1 the equation has two distinct real solutions. What is the greatest value of k for which the equation has at least one real solution?
questions.explanation: Combining the logs (valid only on the common domain 0 < x < 10) turns the equation into x(10 − x) = 10^k. A real solution exists exactly when the constant 10^k lies within the range of the product P(x) = x(10 − x) on (0, 10). This is a downward parabola with vertex at x = 5, so its maximum value is P(5) = 5·5 = 25 (equivalently, by AM–GM the product of two numbers summing to 10 is at most 25). Hence a solution exists iff 10^k ≤ 25; the greatest k is where 10^k = 25, i.e. k = log 25 (≈ 1.398, giving the single solution x = 5). This demands genuine reasoning about the RANGE of the product plus the domain, not a rote extraneous-root reflex. Trap A (k = 2): maximizing the two factors independently — letting x → 10 AND 10 − x → 10 — gives the impossible product 10·10 = 100, so 10^k = 100 and k = 2; it ignores that the factors are coupled (their sum is fixed at 10). Trap C (k = log 5): the student correctly locates the vertex at x = 5 but stops there, using the x-coordinate 5 as the maximum of the product instead of evaluating P(5) = 25. Trap D (k = log 50): multiplying the vertex coordinate by the constant, 5·10 = 50, a mis-formed 'maximum.' Trap E (k = 1): assuming the given case k = 1 is already the boundary, reasoning loosely that a larger right-hand side must fail; but 10^1 = 10 < 25, so k = 1 is not maximal.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: GCD and LCM via prime factorization
questions.skill: Reasoning about exponent structure (min/max per prime) in GCD/LCM decompositions and counting via the multiplication principle
questions.stem: Two positive integers a and b satisfy GCD(a, b) = 2²·3 = 12 and LCM(a, b) = 2³·3²·5 = 360. For every prime, one of a, b carries the GCD exponent (the minimum) and the other carries the LCM exponent (the maximum). How many ordered pairs (a, b) satisfy both conditions?
questions.explanation: Write a = 2^x₂·3^x₃·5^x₅ and b = 2^y₂·3^y₃·5^y₅. For each prime, min(exponents) must equal the GCD exponent and max(exponents) must equal the LCM exponent. Compare the two: prime 2 has GCD exponent 2 and LCM exponent 3 (different), prime 3 has 1 and 2 (different), prime 5 has 0 and 1 (different). Because the min and max differ for ALL THREE primes, each prime's two exponents are a distinct low/high pair that must be split between a and b — and for each prime there are 2 ways to decide which of a, b gets the high exponent. The choices are independent across primes, so the count is 2·2·2 = 2³ = 8 ordered pairs (D). Trap A (1): assuming the two numbers are uniquely determined, forgetting that the assignment is free. Trap B (3): counting the 3 primes once each (adding the choices, 1+1+1) instead of multiplying the independent binary choices. Trap C (6): computing 3! = 6, mis-modeling the problem as permuting three primes rather than making three independent 2-way choices. Trap E (16): using 2⁴ by wrongly including a fourth "prime" or an extra degree of freedom — e.g. also treating a prime where min = max as splittable. Note: if any prime had equal GCD and LCM exponents it would be forced (1 way, not 2); here all three genuinely split, giving 2³.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Ideal gas law and gas transformations
questions.skill: Combining ≥2 gas-law relations (P ∝ nT at constant volume) with Kelvin discipline
questions.stem: A rigid, sealed container holds an ideal gas at 27 °C and a pressure of 1.0×10^5 Pa. The container is then heated to 327 °C. During the heating a faulty seal lets exactly half of the gas (half of the molecules) escape, while the volume of the container stays constant throughout. What is the final pressure of the gas remaining inside?
questions.explanation: At constant volume the ideal-gas law PV = nRT gives P ∝ nT, so the two effects must be combined. Converting temperatures to Kelvin: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 600 K, so the temperature doubles (×2). Half the molecules escape, so n is halved (×½). The final pressure is P₂ = P₁ · (n₂/n₁) · (T₂/T₁) = 1.0×10^5 · (½) · (2) = 1.0×10^5 Pa. The elegant point is that the heating and the leak exactly cancel, so the pressure is unchanged (A). The distractors each isolate one error: B (2.0×10^5) ignores the leak and applies only the Kelvin temperature doubling (pure Gay-Lussac); C (0.5×10^5) ignores the heating and applies only the halving of the amount of gas; D (4.0×10^5) doubles for temperature but inverts the mole ratio, multiplying by 2 for the leak instead of ½ (getting the direction of the amount change wrong); E (6.1×10^5) keeps the ½ factor but forgets to convert to Kelvin, using the Celsius ratio 327/27 ≈ 12.1 (0.5 × 12.1 ≈ 6.1). Only careful Kelvin conversion plus correct combination of the n and T effects yields the "no change" result, which weaker candidates instinctively reject.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Mechanics — Newton's laws, connected bodies over a pulley with friction on an incline
questions.skill: Multi-step reasoning: free-body analysis of a coupled two-body system, deciding direction of motion to fix the kinetic-friction sign, then solving the system Newton's-law equation
questions.stem: The 2 kg block shown rests on a rough incline that rises at 37° to the horizontal (sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8). The coefficient of kinetic friction between this block and the incline is 0.2. A light, inextensible cord runs from the block, passes over the frictionless pulley at the top of the incline, and connects to a second block that hangs freely, exactly as drawn in the figure. The system is released from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.explanation:
First decide the direction of motion. The hanging block's weight (read from the figure: m = 2 kg, so mg = 20 N) pulls the cord one way; gravity's down-slope component on the incline block is Mg sinθ = 2·10·0.6 = 12 N. Since 20 N exceeds 12 N + the maximum friction 0.2·2·10·0.8 = 3.2 N (i.e. 15.2 N), the system moves with the incline block sliding UP the slope, so kinetic friction acts DOWN the slope. Applying Newton's second law to the whole system: mg − Mg sinθ − μMg cosθ = (M+m)a → 20 − 12 − 3.2 = 4a → a = 4.8/4 = 1.2 m/s² (choice B).

Distractor traps: A) 2.0 — dropped friction: (mg − Mg sinθ)/(M+m) = 8/4. C) 4.4 — ignored the hanging block and pulley entirely and used the lone-incline result g(sinθ − μcosθ) = 6 − 1.6 (the pre-rewrite answer). D) 2.8 — assumed the block slides DOWN the incline, flipping the friction sign: |Mg sinθ − μMg cosθ − mg|/(M+m) = |12 − 3.2 − 20|/4; the negative result should have signalled the wrong assumed direction. E) 2.4 — treated the masses independently, taking the tension to equal the full hanging weight (20 N): (20 − 12 − 3.2)/2, ignoring that the hanging block also accelerates so T < mg.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Torque balance about a chosen pivot with variable load position; combining moment and force equilibrium
questions.stem: The free-body diagram shows a uniform ladder in equilibrium. Its foot rests on a rough horizontal floor and its top leans against a smooth (frictionless) vertical wall, so the wall exerts a single horizontal reaction. The ladder's own weight acts at its midpoint, and a person stands on one of the rungs. The angle at the floor, the weights, and the distances along the ladder are all marked on the diagram. Taking the ladder's weight as W, what is the minimum coefficient of static friction between the foot and the floor needed to keep the ladder from slipping? (tan 60° ≈ 1.73)
questions.explanation: Take torques about the foot (this removes the unknown floor forces). The smooth wall gives only a horizontal reaction N_w acting at the top, height L·sin60°, so its lever arm is L·sin60°. The vertical weights have lever arms equal to their horizontal distances from the foot: the ladder's weight W at the midpoint has arm (½L)·cos60°, and the person (weight 2W, read from the figure) stands ¾ of the way up, arm (¾L)·cos60°. Torque balance: N_w·L·sin60° = W·(½L)cos60° + 2W·(¾L)cos60° = W·cos60°·(½ + 3/2)·L = 2W·L·cos60°. So N_w = 2W·cos60°/sin60° = 2W/tan60° = 2W/1.73 = 1.15W. Vertical balance gives the floor normal N = W + 2W = 3W, and horizontal balance requires friction = N_w = 1.15W. Hence μ_min = N_w/N = 1.15/3 = 0.385 ≈ 0.39 (C). The figure is essential: the person's weight (2W) and rung position (¾L) appear only in the diagram. Distractor traps: (B) 0.29 = 1/(2·tan60°) is the memorized uniform-ladder result — it ignores the person entirely. (A) 0.19 reads the person's height from the top instead of the foot, using a ¼L lever arm. (D) 0.58 = 1/tan60° lumps BOTH weights at the top of the ladder (lever L·cos60°), giving N_w = 3W/tan60°. (E) 1.15 either swaps the sine and cosine lever arms (wall arm taken as L·cos60°, weight arms as L·sin60°) or reports N_w/W without dividing by the total normal 3W.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Setting up and solving a small linear system of rates; symmetric elimination
questions.stem: An irrigation reservoir is fed by three pumps A, B and C, each delivering water at its own constant rate. When only pumps A and B run, the reservoir fills in 15 hours; when only A and C run, it fills in 12 hours; and when only B and C run, it fills in 20 hours. How long would pump C, working alone, take to fill the reservoir?
questions.explanation: Work in rates (reservoirs per hour): rate(A+B)=1/15, rate(A+C)=1/12, rate(B+C)=1/20. Adding all three pairwise equations counts every pump exactly twice, so the sum equals 2·rate(A+B+C): 1/15+1/12+1/20 = 4/60+5/60+3/60 = 12/60 = 1/5. Therefore rate(A+B+C) = 1/10 (all three together take 10 h). To isolate C, subtract the pair that does NOT contain C: rate(C) = rate(A+B+C) − rate(A+B) = 1/10 − 1/15 = 3/30 − 2/30 = 1/30, so C alone takes 30 hours → A. Crucially, all three data are load-bearing: dropping any one equation makes rate(A+B+C) unobtainable. Distractor traps: B) 10 h is the all-three-together time — the solver correctly found rate(A+B+C)=1/10 but forgot the final subtraction of the A+B rate. C) 20 h comes from subtracting the wrong pair, rate(A+B+C) − rate(B+C) = 1/10 − 1/20 = 1/20; that isolates pump A, not C. E) 60 h comes from ignoring the B+C datum and just differencing two pairs, rate(A+C) − rate(A+B) = 1/12 − 1/15 = 1/60; that gives C − B, not C (it is in fact B's solo time). D) 5 h comes from subtracting times instead of rates — (A+B time) − (all-three time) = 15 − 10 — a rate/time confusion. Only careful use of all three equations plus the "halve the sum" step yields 30 h.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Recovering a general term from partial sums; arithmetic series
questions.skill: Multi-step reasoning: derive a_n from S_n, recognize arithmetic structure, sum a bounded block with correct indices
questions.stem: The sum of the first n terms of a sequence is S_n = 2n^2 + 3n for every positive integer n. What is the sum of the terms from the 11th through the 20th, inclusive (that is, a_11 + a_12 + ... + a_20)?
questions.explanation:
First recover the general term via a_n = S_n − S_{n−1} = (2n²+3n) − (2(n−1)²+3(n−1)) = 4n+1 (and a_1 = S_1 = 5 fits, so a_n = 4n+1 for all n). The block a_11+…+a_20 is most cleanly obtained as a telescoped difference of partial sums: S_20 − S_10 = (2·400+60) − (2·100+30) = 860 − 230 = 630 (equivalently, the 10-term arithmetic sum (10/2)(a_11+a_20) = 5·(45+81) = 630). So C is correct.
Traps: A) 585 = S_20 − S_11: the student has the identity but mishandles the boundary, subtracting S_11 (matching the start index 11) instead of S_10, which wrongly removes a_11 as well. B) 620 = sum of 4n for n=11..20: the student derives a_n = 4n+1 but drops the "+1" constant, forgetting to add it for each of the 10 terms (10 short of 630). D) 860 = S_20: the student ignores the lower bound and reads the problem as the sum of the first 20 terms. E) 230 = S_10: the student stops at the partial sum being subtracted, reporting S_10 itself instead of the difference. Each distractor is a distinct, plausible slip; none is also correct, and none can be eliminated without actually carrying out the derive-then-sum chain.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Superposition of electric fields; null point between point charges
questions.skill: Interpreting a field-magnitude-vs-position graph and reasoning about where and whether the net field of two like charges vanishes
questions.stem: Two positive point charges are fixed on a line: a charge +4Q at the origin (x = 0) and a charge +Q at x = 0.30 m. The four graphs below (I, II, III, IV) are candidate sketches of the MAGNITUDE of the net electric field, |E|, as a function of position x along the segment between the two charges. In each graph the dashed vertical lines mark the charge locations (+4Q on the left, +Q on the right). Which graph correctly represents |E| versus x on the segment between the charges?

options.E: None of the four graphs is correct

questions.explanation: Between two like charges the two field contributions point in opposite directions, so |E| diverges toward infinity at EACH charge (both dashed lines are vertical asymptotes) and passes through exactly one interior zero where the contributions cancel. Cancellation requires 4Q/d1² = Q/d2², i.e. d1 = 2·d2, so the null point lies TWICE as far from the strong +4Q charge as from the weak +Q charge — it sits at x = 0.20 m, closer to the WEAKER (+Q, right-hand) charge. Graph I is the only curve with two asymptotes and a single zero shifted toward the right/+Q side: correct (A). Graph II (B) places the zero at the midpoint — the trap of assuming the null is equidistant, which ignores the 4:1 magnitude ratio. Graph III (C) puts the zero closer to the strong +4Q charge — the common inversion that the field vanishes nearer the larger charge (it is actually the opposite). Graph IV (D) shows a valley whose minimum never reaches zero — the misconception that two same-sign fields only weaken but never fully cancel between the charges. Option E is the over-rejection trap for a student who computes 0.20 m correctly but fails to recognize that Graph I already displays exactly that asymmetry.

questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Three-set regions and inclusion–exclusion with an added constraint
questions.skill: Reading region counts from a Venn diagram and solving a small constrained linear system
questions.questionType: figure-based multi-step reasoning (three-set Venn with constrained system)
questions.stem:
A tour guide records which of three attractions — the Museum, the Castle and the Gardens — each of 50 tourists visited. Every tourist visited at least one attraction. Across the whole group, 30 people visited the Museum and 25 visited the Castle (the number who visited the Gardens is not recorded). The Venn diagram below gives the exact number of tourists in three of its regions; every region marked "?" is unknown. It is also known that the number of tourists who visited ONLY the Gardens is twice the number who visited all three attractions.

How many tourists visited EXACTLY TWO of the three attractions?
questions.explanation:
Let t be the number who visited all three. From the figure, Museum∩Castle-only = 9, Museum∩Gardens-only = 3, Castle-only = 7. Using the circle totals: Museum 30 = (only-Museum) + 9 + 3 + t, so only-Museum = 18 − t; Castle 25 = 7 + 9 + (Castle∩Gardens-only) + t, so Castle∩Gardens-only = 9 − t. The constraint gives only-Gardens = 2t. Summing all seven regions to the grand total of 50: (18 − t) + 7 + 2t + 9 + 3 + (9 − t) + t = 46 + t = 50, so t = 4. Then Castle∩Gardens-only = 5, and exactly-two = 9 + 3 + 5 = 17 (B). Note the Gardens total is never needed and is deliberately not given, so the memorised identity Σ|sets| = e1 + 2e2 + 3e3 cannot be plugged in directly.

Distractors: A) 12 sums only the two overlap counts printed in the figure (9 + 3) and never recovers the hidden Castle∩Gardens region from the Castle total and constraint. C) 21 solves everything but wrongly counts the all-three region (t = 4) as part of "exactly two" (17 + 4) — the triple-counting trap; the same value arises from ignoring the triple entirely. D) 25 abandons the figure and blind-plugs inclusion–exclusion, inventing a Gardens total of 20 and treating the all-three count as 0: (30+25+20) − 50 − 0 = 25. E) 33 makes the classic sign error in that same identity, adding the triple correction instead of subtracting it: 75 − 50 + 2·4 = 33.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Reading slope/intercept from a graph, finding a line intersection, and computing a triangle's area
questions.stem: The figure shows two straight lines, L1 (rising) and L2 (falling), plotted on a coordinate grid. Each line has two lattice points marked with dots, and the point where the two lines cross is also marked. Together with the y-axis, the two lines enclose a triangle. Read each line's slope and y-intercept from the marked points, then find the EXACT area of the triangle formed by L1, L2 and the y-axis.
questions.explanation: See intendedAnswer rationale.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Identifying the symbolic form of a transformed exponential function from its graph by combining asymptote, a point, and monotonic direction
questions.stem: The solid curve in the figure is obtained by transforming the base function y = 2^x. Read the graph carefully — its horizontal asymptote (dashed line), the single marked point, and the direction in which it runs. Which equation gives the solid curve?
questions.explanation: The curve must simultaneously match THREE features that the figure supplies, and no single feature settles it. (1) Horizontal asymptote y = 4: this fixes the constant term to 4 and eliminates C (asymptote y = 2) and D (asymptote y = -4). (2) Passes through (0, 3), i.e. one unit BELOW the asymptote: since 2^0 = 1, the base term must be subtracted, and the curve must dip below y = 4 — this eliminates E = 4 + 2^(-x), which is decreasing with asymptote y = 4 but sits entirely ABOVE the line (E gives 5 at x = 0, not 3). (3) Decreasing left-to-right with the LEFT tail flattening onto y = 4: to make an increasing base 2^x decrease you reflect in the x-axis, giving -2^x, then shift up 4 → y = 4 - 2^x. This is the only survivor. Distractor traps: B = 4 - 2^(-x) reflects in the WRONG axis (the y-axis), so it shares the same asymptote value AND the same point (0, 3) as the answer but runs the wrong way (increasing) — a student who only plugs in x = 0 cannot tell A from B and must use the direction of decrease. C = 2 + 2^(-x) has the correct decreasing direction and passes (0, 3) but reads the asymptote as y = 2 instead of y = 4. D = 2^x - 4 forgets the reflection and shifts down instead of up (asymptote y = -4, increasing). E = 4 + 2^(-x) keeps the right asymptote line and a decreasing shape but adds instead of subtracts, so the curve lies above the asymptote and misses the marked point. Each pair of cues alone is ambiguous (point → {A,B,C}; direction → {A,C,E}; asymptote → {A,B,E}); only all three together identify A.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Circles and inscribed polygons — composite area
questions.skill: Decomposing a compound shaded figure into sectors, segments and triangles read from a diagram
questions.stem: A regular hexagon and an equilateral triangle are both inscribed in a circle of radius 4, positioned as shown in the figure; the triangle's three vertices are alternate vertices of the hexagon. Some regions are shaded. Using the arrangement shown, find the total area of the shaded regions.
questions.explanation: The figure is essential: the text does not say which regions are shaded — you must read the diagram, which shows (i) the solid central inscribed triangle and (ii) three of the six thin rim segments (the alternating ones), while the three corner "caps" between the triangle and hexagon and the other three rim segments are left white. Decompose with r = 4. The central triangle is equilateral with its vertices at alternate hexagon vertices, so its side is the long chord r√3 = 4√3 and its area is (√3/4)(4√3)² = 12√3. Each shaded rim piece is a 60° circular segment = (60° sector) − (the equilateral triangle on that hexagon side) = (1/6)π(4²) − (√3/4)(4²) = 8π/3 − 4√3. Three of them give 3(8π/3 − 4√3) = 8π − 12√3. Total = 12√3 + (8π − 12√3) = 8π (option B); the triangle's √3 exactly cancels the three segments' triangular deficits. Trap A (8π + 12√3): used full 60° sectors for the rim pieces, forgetting to subtract each side-triangle, i.e. treating a segment as a sector. Trap C (8π − 12√3): shaded only the three segments and missed that the central triangle is also shaded (a pure figure-misread). Trap D (16π − 12√3): counted all six rim segments instead of the three alternating shaded ones (T + 6 segments). Trap E (8π − 8√3): took the central triangle's side as 4 (the hexagon side) instead of the chord 4√3, giving its area as 4√3 rather than 12√3. Every distractor is a distinct, specific decomposition error, and none can be reached — nor the correct value obtained — without reading the figure to identify exactly which pieces are shaded.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: Deriving a closed-form loop count from residue-class structure instead of enumeration
questions.stem:
The following pseudocode counts pairs (i, j) whose index sum is divisible by 3. It runs with N = 20.

  count = 0
  for i from 1 to N do
      for j from 1 to N do
          if ((i + j) mod 3 == 0) then
              count = count + 1
      end for
  end for
  output count

What value is printed?
questions.explanation:
The loop never has to be traced: (i + j) mod 3 depends only on the residues of i and j mod 3, so classify the 20 indices by residue. In 1..20 there are n0 = 6 multiples of 3 (residue 0: 3,6,...,18), n1 = 7 with residue 1 (1,4,...,19), and n2 = 7 with residue 2 (2,5,...,20). A pair satisfies (i + j) ≡ 0 (mod 3) exactly when the residues sum to 0 mod 3: (0,0), (1,2), or (2,1). Counting ordered pairs gives n0·n0 + n1·n2 + n2·n1 = 6·6 + 7·7 + 7·7 = 36 + 49 + 49 = 134. (Cross-check: the three sum-classes hold 134, 133, 133, totalling 400 = 20².)

Distractor traps:
- B) 133 = ⌊20²/3⌋. This is the "exactly one third of all 400 pairs" fallacy — it assumes the three residue classes are equal, which is only true when N is a multiple of 3. Because 20 ≢ 0 (mod 3), residues 1 and 2 are over-represented, and the true count exceeds a clean third by one. (133 is precisely the count for each of the OTHER two sum-classes, which is why it is so tempting.)
- C) 140 = 20 × 7. Recognises "one residue class of j per i" but hands every i the LARGER class ⌈20/3⌉ = 7; only the 14 values of i with residue 1 or 2 actually have 7 partners, while the 6 values with residue 0 have just 6.
- D) 120 = 20 × 6. The symmetric mistake — gives every i the SMALLER class ⌊20/3⌋ = 6.
- E) 36 = 6 × 6 = n0². Misreads "sum divisible by 3" as "both i and j divisible by 3," counting only pairs of multiples of 3.

questions.subject: reading
questions.skill: Distinguishing main purpose from supporting detail, tone, and scope
questions.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question below.

"It is fashionable, in certain circles, to announce that handwriting is a relic with no place in a digital age. I confess I find this verdict both hasty and a little sad. No one denies that a keyboard is faster; the point is that speed was never the whole purpose of writing by hand. When a student forms each letter slowly, the mind lingers over the idea being recorded, and that lingering is precisely where understanding takes root. To abandon the pen altogether is to mistake efficiency for education."

Which of the following best states the author's MAIN purpose in the passage?

options.A: To defend the cognitive value of handwriting against the claim that it is obsolete
options.B: To explain the mechanism by which forming letters slowly deepens a student's understanding
options.C: To lament, from nostalgia, that students today are no longer taught to write by hand
options.D: To concede that the keyboard's greater speed has rendered handwriting outdated
options.E: To argue that reliance on digital tools is damaging education across the board

questions.explanation:
The passage's controlling move is to reject a claim ("handwriting is a relic with no place in a digital age") and to justify that rejection by appeal to what handwriting does for understanding ("that lingering is precisely where understanding takes root"). The main purpose is therefore to DEFEND handwriting's cognitive value against dismissal.

A (correct): Captures both halves of the author's project — the target being rebutted (obsolescence) and the ground of the rebuttal (cognitive value). This is the argumentative claim the whole passage services.

B (too-narrow trap): The slow-lettering-aids-understanding point is real, but it is a SUPPORTING mechanism offered as evidence, not the passage's overall aim. Mistaking a premise for the thesis; it omits the entire polemical framing ("relic," "hasty and a little sad," "mistake efficiency for education").

C (tone/attitude trap): Seizes on the emotional aside "a little sad" and inflates it into the point. The author explicitly subordinates that feeling ("the point is that speed was never the whole purpose"): the passage makes an argument about value, not an elegy about lost practice — and it never claims students are no longer taught.

D (reversed-emphasis trap): Echoes the conceded clause "a keyboard is faster" but flips its function. The author grants speed only to deny that it settles the matter ("speed was never the whole purpose"); D adopts the very verdict the author calls "hasty."

E (over-broad trap): Generalizes from a defense of one practice (handwriting) to a blanket indictment of "digital tools" and all of education. The passage targets a single overreaching claim, not technology at large; "abandon the pen altogether" attacks totality, not digital tools per se.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Multi-step conditional-probability reasoning combined with solving an algebraic inequality (inverting Bayes to find a threshold parameter)
questions.stem: On a multiple-choice question with 4 options, a student knows the correct answer with probability p (and then answers correctly for certain); otherwise the student guesses uniformly at random among the 4 options. A teacher wants the following guarantee to hold: whenever the student answers correctly, the probability that the student genuinely knew the answer is at least 0.9. What is the smallest value of p for which this guarantee is satisfied?
questions.explanation: Set up the posterior. P(correct) = p·1 + (1−p)·(1/4) = (3p+1)/4, and P(knew AND correct) = p, so P(knew | correct) = p ÷ (3p+1)/4 = 4p/(3p+1). This is increasing in p, so the guarantee P(knew|correct) ≥ 0.9 holds for all p at or above the value where equality occurs. Solve 4p/(3p+1) = 9/10: 40p = 27p + 9, giving 13p = 9, so the smallest p is 9/13 ≈ 0.692 → A. The distractors each encode a specific error: B (9/11) comes from using a guessing success rate of 1/2 instead of 1/4 (treating the guess as if between two plausible options), giving 2p/(p+1)=9/10. C (3/4) comes from using 1/3 as the guess-success rate — miscounting the four options as "three wrong ones" — giving 3p/(2p+1)=9/10. D (13/15) comes from constraining the wrong probability: setting the overall accuracy P(correct)=(3p+1)/4 ≥ 0.9 instead of the posterior, giving 3p+1 ≥ 3.6. E (9/10) is the posterior-equals-prior fallacy: ignoring that guessing also produces correct answers and simply demanding p ≥ 0.9, so a correct response is wrongly assumed to leave the prior unchanged.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Combining momentum conservation with the elastic relative-velocity relation and sign reasoning to solve for an unknown mass
questions.stem: On a frictionless horizontal track, a 2.0 kg ball moving at 3.0 m/s makes a head-on, perfectly ELASTIC collision with a second ball that is initially at rest. After the collision the 2.0 kg ball is observed to REBOUND, moving at 1.0 m/s in the direction opposite to its original motion. What is the mass of the second (target) ball? (Take the original direction of motion as positive.)
questions.explanation:
Two invariants are needed. For a 1D elastic collision the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach: v2' − v1' = u − 0 = 3.0 m/s. The 2.0 kg ball rebounds, so v1' = −1.0 m/s, giving the target's velocity v2' = 3.0 + (−1.0) = +2.0 m/s. Then momentum conservation: (2.0)(3.0) = (2.0)(−1.0) + m2(2.0) → 6.0 = −2.0 + 2.0·m2 → m2 = 4.0 kg (D). Check: KE before = ½·2·3² = 9 J; after = ½·2·1² + ½·4·2² = 1 + 8 = 9 J, confirming the collision is elastic.

Distractor traps: (A) 1.0 kg — uses the memorized formula v1'/u = (m1−m2)/(m1+m2) but plugs the rebound speed as +1.0 instead of −1.0, i.e. ignores that rebound means a negative velocity. (B) 2.0 kg — finds v2' = 2.0 correctly but makes a sign error in momentum, writing 6.0 = +2.0 + 2.0·m2 (treating the rebounding ball's final momentum as positive); this also wrongly implies equal masses. (C) 3.0 kg — finds v2' = 2.0 but drops the incoming ball's post-collision momentum entirely, writing 6.0 = 2.0·m2. (E) 8.0 kg — never applies separation = approach; instead assumes the target leaves at the same 1.0 m/s the incoming ball rebounds, giving 6.0 = −2.0 + m2·1.0.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Newton's second law: connected bodies, inclined plane with kinetic friction
questions.skill: Resolving gravity along/normal to an incline, determining direction of motion, applying friction with the correct sign, and analyzing a connected two-body system
questions.stem: Two blocks, each of mass m₁ = m₂ = 3 kg, are connected by a light inextensible string that passes over an ideal (massless, frictionless) pulley mounted at the top of a fixed inclined plane, as shown. Block m₁ rests on the inclined surface; block m₂ hangs vertically. The slope of the incline and the coefficient of kinetic friction between m₁ and the surface are given ONLY in the figure. The system is released from rest. Take g = 10 m/s². What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.explanation:
The figure supplies the two facts missing from the text: the incline's slope is rise:run = 3:4, so sinθ = 3/5 = 0.6 and cosθ = 4/5 = 0.8, and the coefficient of kinetic friction is μ = 0.25. With m₁ = m₂ = 3 kg and g = 10: normal force N = m₁g·cosθ = 3·10·0.8 = 24 N, so kinetic friction f = μN = 0.25·24 = 6 N.

Determine the direction first. The hanging weight m₂g = 30 N tends to pull the system one way; the weight component of m₁ along the incline, m₁g·sinθ = 3·10·0.6 = 18 N, opposes it. Since 30 N > 18 N, m₂ descends and m₁ slides UP the incline, so kinetic friction acts DOWN the incline (opposing m₁'s actual motion).

Check that it actually moves: the net driving force before friction is 30 − 18 = 12 N, which exceeds the maximum friction 6 N, so the system is NOT static. Applying Newton's second law to the whole system:
a = (m₂g − m₁g·sinθ − μ·m₁g·cosθ)/(m₁ + m₂) = (30 − 18 − 6)/6 = 6/6 = 1 m/s². Answer B.

Distractor traps:
A) 0 m/s²: assumes friction holds the system static, without comparing the 12 N net drive to the 6 N maximum friction — the motion condition is never checked.
C) 2 m/s²: reads the incline correctly but ignores friction: (30 − 18)/6.
D) 3 m/s²: gives friction the wrong sign, treating it as if it aids the motion: (30 − 18 + 6)/6.
E) 5 m/s²: ignores the incline entirely and pattern-matches to the flat-table pulley formula a = m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 30/6 — the pure recognition shortcut this item is built to defeat.

verifyDefect.reason: The coefficient of kinetic friction (intended μ=0.25) is occluded by the m₁ block; only "μk = 0" is legible, so the figure fails to supply data the stem says is given ONLY there, and the two readings (μ=0→C, μ=0.25→B) both hit listed options, making the item ambiguous/unanswerable as drawn.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Parallelograms in the coordinate plane / midpoint of diagonals
questions.skill: Reading coordinates from a grid; enumerating all valid parallelogram completions of three points; applying a quadrant constraint
questions.stem: The coordinate grid shows three fixed points A, B and C, together with five candidate points labelled P1 to P5. All coordinates must be read from the grid (they are not given in words). A point D is called a *completion* if A, B, C and D — in some order — are the four vertices of a parallelogram. Among the marked candidate points, which one is a completion AND lies in the fourth quadrant (the region where x > 0 and y < 0)?
questions.explanation:
Read from the grid: A(-3,-1), B(1,4), C(5,0). Three vertices of a triangle can be completed to a parallelogram in exactly THREE ways, one for each choice of which pair of the given points are opposite (their diagonals must share a midpoint):
• B and D opposite: D = A + C − B = (1, −5)  → this is P4.
• C and D opposite: D = A + B − C = (−7, 3)  → this is P2.
• A and D opposite: D = B + C − A = (9, 5)   → this is P1.
So P1, P2 and P4 are all genuine completions, but only ONE of them lies in the fourth quadrant. P1(9,5) is in the first quadrant and P2(−7,3) is in the second quadrant, so both fail the x>0, y<0 condition — they trap students who find one valid completion and stop without checking where it lies. P4(1,−5) satisfies both conditions, so P4 is correct.
Distractor traps: P3(2,−1) is A + C = (2,−1), i.e. the correct formula A + C − B with the −B term forgotten; it deliberately sits in the fourth quadrant, so it survives the quadrant filter and catches students who apply the constraint but mis-derive D — yet it forms no parallelogram with A, B, C. P5(1,1) is the centroid (A+B+C)/3 = (1,1), the "just average the vertices" error, and it is not a completion (and lies in the first quadrant). Only P4 is simultaneously a valid completion and in the fourth quadrant.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Coupling the radial form of Newton's second law (tension = 0 condition) with mechanical-energy conservation
questions.stem: A small ball is attached to the end of a light, inextensible string of length r = 0.90 m and swung in a vertical circle. At the LOWEST point of the circle the ball is moving at 6.0 m/s. This speed is too small to keep the string taut all the way around, so at some point in the upper part of the circle the string suddenly goes slack. How far ABOVE the lowest point of the circle is the ball at the instant the string first goes slack? (g = 10 m/s².)
questions.explanation: See above.

questions.subject: reading
questions.subtopic: Inference and application of an author's argument to a novel case
questions.skill: Applying a text's central principle to an unstated scenario
questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

It is tempting to picture evolution as a ladder of progress, climbing from 'simple' bacteria at the bottom toward 'complex' humans at the top. Biologists resist this image. A bacterium alive today is not a leftover from an earlier rung; it is the product of exactly as many generations of selection as we are, and it is exquisitely adapted to its own way of life. Complexity is one answer to the problem of survival, but it is not the goal, and often not even the best answer. Evolution has no summit toward which everything strives — only a vast, branching bush of lineages, each living tip equally modern.

Researchers discover a cave-dwelling fish whose ancestors had fully functional eyes, but which has itself lost its eyes entirely over many generations in the dark. A commentator argues this proves the fish is "evolutionarily backward" — a species sliding down the ladder rather than climbing it. Based on the passage, how would the author most likely respond to the commentator?

A) The author would agree, because losing a complex organ like an eye is a clear step backward down the evolutionary ladder.
B) The author would disagree, arguing that the eyeless fish has undergone just as much selection as any sighted species and is well adapted to its dark niche, so "backward" misapplies a ladder the author rejects.
C) The author would agree that the fish is less evolved, since it is now simpler than its sighted ancestors were.
D) The author would disagree, arguing that the fish will eventually regrow its eyes because evolution always trends toward greater complexity over time.
E) The author would say the question cannot be answered, because the passage claims only bacteria — not animals like fish — can be judged "equally modern."

options.A: The author would agree, because losing a complex organ like an eye is a clear step backward down the evolutionary ladder.
options.B: The author would disagree, arguing that the eyeless fish has undergone just as much selection as any sighted species and is well adapted to its dark niche, so "backward" misapplies a ladder the author rejects.
options.C: The author would agree that the fish is less evolved, since it is now simpler than its sighted ancestors were.
options.D: The author would disagree, arguing that the fish will eventually regrow its eyes because evolution always trends toward greater complexity over time.
options.E: The author would say the question cannot be answered, because the passage claims only bacteria — not animals like fish — can be judged "equally modern."

questions.explanation:
The passage rejects the "ladder of progress" and holds that (1) every surviving lineage is the product of exactly as many generations of selection as any other ("each living tip equally modern"), (2) organisms are judged by adaptation to their own way of life, and (3) complexity is "not the goal, and often not even the best answer." Applying these principles to the novel case, the author would reject the "backward" label: the eyeless fish is not sliding down a nonexistent ladder — it has been selected just as long as sighted fish and is adapted to darkness, where eyes are costly and useless. B operationalizes all three principles against the new case, which is stated nowhere in the text and must be inferred.

Trap A: adopts the very ladder-and-summit image the author explicitly rejects, treating loss of complexity as regression. Trap C: relies on "simpler = less evolved," but the passage denies that complexity measures evolutionary standing and insists all lineages are equally modern. Trap D: correctly senses the author would disagree with the commentator, but supplies the opposite of the author's view — it smuggles in "evolution always trends toward greater complexity," precisely the directed progress the passage denies (a careless reader picks the right verdict for the wrong, contradictory reason). Trap E: fabricates a scope restriction; the passage uses bacteria only as an illustration and applies "equally modern" to all lineages ("each living tip"), so nothing limits the thesis to bacteria. Each distractor is defensible only to a reader who has not weighed the passage's actual claims.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Interpreting signed area under a v–t graph (motion with reversal)
questions.stem: The velocity–time graph shows a cart moving along a straight line, where positive velocity means motion in the +x direction. The cart speeds up from rest, cruises at constant velocity, slows to rest, then REVERSES and moves back before finally stopping. Reading the values from the graph, determine the cart's NET displacement (its final position measured from the starting point) over the whole 12 s interval.
questions.explanation: Displacement is the SIGNED area under the v–t graph. Above-axis (forward) area: triangle 0–2 s = ½·2·6 = 6; rectangle 2–6 s = 4·6 = 24; triangle 6–8 s = ½·2·6 = 6 → +36 m. Below-axis (reverse) area, which counts as NEGATIVE displacement: triangle 8–9 s = ½·1·4 = 2; rectangle 9–11 s = 2·4 = 8; triangle 11–12 s = ½·1·4 = 2 → −12 m. Net displacement = 36 − 12 = 24 m (C). Traps: (E) 48 m adds the absolute areas 36 + 12 — that is the TOTAL DISTANCE, the sign-blind student who treats below-axis area as positive. (D) 36 m ignores the reversal entirely, counting only the forward region. (B) 20 m reads the below-axis part as a full rectangle 4 m/s × 4 s = 16 m (forgetting the two ramp triangles) giving 36 − 16. (A) 12 m reports only the magnitude of the return leg, mistaking "net" for the reversal contribution alone. The item is selective because the arithmetic is trivial; the discriminating step is recognizing that area below the axis subtracts.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Coulomb's law and vector superposition of forces
questions.skill: Resolving perpendicular Coulomb forces into components and adding them vectorially, including correct attractive/repulsive directions
questions.stem: Three point charges are fixed in the xy-plane as shown in the figure. The target charge q₂ sits at the origin O; the other two charges lie on the coordinate axes at the distances marked. Using k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C², determine the magnitude AND direction of the net electrostatic force on q₂. (All positions, distances, and which axis each charge lies on must be read from the figure.)

options.A: 1.35 N, directed along the −x-axis (straight toward the left)
options.B: 1.41 N, directed up and to the left, about 17° above the −x-axis
options.C: 1.41 N, directed down and to the left, about 17° below the −x-axis
options.D: 1.75 N, directed up and to the left
options.E: 0.95 N, directed up and to the left

questions.explanation: Read the geometry from the figure: q₁ = +6 μC lies on the +x-axis at 0.20 m, and q₃ = −4 μC lies on the +y-axis at 0.30 m, so the two forces on q₂ act along perpendicular directions. Force from q₁ (both positive → repulsion): F₂₁ = k·q₁·q₂/r² = (9×10⁹)(6×10⁻⁶)(1×10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = 1.35 N, pointing in the −x direction (pushed away from q₁). Force from q₃ (opposite signs → attraction): F₂₃ = (9×10⁹)(4×10⁻⁶)(1×10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 0.40 N, pointing in the +y direction (pulled toward q₃). These are perpendicular, so the net magnitude is √(1.35² + 0.40²) = √1.9825 = 1.41 N, and the direction is atan(0.40/1.35) ≈ 16.5° above the −x-axis — up and to the left. That is B. Trap C has the correct magnitude (1.41 N) but the wrong direction: it comes from treating the negative charge q₃ as if it repelled q₂ (force pushed to −y instead of +y), putting the resultant below the −x-axis — a sign/direction error that a scalar magnitude check cannot catch. Trap A (1.35 N) drops q₃ entirely and reports only the force from q₁. Trap D (1.75 N) adds the two magnitudes as if they were parallel (scalar sum), ignoring that they are perpendicular. Trap E (0.95 N) subtracts the magnitudes (1.35 − 0.40) as if the two forces were antiparallel rather than at 90°.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Hypothesise, test, and eliminate competing generating rules against all given terms
questions.stem:
In the sequence below, the numbers in odd positions count up (1, 2, 3, 4, 5). Each number in an even position is generated from that count by a fixed rule. What number should replace the question mark?

1, 6, 2, 24, 3, 60, 4, 120, 5, ?
questions.explanation:
Separate the two interleaved streams. The odd positions are the counter n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The even positions are the "result" terms 6, 24, 60, 120, ?, each produced from the current counter n. Test candidate rules against ALL four known results, not just the first one or two.

The rule that fits every given result is the product of three consecutive integers, r(n) = n(n+1)(n+2): 1·2·3 = 6, 2·3·4 = 24, 3·4·5 = 60, 4·5·6 = 120. It is the unique rule consistent with all four values (equivalently, the first differences 18, 36, 60 grow by 18, 24, so the next difference is 90, giving 120 + 90 = 210). For n = 5 the result is 5·6·7 = 210. Correct answer: B.

Trap analysis:
- E) 720 — the "factorial recall" trap. Seeing 6 = 3! and 24 = 4!, a candidate who recognises the familiar factorial-interleave template leaps to 5!, 6! and answers 6! = 720. But the template is refuted by the sequence itself: the third result is 60, not 5! = 120, and the fourth is 120, not 6! = 720. Recognition here gives the wrong answer; only verifying against 60 and 120 saves you.
- A) 180 — constant-difference error. Takes the last gap (120 − 60 = 60) and adds it once more (120 + 60), missing that the gaps grow (18, 36, 60, 90).
- C) 240 — constant-ratio error. The last two results 60 and 120 look like ×2, so the candidate predicts 120 × 2, ignoring that the earlier ratios (6→24 is ×4, 24→60 is ×2.5) are not constant.
- D) 336 — counter-misalignment error. Correctly identifies the triple-product rule but pairs the missing term with counter 6 instead of 5, computing 6·7·8 = 336.

Only 210 continues the rule that matches all four visible results, so the item rewards hypothesise-test-reject reasoning over pattern recognition.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Contact/pushed blocks with non-uniform kinetic friction; free-body isolation
questions.skill: Isolating one block of a connected system and selecting the correct friction term acting on it
questions.stem: Two blocks rest in contact on a horizontal floor, with m₁ = 3.0 kg directly behind m₂ = 2.0 kg. A horizontal force F = 30 N pushes on m₁, driving both blocks forward together so that m₁ presses on m₂. The floor is NOT uniform: beneath each block the coefficient of kinetic friction has a different value, as labelled in the figure. Taking g = 10 m/s², what is the magnitude of the horizontal contact force that m₁ exerts on m₂?
questions.explanation:
Treat the two blocks as one system to get the shared acceleration, then isolate m₂ using the friction that actually acts beneath IT. Total floor friction = μ₁m₁g + μ₂m₂g = (0.25)(3.0)(10) + (0.50)(2.0)(10) = 7.5 + 10 = 17.5 N. System: a = (F − 17.5)/(m₁+m₂) = (30 − 17.5)/5.0 = 2.5 m/s². Now isolate m₂: the only horizontal forces on it are the forward contact force N from m₁ and its own backward kinetic friction μ₂m₂g = (0.50)(2.0)(10) = 10 N. Newton's 2nd law: N − 10 = m₂a = (2.0)(2.5) = 5.0, so N = 15.0 N (D). Cross-check by isolating m₁: F − N − μ₁m₁g = m₁a → 30 − N − 7.5 = 7.5 → N = 15.0 N. ✓

Distractor traps:
A) 5.0 N — computes only m₂a and forgets that m₂ has its own friction to overcome (drops the +μ₂m₂g term).
B) 10.0 N — correct method but reads the WRONG coefficient off the figure, using μ₁ = 0.25 (the value under m₁) for m₂'s friction: 2.0·2.5 + 0.25·2.0·10 = 5 + 5 = 10. This is why the per-block labels are load-bearing.
C) 12.0 N — the classic friction-blind answer: N = m₂F/(m₁+m₂) = 2.0·30/5.0 = 12.0, obtained by ignoring friction entirely. With uniform friction this coincidentally equals the true answer, but here the differing μ's make it a genuinely wrong 12.0 N, so the friction-blind student is now caught.
E) 17.5 N — mistakes the total system friction force (μ₁m₁g + μ₂m₂g) for the contact force.

questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Multi-step deduction: enumerate all admissible arrangements and intersect properties across cases
questions.questionType: must-be-true / constraint satisfaction with case enumeration
questions.stem:
Six friends — P, Q, R, S, T and U — sit around a circular table, all facing the centre. For anyone facing the centre, 'right' means the clockwise direction and 'left' the anticlockwise direction. The only facts known about the seating are:

(1) P sits directly opposite S.
(2) T is the second person to Q's right.
(3) U does NOT sit immediately to S's left.

These three conditions do not fix a unique seating. Which one of the following statements MUST be true in EVERY seating that satisfies them?

options.A: T sits immediately to S's right.
options.B: R and U do not sit next to each other.
options.D: T and U do not sit next to each other.
options.E: P and R sit next to each other.

questions.explanation:
Fix P by rotational symmetry; condition (1) places S directly opposite P. Condition (2) means T sits two seats clockwise from Q, so among the remaining seats {Q,T} can only be {Q at P's 2nd-right, T at P's 4th-right} in one of two ways, giving {Q,T}={one pair} or the diametric alternative. Working it through, the free seats admit exactly three valid seatings (listed clockwise from P):
• S1: P, R, Q, S, T, U
• S2: P, U, Q, S, T, R
• S3: P, T, R, S, U, Q
(The would-be fourth seating is killed by condition (3), which bars U from S's immediate left.) You cannot answer from one seating, because in S1 every option below happens to be true — the item demands that you enumerate ALL valid seatings and keep only what survives in each.

Correct: (B). In S1 and S2, R and U are separated by P; in S3 they are separated by S. In no valid seating are they neighbours, so 'R and U are not adjacent' holds in all three — the structural invariant that R and U always end up in the two seats flanked by the fixed pair P/S.

Trap (A): true in S1 and S2 but false in S3, where the person on S's right is U, not T. It catches candidates who find only the two 'near' seatings and never construct S3.
Trap (C): true only in S1. It catches candidates who build a single seating and read the answer straight off it.
Trap (D): true in S2 and S3 but false in S1, where T and U are in fact adjacent. It catches candidates who miss S1 while checking a negative statement.
Trap (E): true in S1 and S2 but false in S3. It catches candidates who assume R must stay beside P, an incidental feature of the first seatings rather than a forced one.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: tracing nested loops with a dependent inner bound and a parity filter to count executions
questions.explanation:
i + j is even exactly when i and j have the SAME parity. For a fixed i, the inner variable j ranges over i, i+1, ..., 10, and the values sharing i's parity are j = i, i+2, i+4, ..., up to 10. Their count is floor((10 - i)/2) + 1 (the "+1" includes j = i itself, which always satisfies the condition since i + i = 2i is even). Summing over i = 1..10: 5+5+4+4+3+3+2+2+1+1 = 30. Correct: B.

Distractor traps:
A) 20 — off-by-one: the student computes the number of valid j as floor((10 - i)/2) but forgets the "+1" that counts j = i, undercounting every row by one (30 - 10 = 20).
C) 25 — parity inversion: the student filters for i + j ODD (opposite-parity j) instead of even. Those are the complementary pairs, 55 - 30 = 25.
D) 50 — drops the j >= i restriction: for each i there are exactly 5 same-parity values in the full range 1..10 (five odds or five evens), giving 10 x 5 = 50; this ignores that j must start at i, so it wrongly includes pairs with j < i.
E) 55 — ignores the parity condition entirely and just sums the inner-loop lengths 10+9+8+...+1, the plain triangular number n(n+1)/2 that the original easy version rewarded.

A student who recognizes the pattern but does not carefully model the same-parity inner-loop cardinality lands on a plausible-looking wrong value (20, 25, or 55); the correct answer requires actually reasoning about parity within the dependent, shrinking inner range.

questions.subject: computer_science
questions.skill: structural reasoning about a recursion (call) tree
questions.questionType: conceptual-analytical (general closed form, not a single trace)
questions.stem:
The naive recursive Fibonacci function is defined, for integer n, by:

  fib(0) = 0
  fib(1) = 1
  fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)   for n >= 2

Consider evaluating fib(n) for some fixed n >= 2. During the whole computation let:

  A = the number of times the base case fib(0) is reached,
  B = the number of times the base case fib(1) is reached,
  P = the number of additions (the "+" in fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)) actually performed.

Which statement gives ALL THREE quantities correctly, in terms of Fibonacci numbers, for every n >= 2?

options.A: A = fib(n-1),  B = fib(n),  P = fib(n+1) - 1
options.B: A = fib(n),  B = fib(n-1),  P = fib(n+1) - 1
options.C: A = fib(n-1),  B = fib(n),  P = fib(n+1)
options.D: A = fib(n-1),  B = fib(n),  P = fib(n) - 1

questions.explanation: The call tree of fib(n) is a FULL binary tree: every fib(k) with k>=2 makes exactly two recursive calls, and the base cases make none. The leaves are exactly the base-case calls. Since the returned value fib(n) is the sum of the leaf values, and each fib(1) leaf contributes 1 while each fib(0) leaf contributes 0, the number of fib(1) leaves is B = fib(n). The total leaf count L satisfies L(0)=L(1)=1 and L(n)=L(n-1)+L(n-2), so L = fib(n+1); hence A = L - B = fib(n+1) - fib(n) = fib(n-1). Every addition happens at exactly one internal (non-leaf) node, and in a full binary tree the number of internal nodes = leaves - 1, so P = fib(n+1) - 1. All three: A=fib(n-1), B=fib(n), P=fib(n+1)-1 (sanity check n=5: A=3, B=5, leaves=8, P=7). Distractor traps: (B) swaps A and B, assuming fib(0) is reached at least as often as fib(1) — but the tree is skewed and fib(1) is the more frequent base case (fib(n) > fib(n-1)). (C) gets the base-case counts right but sets P = leaves, forgetting that internal nodes = leaves - 1 (one fewer addition than there are base-case calls). (D) gets the base-case counts right but computes P = B - 1, counting one addition per fib(1) leaf only instead of per internal node. (E) assumes the recursion tree is balanced so the two base cases occur equally (A = B); it is skewed, so A = fib(n-1) is strictly less than B = fib(n). Only option A requires holding BOTH structural facts at once — which base case dominates, and that additions equal leaves minus one — so it separates students who reason about the tree from those who match a single remembered clause.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Perpendicular bisector / locus of equidistant points
questions.skill: Reading point coordinates off a grid and identifying the perpendicular bisector by midpoint and slope
questions.stem: The coordinate grid shows two points A and B and five straight lines labelled ℓ1, ℓ2, ℓ3, ℓ4 and ℓ5. Read the positions of A and B from the grid. Exactly one of the drawn lines is the locus of all points that are equidistant from A and from B (that is, the perpendicular bisector of segment AB). Using only the figure, which line is it?
questions.explanation: From the grid, A = (1, 1) and B = (5, 3). The locus of points equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector of AB, which must (i) pass through the midpoint M = (3, 2) and (ii) be perpendicular to AB. Since AB has slope (3−1)/(5−1) = ½, the bisector has slope −2. Only ℓ3 passes through M(3,2) with slope −2 (equation 2x + y = 8); a quick check confirms equidistance, e.g. (0,8) and (4,0) are each the same distance from A and B. Distractor traps: ℓ1 is the line through A and B itself (slope ½) — it passes through the midpoint but has the wrong direction, catching students who pick the line joining the two points rather than the one perpendicular to it. ℓ2 passes through the correct midpoint M but has slope +2 (2x − y = 4): the sign of the perpendicular slope has been flipped. ℓ4 has the correct slope −2 but is drawn through A(1,1) instead of the midpoint (2x + y = 3): right direction, wrong location, so points on it are not equidistant. ℓ5 passes through M with slope −½ (x + 2y = 7): the AB slope was merely negated instead of taking the negative reciprocal, giving a line that is not perpendicular to AB.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Reading a vertex and arm-slope off a grid and reconstructing y = a|x−h|+k
questions.stem: The figure shows the graph of a function of the form y = a|x − h| + k (obtained from y = |x| by a reflection, a vertical stretch/compression, and translations). Using the grid, read off the vertex and the slope of the two arms, then choose the formula that produces the graph.
questions.explanation: Two independent features must be read from the grid. Vertex: the peak sits at (2, 3), so h = 2 and k = 3. Slope: each arm drops 2 units of y per 1 unit of x — the graph passes through (1, 1) and (3, 1) — and it opens downward, so a = −2. This gives y = −2|x − 2| + 3 (A). Each distractor is a specific misread that survives a single-feature check: B reads the vertex correctly but ignores the marked second point, taking the slope as −1 instead of −2 (the classic "translation-only" error); C swaps the vertex coordinates to (3, 2); D commits the horizontal-shift sign error, |x + 2|, placing the vertex at (−2, 3) while matching slope and orientation; E commits the vertical-shift sign error, putting the vertex at (2, −3). Because B agrees with A on the vertex and C/D/E agree with A on the slope and orientation, no single feature eliminates the whole set — the student must combine the vertex reading and the slope reading to select A.

questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Newton's laws — connected bodies on an inclined plane with friction
questions.skill: Resolving forces on an incline, extracting geometry from a figure, applying Newton's second law to a two-body system with kinetic friction
questions.stem: A block of mass m₁ = 2.0 kg sits on the surface of a fixed inclined wedge. An ideal (massless, inextensible) string runs from m₁ up the slope, passes over a frictionless pulley at the top of the incline, and connects to a hanging block of mass m₂ = 3.0 kg, as shown. The coefficient of kinetic friction between m₁ and the incline is μ = 0.25; the incline angle θ is defined by the right triangle in the figure. The system is released from rest. Taking g = 9.8 m/s², what is the magnitude of the acceleration of the blocks?
questions.explanation: The incline angle is not stated in words — it must be read from the labeled right triangle: rise = 3, run = 4, so the hypotenuse ratio is 3-4-5 and sinθ = 3/5 = 0.6, cosθ = 4/5 = 0.8. First check which way the system moves: the driving weight is m₂g = 29.4 N, while the maximum it must overcome (gravity component down the slope plus friction) is m₁g·sinθ + μm₁g·cosθ = 11.76 + 3.92 = 15.68 N. Since 29.4 > 15.68 the system accelerates, m₁ slides UP the incline, and kinetic friction therefore acts DOWN the incline (shown by f in the figure). Applying Newton's second law to the two-block system: a = (m₂g − m₁g·sinθ − μm₁g·cosθ)/(m₁ + m₂) = (29.4 − 11.76 − 3.92)/5.0 = 13.72/5.0 = 2.7 m/s² (B).\n\nDistractor traps: (A) 4.9 m/s² — treats the surface as a HORIZONTAL table, dropping the m₁g·sinθ gravity term entirely and using a = (m₂g − μm₁g)/(m₁+m₂); this is the answer a student gets by ignoring the incline and never reading the triangle. (C) 4.3 m/s² — flips the friction sign, wrongly assuming m₁ slides DOWN so friction adds to the drive: (m₂g − m₁g·sinθ + μm₁g·cosθ)/(m₁+m₂); fails the direction-of-motion reasoning. (D) 2.2 m/s² — swaps sine and cosine, using sinθ = 0.8 in the gravity term and cosθ = 0.6 in friction (misreads which leg is opposite θ). (E) 3.5 m/s² — resolves gravity correctly but forgets kinetic friction altogether: (m₂g − m₁g·sinθ)/(m₁+m₂).

verifyDefect.reason: Physics, answer (B, a=2.7 m/s²), and distractors are all correct, but the figure has a visible label-collision glitch where "rise = 3" overlaps "m₂ = 3.0 kg" (rendering as a jumbled "rise = 3.0 kg"), a cosmetic quality flag for a final publish gate.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Reading circuit topology from a schematic and recognising a balanced Wheatstone bridge
questions.stem: The figure shows an ideal battery connected to a network of five resistors. The resistor values are R₁ = 2 Ω, R₂ = 4 Ω, R₃ = 3 Ω, R₄ = 6 Ω and R₅ = 5 Ω, but how each one is wired must be read from the diagram. What is the equivalent resistance seen by the battery?
questions.explanation: The network is a Wheatstone bridge: R₁ and R₂ form the upper path A→C→B, R₃ and R₄ form the lower path A→D→B, and R₅ is the bridge between the middle nodes C and D. Read the arm values from the figure and test the balance condition R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄: here 2/4 = 3/6 = 1/2, so the bridge is BALANCED. When balanced, nodes C and D sit at the same potential, so no current flows through R₅ — it can be deleted (equivalently, shorted; both give the same result). The circuit collapses to two series branches in parallel: (R₁+R₂) ∥ (R₃+R₄) = 6 ∥ 9 = 54/15 = 3.6 Ω (A, correct). Distractor B (8.6 Ω) keeps R₅ and adds it in series with the reduced 3.6 Ω — the exact error of not recognising the zero-current bridge arm. Distractor C (15 Ω) correctly drops R₅ but then combines the two 6 Ω and 9 Ω branches in series (6+9) instead of in parallel — a series/parallel confusion. Distractor D (20 Ω) simply sums all five resistors (2+4+3+6+5) as though the whole network were one series chain, ignoring every parallel structure. Distractor E (2.1 Ω) handles R₅ by throwing it in parallel across the network, 6 ∥ 9 ∥ 5 ≈ 2.1 Ω — the mirror-image mishandling of the bridge arm. Only a student who reads the topology from the figure and spots the balance ratio reaches 3.6 Ω; the text alone (values with no wiring) is under-determined, so the diagram is essential. No calculus is used — only ratio reasoning and series/parallel rules.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Recognizing bridge balance / equipotential-node reasoning instead of blind series-parallel reduction
questions.stem: In the circuit shown, an ideal 12 V battery drives a bridge network of five resistors whose values are labelled in the figure. The upper node A and lower node C are the battery terminals; nodes B and D are joined by the bridge resistor R5. What is the magnitude of the current flowing through R5?
questions.explanation: This is a Wheatstone bridge. The bridge resistor R5 carries current only if nodes B and D are at different potentials. Test the balance condition on the two arms as drawn: left arm A–B–C has R1 = 2 Ω and R2 = 3 Ω; right arm A–D–C has R3 = 8 Ω and R4 = 12 Ω. Since R1/R2 = 2/3 and R3/R4 = 8/12 = 2/3, the ratios are equal, so the bridge is BALANCED. Each arm acts as an identical voltage divider: V_B = 12·R1/(R1+R2)... equivalently V_B = 12 − (12/5)(2) = 7.2 V and V_D = 12 − (12/20)(8) = 7.2 V. B and D are equipotential, so no current flows through R5 regardless of its 5 Ω value. Answer: A (0 A). Distractor traps: B = 1.8 A assumes the bridge must carry the DIFFERENCE of the two branch currents (2.4 A − 0.6 A) — the classic error of forgetting to test for balance and misapplying node conservation. C = 0.6 A mistakes the bridge current for the current in the weaker (right) arm. D = 2.4 A mistakes it for the current in the stronger (left) arm. E = 3.0 A is the total current drawn from the battery, chosen by a student who imagines all the current funnels through the central resistor. Only balance-recognition (or computing that V_B = V_D) yields the correct zero; the resistor values are deliberately non-symmetric so the balance must be verified by ratio, not read off by eye.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Applying Newton's second law / work–energy with friction across a compound incline and recognising the constant-velocity condition tanθ = μ
questions.stem: A small block is released from rest at the top of the two-segment ramp shown and slides all the way down. The SAME coefficient of kinetic friction, μ = 0.25, applies on both segments. Take g = 9.8 m/s² (use sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8 as reference values). All lengths and slopes must be read from the figure. What is the block's speed when it reaches the bottom of the second (lower) segment?
questions.explanation: Segment 1 (37°, L₁ = 5.0 m, from figure): a₁ = g(sin37° − μcos37°) = 9.8(0.6 − 0.25·0.8) = 3.92 m/s². Speed at the kink: v₁² = 2a₁L₁ = 2(3.92)(5.0) = 39.2 → v₁ = 6.26 ≈ 6.3 m/s. Segment 2 (rise 1.0 m over run 4.0 m, from figure): tanθ₂ = 1.0/4.0 = 0.25 = μ. Since sinθ₂ = μcosθ₂, the along-slope weight component exactly cancels kinetic friction, so the NET force on segment 2 is zero. The block therefore coasts at constant velocity down segment 2 no matter how long it is — its length is a red herring. Speed at the bottom = v₁ = 6.3 m/s (C). This is the selective step: only a student who tests μ vs tanθ₂ realises segment 2 adds nothing. Trap A (8.9): ignored friction on both segments and used the total vertical drop H = 3.0 + 1.0 = 4.0 m in v = √(2gH). Trap B (7.7): kept friction on segment 1 but treated segment 2 as frictionless, so the block seems to speed up: v² = v₁² + 2g·h₂ = 39.2 + 19.6 = 58.8. Trap D (5.9): on segment 1 used μg instead of μg·cosθ₁ for friction (forgot to project the weight onto the normal): a₁ = 9.8·0.6 − 0.25·9.8 = 3.43, v² = 34.3. Trap E (4.4): correct on segment 1 but on segment 2 dropped the gravity driving term and treated friction as if on flat ground: v² = v₁² − 2μg·cosθ₂·L₂ = 39.2 − 2(0.25)(9.8)(4.0) = 19.6.

questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Two-dimensional projectile reasoning: distinguishing height AT a point from maximum height, recognizing the descending branch, and testing a clearance condition
