questions.stem: A data-center audit sorts every server by three independent properties, drawn as the three overlapping circles in the diagram (E, R and P are defined in the legend). Exactly one region is hatched: the audit found that **no server falls in the hatched region — that combination of properties never occurs**. Everywhere else in the diagram, servers do exist. Reading the hatched region off the figure, which statement is logically EQUIVALENT to the fact it records?

options.A: No server that is cleared for remote access lacks encryption.
options.B: Every encrypted server is cleared for remote access.
options.C: At least one server cleared for remote access has encryption disabled.
options.D: Every server that stores production data has encryption enabled.
options.E: A server can be granted remote access only after encryption has first been enabled.

questions.explanation:
The hatched region is the whole crescent of circle R lying OUTSIDE circle E — that is, both the "R-only" lens and the "R∩P but not E" lens. Its emptiness means ¬∃x(Rx ∧ ¬Ex), equivalently ∀x(Rx → Ex): every remote-access server is encrypted. Recognizing that this crescent spans two subregions across three circles (not a single simple lens) is the diagram-reading step.

A — CORRECT. "No R-server lacks E" is exactly ¬∃x(Rx ∧ ¬Ex), the canonical "no P is non-Q" form of the depicted conditional.

B — Trap: illicit conversion. It states ∀x(Ex → Rx), the CONVERSE. This corresponds to a different empty region (E∖R, the left crescent), which is NOT hatched; the diagram in fact shows E-servers existing outside R, so B is both non-equivalent and false.

C — Trap: reads the hatched region as "these servers exist" instead of "this region is empty." It asserts ∃x(Rx ∧ ¬Ex) — the exact logical NEGATION of the depicted fact, not its equivalent.

D — Trap: transfers the emptiness constraint to the wrong circle, giving ∀x(Px → Ex) from the un-hatched P∖E region. Only by reading the figure (the hatched crescent belongs to R, and P clearly extends outside E un-hatched) can this be rejected; it is the key three-predicate distractor.

E — Trap: temporal/modal misreading of the conditional R→E as a sequence in time ("remote access only after encryption"). A universal conditional states co-occurrence, not chronological ordering, so this is an unrelated modal claim, not an equivalence.

questions.competency: Constraint-satisfaction over self-referential truth-value assertions (knights-and-knaves): propagating a system of mutually-referential "X is lying/telling the truth" claims under a global cardinality constraint (exactly k statements true), using contradiction detection to eliminate impossible assignments.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Propagating mutually-referential truth-value claims under a global cardinality constraint
questions.stem: At a coding competition, five judges — F, G, H, J, and K — are each either reliable (every claim they make is true) or unreliable (every claim they make is false). During deliberation each judge makes exactly one claim about a colleague. These claims are encoded ONLY in the claim graph below: a solid arrow from X to Y means "X asserts that Y is unreliable (Y lies)," and a dashed arrow from X to Y means "X asserts that Y is reliable (Y is honest)." The competition's audit log independently confirms that exactly three of the five judges are reliable. Reading the accusation network from the diagram, which three judges are the reliable ones?
questions.explanation:
The figure encodes a 4-cycle of accusations F→G→H→J→F ("X says Y lies") plus one vouch K→F ("K says F is honest"). Propagating gives two internally consistent worlds. If F is reliable: F's "G lies" is true → G unreliable → G's "H lies" is false → H reliable → H's "J lies" is true → J unreliable → J's "F lies" is false → F reliable (closes consistently); K's vouch "F is honest" is true → K reliable. That world is {F, H, K} = 3 reliable. If F is unreliable: G reliable → H unreliable → J reliable → J's "F lies" true → F unreliable (also consistent); K's vouch is false → K unreliable. That world is {G, J} = 2 reliable. Both worlds satisfy every statement, so the accusation graph alone is under-determined; the audit constraint "exactly three reliable" selects the size-3 world, giving C) F, H, K.
Trap A (F, G, H): keeps G reliable alongside the reliable accuser F, forgetting that a reliable accuser forces its target to lie (F reliable ⇒ G unreliable via edge F→G).
Trap B (G, J, K): correctly finds the alternative stable world {G, J} but pads it with K to force the count up to three, ignoring that K vouches for F, so K is unreliable in exactly the world where F is unreliable.
Trap D (F, H, J): right about F and H but mis-signs J — treats J's accusation of F as true; since F is reliable, J's "F lies" is false, so J must be unreliable, not reliable.
Trap E (G, H, K): an inconsistent splice that borrows H and K from the first world and G from the second without committing to one assignment; it violates edge G→H, since a reliable G forces H to be unreliable.

questions.competency: Negating a quantified categorical proposition: contradictory of a universal affirmative is a particular negative; distinguishing contradictory from contrary via the square of opposition.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Categorical propositions and the square of opposition
questions.skill: Negating a universal affirmative via its contradictory; distinguishing contradictory from contrary using Euler-diagram set relationships
questions.stem: A logician asserts the categorical proposition "All S are P." A colleague replies that this assertion is FALSE. The four Euler diagrams below (I, II, III, IV) each depict one possible relationship between set S and set P. Reading the diagrams, which of them represent situations that are logically consistent with the colleague's claim — that is, with "All S are P" being false?
questions.explanation: "All S are P" is a universal affirmative. Its CONTRADICTORY (not its contrary) is the particular negative "Some S are not P." By the square of opposition a proposition and its contradictory always have opposite truth values, so "All S are P" is false EXACTLY when at least one member of S lies outside P. Testing each figure: I shows S entirely inside P (S ⊆ P) — every S is a P, so the universal is TRUE and this is the one case inconsistent with its falsity, hence excluded. II (partial overlap), III (disjoint), and IV (P strictly inside S) all contain at least one S outside P, making "Some S are not P" true and the universal false. Correct answer: D (II, III, IV). Distractor traps — A: selects the single diagram where the claim is TRUE, reversing the question. B (the central trap): confuses the contradictory with the CONTRARY, reading "All S are P is false" as "No S are P is true," which matches only the disjoint diagram III. C: wrongly imports existential overlap into "Some S are not P," assuming it also requires "Some S are P," so it drops the disjoint case III. E: treats falsity as consistent with every configuration, forgetting that the subset diagram I actually makes the universal true. Only figure-reading distinguishes these; the text alone cannot say which diagram is which.

questions.competency: Manipulating conditional statements via logical equivalence — forming the contrapositive (negate both terms AND swap antecedent/consequent) and distinguishing it from the converse and inverse, i.e. understanding that P→Q is equivalent to ¬Q→¬P but not to Q→P or ¬P→¬Q.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Deriving the contrapositive of a chained implication from set-containment, and distinguishing it from converse and inverse
questions.stem: In a turbine-blade quality lab, each blade in a batch is classified by the Euler diagram shown. A region drawn entirely inside another means "every blade in the inner region also belongs to the outer region"; two regions with no overlap share no blade. Reading ONLY the containment relationships in the figure, which statement must be true for every blade in the batch?

options.A: If a blade was not Inspected, then it is not Precision-cast.
options.B: If a blade is Inspected, then it is Precision-cast.
options.C: If a blade is not Precision-cast, then it was not Inspected.
options.D: If a blade is Titanium-alloy, then it is Precision-cast.
options.E: If a blade is Ceramic-coated, then it is Titanium-alloy.

questions.explanation: The nesting encodes two conditionals: Precision-cast ⊆ Titanium-alloy gives "Cast → Titanium", and Titanium-alloy ⊆ Inspected gives "Titanium → Inspected". Chaining yields "Precision-cast → Inspected". Its contrapositive — negate BOTH terms AND swap them — is "not Inspected → not Precision-cast", which is option A. It is the only statement logically equivalent to the diagram. Traps: B is the CONVERSE of the chain (Inspected → Cast); the diagram shows the Inspected region strictly larger, so inspected blades need not be cast. C is the INVERSE (not-Cast → not-Inspected); negating without swapping is not equivalent — a Titanium-but-not-cast blade is not-cast yet still Inspected. D reverses a single containment (treats Titanium ⊆ Cast, the converse of Cast→Titanium); the cast region is strictly smaller, so it fails. E misreads the DISJOINT Ceramic-coated set as if it were nested; being disjoint from Inspected, Ceramic-coated blades are not Titanium-alloy, so the implication is false. Only A survives.

questions.competency: Constructing and extending a second-order additive recurrence (Fibonacci-type sequence, a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}) from given seeds and evaluating a specified indexed term.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Constructing and back-solving a second-order additive (Fibonacci-type) recurrence from non-initial terms
questions.stem: An engineer's assembly log records, for a modular steel truss, the number of support rods R_n installed in the n-th segment. By design each segment uses as many rods as its two immediately preceding segments combined, so R_n = R_{n-1} + R_{n-2} for every n ≥ 3. Water damage destroyed most of the log; only two intact entries survive: the 3rd segment used 11 rods and the 7th segment used 79 rods. How many rods were installed in the 5th segment?
questions.explanation:
Because the two known entries are NOT the seeds, you must recover the starting values. Let R_1 = a and R_2 = b. Expanding the recurrence gives R_3 = a + b and R_7 = 5a + 8b (the coefficients are Fibonacci numbers). The surviving data yield the system a + b = 11 and 5a + 8b = 79. Substituting a = 11 − b: 5(11 − b) + 8b = 55 + 3b = 79, so b = 8 and a = 3. Then R_4 = 19 and R_5 = 30 (option B is correct). This solution is unique in integers.

Distractor traps:
• 25 (A): solves the same 2×2 system but assigns the seeds in the wrong order (a = 8, b = 3), giving R_5 = 2(8) + 3(3) = 25 — a seed-swap error.
• 45 (C): abandons the additive rule and assumes an arithmetic progression, taking R_5 as the value midway between the knowns, (11 + 79)/2 = 45 (equivalently R_3 + 2d with common difference d = 17). This is the "sequence is arithmetic" misconception.
• 49 (D): correctly recovers the seeds but reads off the wrong index, reporting R_6 = 49 instead of R_5 — an off-by-one slip.
• 68 (E): over-generalizes the recurrence to alternate terms, wrongly assuming R_7 = R_5 + R_3 and hence R_5 = 79 − 11 = 68. The additive rule holds only for consecutive terms, so this is false (R_5 + R_3 = 41 ≠ 79).

questions.competency: Modeling a round-robin (each pair meets once) as the combination count C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 and inverting it to solve for the population size n — i.e. recognizing pairwise-counting structure and back-solving a quadratic from a total-count constraint.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Combinations and pairwise counting (complete graphs / full mesh)
questions.skill: Modeling pairwise counts as C(n,2) and back-solving for the population size from a total-count constraint
questions.stem: In a data center, the servers of a cluster are wired in a full mesh: every pair of servers is joined by exactly one direct cable, and no other cables exist. Engineers install 3 additional servers into an existing cluster and re-wire it so that the full mesh is preserved. This expansion requires exactly 27 new cables (no existing cable is removed). How many servers were in the cluster before the expansion?
questions.explanation: A full mesh of k servers uses C(k,2)=k(k-1)/2 cables. Expanding an original n by 3 servers raises the count to C(n+3,2), so the number of NEW cables is the difference of two combinations: C(n+3,2) - C(n,2) = [(n+3)(n+2) - n(n-1)]/2 = (6n+6)/2 = 3n+3. Notice the n^2 terms cancel, so the constraint is linear: 3n+3 = 27, giving n = 8. Structurally, the 3 new servers add 3n cables to the original servers plus C(3,2)=3 cables among themselves: 3n+3 = 27. Check: C(11,2) - C(8,2) = 55 - 28 = 27. Distractor traps: (A) 6 comes from modeling the new cables as 3(n+3)=27 — treating each new server as connecting to all n+3 machines, failing to exclude itself and over-counting. (B) 7 comes from 3(n+2)=27 — cabling each new server to every OTHER machine, which counts the 3 cables among the new servers twice. (D) 9 comes from 3n=27 — counting only new-to-original cables and forgetting the C(3,2)=3 cables among the three new servers. (E) 11 solves the model correctly but reports the expanded size n+3 instead of the original count. Only n=8 produces exactly 27 added cables; the neighbouring values give 21, 24, 30, and 36, so no distractor is also-correct.

questions.competency: Worst-case guarantee reasoning via the pigeonhole/extremal principle: to guarantee representation of every category, the solver must model the adversarial worst case — an opponent hands out every item from the largest categories first, deliberately withholding the last-needed category — then add one. The general skill is recognizing that a "minimum to ensure at least one of each" question is solved by summing the counts of all-but-the-smallest-necessary categories (here the two most-populous colors) and adding 1, rather than by averaging or by best-case counting.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Worst-case extremal reasoning with a required-subset filter
questions.stem: An automated pick-and-place machine empties a sealed hopper by drawing components one at a time in random order; drawn parts cannot be returned. The hopper holds 20 resistors, 15 capacitors, 12 diodes, 9 transistors, and 6 relays. To assemble one control board the machine needs at least one diode, at least one transistor, and at least one relay — resistors and capacitors are not used on this particular board. What is the minimum number of components the machine must draw to be CERTAIN it has collected everything required for one control board?
questions.explanation:
The guarantee is set by the largest possible "incomplete" draw — a draw still missing an entire required type. Only diodes, transistors, and relays are required; resistors and capacitors, though present, must all be pulled in the adversarial worst case because they carry no requirement. To stall longest, the worst case withholds the required type with the FEWEST parts — relays (6). The machine could then draw every other component: 20 resistors + 15 capacitors + 12 diodes + 9 transistors = 56 parts, still with zero relays. The 57th draw must be a relay, and at that point the diodes and transistors are already in hand, so 57 guarantees a full set. B (57) is correct.

Trap map:
- A) 36 = 20 + 15 + 1: blindly applied the "two largest categories + 1" template to the two most-populous bins (resistors, capacitors) without noticing those categories aren't required at all.
- C) 22 = 12 + 9 + 1: applied the classic template only to the required types, forgetting that the 35 non-required parts can (and in the worst case will) be drawn before a complete set appears.
- D) 51 = 62 − 12 + 1: modeled the worst case correctly in form but withheld the LARGEST required type (diodes, 12) instead of the smallest — the extremal choice is inverted, so it undercounts.
- E) 56 = 62 − 6: correct worst-case model but forgot the final "+1"; 56 parts is exactly the biggest draw that can still be missing a relay, so it does NOT yet guarantee the set.

questions.competency: Interpreting an "only" statement as a conditional and extracting the correct necessary-vs-sufficient relationship: "Only P can be Q" means Q implies P, so P is necessary (not sufficient) for Q.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Conditional reasoning: necessary vs. sufficient conditions and set logic
questions.skill: Translating set-containment (nesting) in an Euler diagram into correct necessary/sufficient ("only ... can ...") relationships, distinguishing necessity from sufficiency and containment direction.
questions.stem: A factory classifies its components using the Euler diagram below. Each labelled region is the set of components of that type. Reading only the containment and overlap shown in the diagram, which one of the following statements is necessarily true?

options.A: Being made of steel is a necessary condition for being aerospace-grade.
options.B: Being hardened is a sufficient condition for being aerospace-grade.
options.C: Being aerospace-grade is a necessary condition for being hardened.
options.D: Being coated is a sufficient condition for being made of steel.
options.E: Being a polymer is a necessary condition for being coated.

questions.explanation: The diagram shows the strict nesting Aerospace-grade ⊆ Hardened ⊆ Steel, a Polymer set disjoint from Steel, and a Coated set that overlaps both Steel and Polymer while extending outside both. "Only P can be Q" / "P is necessary for Q" means Q ⊆ P. A (correct): by transitivity of the two nestings, every aerospace-grade component lies inside Steel, so Aerospace ⊆ Steel — steel is necessary for aerospace-grade. This requires reading BOTH nestings, not the text. B (trap — the core necessary/sufficient confusion): the same nesting makes "only hardened components can be aerospace-grade" true (hardened is NECESSARY), but Hardened has a large non-aerospace region, so being hardened does NOT guarantee aerospace-grade; it is not sufficient. C (containment-direction reversal): sufficiency/necessity flipped — this would require Hardened ⊆ Aerospace, but the nesting runs the other way. D (overlap read as subset): Coated extends outside Steel, so a coated component need not be steel; sufficiency fails. E (overlap read as necessity): Coated has a region outside Polymer (e.g. steel-coated components), so being coated does not require being a polymer. Each distractor encodes a distinct misreading of the same figure, and none can be eliminated without actually reading the nesting.

questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Similar triangles and the intercept (Thales) theorem in a trapezoid
questions.skill: Applying the intercept theorem and similar-triangle proportionality to intersecting/parallel lines to compute an unknown length
questions.stem: In the trapezoid shown, the two horizontal sides are parallel and their lengths are the values marked in the figure. The diagonals of the trapezoid intersect at point O. A segment EF is drawn through O parallel to those two horizontal sides, with its endpoints E and F lying on the two slanted sides. Using only the measurements given in the figure, what is the length of EF?
questions.explanation: The two horizontal sides are AB = 6 (top) and CD = 12 (bottom). Because AB ∥ CD, triangles AOB and COD are similar, so AO/OC = AB/CD = 6/12 = 1/2; thus O divides each diagonal in ratio 1:2, i.e. AO/AC = 1/3 and CO/CA = 2/3. Segment EF passes through O parallel to the bases, so it splits into EO and OF. In triangle ACD, EO ∥ CD gives EO = CD·(AO/AC) = 12·(1/3) = 4. In triangle CAB, OF ∥ AB gives OF = AB·(CO/CA) = 6·(2/3) = 4. Hence EF = EO + OF = 4 + 4 = 8 (this is the harmonic mean 2·6·12/(6+12) of the parallel sides). Distractor traps: (A) 4 stops after computing only one half, EO (or OF), forgetting the segment has two pieces. (B) 6 assumes EF simply equals the shorter parallel side, imagining the diagonal-intersection segment collapses to the top base. (D) 6√2 = √(6·12) applies the geometric mean, misremembering the similar-triangle relation as the altitude-on-hypotenuse (mean-proportional) result. (E) 9 = (6+12)/2 uses the arithmetic mean, confusing EF with the midsegment (median) of the trapezoid, which does average the bases but does not pass through the diagonal intersection O.

questions.competency: Computing the angle between clock hands via relative angular rates and proportional reasoning about rotational position.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Clock-hand angles via relative angular rates and proportional reasoning
questions.stem: An analogue clock is shown at a certain instant. The minute hand lies exactly on one of the small (one-minute) tick marks, and the hour hand lies between two numerals. Read both hand positions from the figure to determine the time being shown, then find θ, the smaller angle between the two hands (marked by the dashed arc). What is θ?
questions.explanation:
Reading the figure: the minute hand sits on the tick 4 marks past the numeral 4, i.e. the 24-minute mark, so the minute value is 24; the hour hand lies between 8 and 9 (past the 8), so the completed hour is 8. The time is 8:24.

Angular positions (measured clockwise from the 12): each minute is 6°, so the minute hand is at 24 × 6 = 144°. The hour hand advances 30° per hour AND a proportional 0.5° per minute (30° ÷ 60 min), so it is at 8 × 30 + 24 × 0.5 = 240 + 12 = 252°. The smaller angle between them is |252 − 144| = 108°, which matches the dashed (minor) arc. Correct = C.

Distractor traps:
A) 90° — crude numeral-gap count: rounds both hands to the nearest numerals (minute → 5, hour → 8) and multiplies the 3 whole gaps by 30°, ignoring that each hand sits partway between marks.
B) 96° — reads the minute hand correctly (144°) but leaves the hour hand exactly on the 8 (240°): |240 − 144|. This ignores the hour hand's proportional drift of 0.5°/min — the single most common error and the reason the figure shows the hour hand clearly past the 8.
D) 120° — applies the hour-hand drift at the wrong rate, 1°/min instead of 0.5°/min (hour at 240 + 24 = 264°): |264 − 144|. Confuses the hour-hand rate with the minute-scale.
E) 252° — reports the reflex (major) angle, 360 − 108 = 252° (numerically also the hour hand's raw bearing from 12), failing to take the smaller angle indicated by the dashed arc.

questions.competency: Counting permutations under two simultaneous constraints: a relative-order condition resolved by symmetry (half of all permutations have A before D) combined with an adjacency restriction resolved by complementary counting via the glue-block method.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: relative-order symmetry (divide by k!) combined with adjacency restriction via complementary counting and the glue-block method
questions.stem: A curator hangs 6 distinct paintings in a single row along a corridor. Three of them form a triptych and, to preserve its narrative, must hang so that panel I is somewhere to the left of panel II, and panel II is somewhere to the left of panel III (the three panels need not be adjacent to one another). Two of the remaining paintings are lit by heat-sensitive lamps and must not hang next to each other. The last painting has no restriction. In how many different orders can the 6 paintings be hung?
questions.explanation: Two constraints act on the 6 items. Relative order (by symmetry): of the 6! = 720 total arrangements, the three triptych panels I, II, III fall into each of their 3! = 6 possible relative orders equally often, so exactly 720/6 = 120 arrangements have them in the required order I–II–III. Non-adjacency (by complement/glue-block): from these 120, remove those where the two fragile paintings are adjacent. Glue the fragile pair into one block (2 internal orders) to get 5 units; among the 5 units the three panels must still keep their fixed relative order, giving 5!/3! = 20 unit-arrangements, times 2 internal orders = 40 forbidden arrangements. Answer: 120 − 40 = 80 (B).\n\nTrap analysis: (A) 40 is the count of forbidden (fragile-adjacent) arrangements — the student computed the complement but forgot to subtract it from 120. (C) 100 forgets the factor 2 for the internal order of the glued fragile pair, counting only 20 forbidden arrangements (120 − 20). (D) 120 applies only the triptych order constraint and ignores the non-adjacency rule entirely. (E) 240 mistakenly treats the three-panel ordering as a single before/after pair (dividing by 2 instead of 3! = 6): 720/2 = 360 with forbidden 240/2 = 120, giving 360 − 120 = 240 — punishing the reflex of 'relative order means halve.'

questions.competency: Counting ordered arrangements without repetition — applying the multiplication principle / permutations P(n,k) to select and order k distinct items from n (here forming sequences of distinct digits), including correctly treating positions as ordered and elements as non-repeating.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Counting ordered arrangements without repetition under structural constraints
questions.stem: A laboratory sample tube is labelled with a 5-symbol code read left to right. The first two positions are letters chosen from {A, B, C, D} and the last three positions are digits chosen from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. No letter may repeat and no digit may repeat within a code. A code is valid only if its very first symbol (the leftmost letter) is NOT A. How many valid codes are possible?
questions.explanation:
Count the letter block and digit block separately, then multiply. Letters: two distinct letters from {A,B,C,D} placed in ordered positions 1 and 2, with position 1 not equal to A. Position 1 has 3 choices (B, C, or D); position 2 then has 3 remaining letters (any of the other three, including A). So letter arrangements = 3 x 3 = 9. Digits: three distinct digits from six in ordered positions = P(6,3) = 6 x 5 x 4 = 120. Total valid codes = 9 x 120 = 1080 (option A).

Distractor traps: (B) 1440 = 12 x 120 ignores the 'first symbol not A' restriction entirely, using the full P(4,2)=12 for the letters — the classic 'forgot the constraint' path. (C) 2160 = P(4,2) x 6^3 / ... actually 2160 = 18 x 120 double-counts by treating position-1 as 3 choices but position-2 as 6 (mixing letters with digit count) — a slot-confusion error. More cleanly, 2160 also arises as 12 x 180: using P(4,2)=12 letters AND wrongly computing digits as 6 x 5 x 6, i.e., forgetting the second digit-repetition removal. (D) 1728 = 12 x 144 treats digits with one repetition allowed and keeps all 12 letter pairs — combines two independent slips. (E) 720 = 6 x 120 subtracts too aggressively: it counts only 6 letter arrangements by forbidding A from BOTH letter positions (over-applying the restriction to position 2 as well) instead of only position 1, then multiplies by the correct P(6,3)=120.

questions.competency: Modeling pairwise interactions as unordered combinations C(n,2) and solving the resulting equation n(n-1)/2 = k for n — i.e., recognizing a "count all distinct pairs" situation and inverting the triangular/combination formula.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Modeling pairwise links as C(n,2) and inverting the triangular formula to solve for n, applied to a partitioned (disjoint-clique) structure read from a figure
questions.stem: An IT auditor mapped every direct communication link inside a company. The complete map is shown in the diagram, and it contains 55 links in total. Using only the structure shown, how many people work at the company altogether?
questions.explanation:
The figure is essential: it shows the network is split into two SEPARATE fully-connected teams with NO links crossing between them, and that the management team has exactly 5 members. Management is a complete graph on 5 people, contributing C(5,2)=10 links. The staff team is a separate complete group of unknown size s, contributing C(s,2) links. Since the teams are disjoint, total = 10 + C(s,2) = 55, so C(s,2)=45. Inverting the triangular/combination formula: s(s-1)/2=45 → s^2-s-90=0 → s=10. Total people = 5 managers + 10 staff = 15 (B).

Distractor traps:
- A) 13: miscounts by treating the map as if only 45 staff links matter and pairing with a wrong small manager figure / general off-by-two arithmetic slip when adding teams — does not follow the exact 5+10 split.
- C) 11: partition-blind — ignores that the figure shows two DISJOINT cliques and treats all 55 links as one single complete graph, solving C(n,2)=55 → n=11. This is the key figure-reading failure the item targets.
- D) 10: correctly inverts the staff cluster (C(s,2)=45 → s=10) but forgets to add the 5 managers, reporting the staff subgroup as the whole company.
- E) 16: fails to subtract the 10 management links before inverting — assigns all 55 links to the staff group, C(s,2)=55 → s=11, then adds 5 → 16.

Only B correctly reads the disjoint-clique structure from the figure, removes the management edges, inverts C(s,2)=45, and recombines the two teams.

questions.competency: Counting arrangements of n distinct objects into n labeled positions: recognizing that placing 15 distinct items into 15 fixed cells is a permutation of all elements (n!), and that the grid's 3×5 shape is structurally irrelevant because every cell is a distinct labeled slot. The elite version should force genuine reasoning by adding constraints (e.g., adjacency/row-block/forbidden-position or symmetry conditions) so the count is no longer a bare n! recall but requires decomposing the arrangement into cases or applying the multiplication/division principle under restrictions.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Counting arrangements of distinct objects in labeled positions under a restriction via the multiplication principle
questions.stem: A laboratory technician mounts 6 distinct diagnostic instruments into a rack of 6 labeled bays arranged in 2 rows and 3 columns, with each bay holding exactly one instrument. For correct signal routing, the calibrator and the reference unit must be installed in the same column (in either order); the other four instruments have no restriction. In how many different ways can all 6 instruments be mounted in the rack?
questions.explanation: Every bay is a distinct labeled slot, so without restriction there are 6! = 720 mountings; the constraint is what earns the difficulty. Decompose by the multiplication principle: (1) choose the shared column for the calibrator and reference — 3 ways; (2) order those two units within that column's 2 cells — 2 ways; (3) place the remaining 4 instruments in the 4 remaining bays — 4! = 24 ways. Total = 3 × 2 × 24 = 144. (Check: after the calibrator is placed, the reference must land in the 1 of the 5 remaining bays that shares its column, so exactly 720 × 1/5 = 144.) Distractor traps: A) 720 = 6! ignores the same-column constraint entirely — the bare-permutation recall trap the competency targets. B) 288 misreads "same column" as "same row": a row holds 3 cells, giving 2 rows × P(3,2)=6 × 4! = 288, confusing the capacity of a column (2 cells) with that of a row (3 cells). D) 72 = 3 × 4! correctly picks the column and arranges the rest but forgets the pair can sit in 2 internal orders. E) 48 = 2 × 4! orders the pair but fixes one specific column, forgetting the 3 possible column choices.

questions.competency: Constructing the contrapositive of a conditional statement — recognizing that "P → Q" is logically equivalent to "¬Q → ¬P", requiring correct negation of antecedent/consequent (including a negated consequent) and swapping their roles. More broadly, reasoning about logical equivalences among a conditional, its converse, inverse, and contrapositive.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Contrapositive of a chained conditional read from an implication diagram
questions.stem: The directed diagram below records the ONLY implications known to hold in a pump-control system, where an arrow "→" means "logically implies". Assuming every implication shown is true, which one of the following statements is GUARANTEED to be true?

options.A: If the intake sensor is not triggered, then no overflow warning is shown.
options.B: If an overflow warning is shown, then the intake sensor is triggered.
options.C: If the drain valve is open, then an overflow warning is shown.
options.D: If no overflow warning is shown, then the intake sensor is not triggered.
options.E: If the intake sensor is triggered, then the drain valve is open.

questions.explanation:
The figure gives two links: P ("intake sensor triggered") → ¬Q ("drain valve NOT open"), and ¬Q → T ("overflow warning shown"). Chaining them yields P → T, whose contrapositive ¬T → ¬P is: "If no overflow warning is shown, then the intake sensor is not triggered" — option D, the only guaranteed statement.
A is the INVERSE of the chain (¬P → ¬T): negating without swapping is not valid. B is the CONVERSE (T → P): swapping without a valid basis. C drops the negation on the middle node, reading Q → T instead of the given ¬Q → T — the diagram never asserts anything about the valve being OPEN implying a warning. E also mishandles the middle node's negation, reading P → Q; in fact the figure states P → ¬Q, so E is not merely unproven but contradicted. Only D correctly negates BOTH ends of the composed conditional and swaps their roles, so the figure (which alone tells you which node is negated and how the arrows chain) is required to answer.

questions.competency: Determining the minimum size of the intersection of two subsets given their cardinalities and the size of the enclosing universe — i.e. inclusion-exclusion / pigeonhole bounding of overlap (|A∩B| ≥ |A|+|B|−|U|).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Determining the minimum size of the intersection of two subsets given their cardinalities and the size of the enclosing universe (inclusion-exclusion / pigeonhole bounding of overlap)
questions.stem: At a summer STEM camp, every participant is represented exactly once inside the bounded rectangle (the whole camp) shown in the diagram. Circle R contains those who attended the robotics workshop and circle C contains those who attended the coding workshop; the count in each circle, the total camp size, and the number who attended neither workshop are all marked on the figure. Reasoning only from the values shown, at least how many participants must have attended BOTH workshops?
questions.explanation: Read from the figure: U = 120, |R| = 78, |C| = 66, and 18 attend neither workshop. Those 18 sit outside both circles, so R ∪ C can occupy at most 120 − 18 = 102 participants. Since |R ∪ C| = |R| + |C| − |R ∩ C| = 144 − |R ∩ C| ≤ 102, the overlap is forced to be at least 144 − 102 = 42. This requires combining the complement/"neither" region with the inclusion–exclusion bound — the key selective step. (B) 42 is correct. (A) 24 comes from applying |R|+|C|−|U| = 144 − 120 and ignoring that the 18 outsiders shrink the usable pool. (C) 6 adds the 18 to the universe instead of removing it from it: 144 − (120+18). (D) 60 subtracts the 18 twice, treating 144 − (120 − 36). (E) 66 confuses the *minimum forced* overlap with the *maximum possible* overlap, which equals the smaller set |C| = 66 (an upper bound, not the answer). Every distractor stays at or below 66, the true ceiling min(|R|,|C|), so none can be eliminated without doing the reasoning.

questions.competency: Combining individual work rates as additive reciprocals to find joint completion time.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining individual work rates as additive reciprocals to find joint completion time
questions.stem: Two technicians, Elif and Marco, service turbines. Working simultaneously, they can service one turbine in 4 hours. One morning, however, Elif started alone and worked for the first 3 hours; she then handed over to Marco, who worked alone and needed a further 6 hours to finish servicing that same turbine. Assuming each technician always works at her or his own constant rate, how long would Marco take to service one turbine entirely on his own?
questions.explanation: Let e and m be Elif's and Marco's rates (turbines per hour). Two facts must be combined. (1) Working together: e + m = 1/4. (2) The phased day: Elif worked 3 h and Marco 6 h to complete exactly one turbine, so 3e + 6m = 1. Substitute e = 1/4 - m into (2): 3(1/4 - m) + 6m = 1 -> 3/4 + 3m = 1 -> 3m = 1/4 -> m = 1/12. Marco alone needs 1 / (1/12) = 12 hours (D). Each distractor is a specific error. A (6 h) is Elif's solo time, e = 1/4 - 1/12 = 1/6 -> 6 h: the solver correctly builds the system but reports the wrong technician. B (8 h) assumes the two rates are equal, splitting the combined 1/4 evenly into 1/8 each, so 8 h per person -- this ignores the phased data entirely. C (9 h) simply adds the two phase durations 3 + 6 and misreads that elapsed time as Marco's solo time. E (24 h) misuses the combined rate as Elif's individual rate: it assumes Elif does 3 x 1/4 = 3/4 of the turbine in her 3 hours, leaving 1/4 for Marco in 6 hours -> 24 h. Only D correctly treats the rates as additive reciprocals AND uses the partial-work equation to isolate Marco's rate.

questions.competency: Quantifier equivalence in categorical logic: recognizing that a universal-affirmative obligation is equivalent to the negated existential (∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x)) and separating true equivalence from contraries, subcontraries, and unrelated conditionals.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Categorical logic and the square of opposition
questions.skill: Reading set relations from an Euler diagram and translating an entailed universal-affirmative into its equivalent negated-existential form, while rejecting contrary, contradictory, converse and inverse claims
questions.stem:
The Euler diagram represents the members of a robotics club. The outer rectangle is the set of all club members. The large circle is the set of members who passed the safety test, and the smaller circle is the set of certified operators. A cross (×) marks a member who is neither, and the shaded band shows members who lie inside the large circle but outside the small one.

Reading only the relationships fixed by the diagram, exactly one of the following statements about certified operators is logically GUARANTEED to be true. Which one?

options.A: Every club member who passed the safety test is a certified operator.
options.B: No certified operator failed the safety test.
options.C: Some certified operators failed the safety test.
options.D: No certified operator passed the safety test.
options.E: Every club member who is not a certified operator failed the safety test.

questions.explanation:
The diagram fixes the small circle (certified operators, C) entirely inside the large circle (passed the safety test, P), with a non-empty shaded band inside P but outside C, and at least one member (×) outside both. The only relationship this forces is C ⊆ P, i.e. the universal affirmative ∀x(Cx → Px), "every certified operator passed."

Correct — B: "No certified operator failed" is ¬∃x(Cx ∧ ¬Px), the exact negated-existential equivalent of ∀x(Cx → Px). This is the competency being tested: ∀x P(x) ≡ ¬∃x ¬P(x). Because C ⊆ P, no point of C can lie outside P, so B is guaranteed.

A — Converse error: asserts ∀x(Px → Cx). The shaded band (in P, outside C) is exactly a counterexample; the diagram never makes P ⊆ C.

C — Contradictory: asserts ∃x(Cx ∧ ¬Px). This is the direct negation of the entailed universal; since C is wholly inside P, no such member exists, so it is false, not merely unproven.

D — Contrary: asserts ∀x(Cx → ¬Px), "no certified operator passed." It confuses the entailed universal with its contrary (reversing which set contains which); the diagram shows the opposite, C inside P.

E — Inverse error: asserts ∀x(¬Cx → ¬Px), "every non-certified member failed." The shaded band is a member who is not certified yet passed, a direct counterexample; an entailment about C→P says nothing that forces ¬C→¬P.

Only B survives, and it survives precisely as the ¬∃ restatement of the universal the figure entails.

questions.competency: Recognizing the logical equivalence between a conditional and its contrapositive (¬Q → ¬P), and distinguishing contrapositive from converse and inverse.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Contrapositive equivalence vs converse/inverse across an implication chain with a branching cause
questions.stem: In a hydraulic monitoring system, four conditions V, S, P, and A are related as shown in the diagram, where each arrow X → Y means "if X is true, then Y is true." An arrow expresses only that one-directional conditional: it does not mean Y can arise solely from X, and it is not a biconditional. Assuming ONLY the relationships drawn, which one of the following statements is logically guaranteed to be true?

options.A: If the alarm does not trigger, then valve V is not open.
options.B: If the alarm triggers, then valve V is open.
options.C: If valve V is not open, then the alarm does not trigger.
options.D: If the supply is not active, then the alarm does not trigger.
options.E: If valve V is not open, then the line pressure does not drop.

questions.explanation:
The diagram gives three conditionals: V→P (valve open ⇒ pressure drops), S→P (supply active ⇒ pressure drops), and P→A (pressure drops ⇒ alarm triggers). Chaining the V-branch gives V→P→A, i.e. V→A. The contrapositive of V→A is ¬A→¬V, which is logically equivalent to it — so (A) "if the alarm does not trigger, then valve V is not open" is guaranteed. This requires reading the arrow directions in the figure (a two-step chain) and then contraposing; it is unsolvable from the stem text alone.

Each distractor encodes a specific error:
B) A→V is the CONVERSE of V→A, not the contrapositive. It fails because P (hence A) can be produced by the S-branch instead of V — the alarm can fire with the valve closed. Choosing it means confusing contrapositive with converse.
C) ¬V→¬A is the INVERSE of the chain V→A. It fails for the same branch reason: with V false, S can still drive P→A. This is the classic contrapositive/inverse confusion.
D) ¬S→¬A negates the antecedent of the S-branch (inverse form of S→A) and treats a sufficient cause as necessary; with S false, V can still trigger the alarm. Trap: forgetting A has a second possible cause.
E) ¬V→¬P is the INVERSE of the first link V→P; with V false, S can still make P true. Trap: contraposing the wrong link and ignoring the branch feeding P.
Only (A) contraposes a valid forward chain, so it alone is forced by the diagram.

questions.competency: Combining additive reciprocal work-rates (1/t1 + 1/t2 = 1/t_together) to solve for an unknown individual completion time given the combined rate and one worker's rate.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining additive reciprocal work-rates to solve for an unknown individual completion time
questions.stem: On an automated assembly line two robots, R1 and R2, work simultaneously and together assemble one complete batch of components in 6 hours. At the start of a certain shift both robots begin a fresh batch together, but after exactly 4 hours R2 is pulled offline for maintenance. R1 keeps working alone and finishes the remaining components in a further 5 hours. If R2 had been required to assemble an identical batch entirely on its own, how long would it have taken?
questions.explanation:
The combined rate is 1/6 batch per hour. In the 4 hours worked together they finish 4 × 1/6 = 2/3 of the batch, so 1/3 remains. R1 completes that 1/3 alone in 5 hours, so R1's solo rate is (1/3)/5 = 1/15 batch per hour (R1 alone = 15 h). R2's rate is therefore 1/6 − 1/15 = 5/30 − 2/30 = 3/30 = 1/10, so R2 alone takes 10 hours (B).

Distractor traps: (A) 9 h subtracts times instead of rates (t_R1 − t_together = 15 − 6), a common rate/time confusion. (C) 15 h correctly finds a solo rate but reports R1's time — the robot still working — instead of R2's, the requested one. (D) 18 h treats R1's total time on the job (4 h joint + 5 h solo = 9 h) as R1's solo completion time, then does 1/6 − 1/9 = 1/18. (E) 30 h ignores the fraction-of-work step and treats R1's 5-hour finish as its whole-batch solo time (rate 1/5), giving |1/6 − 1/5| = 1/30. Only 10 h uses the correct sequence: combined rate → work done in the shared interval → remaining fraction → R1's true solo rate → subtract reciprocals for R2.

questions.competency: Negating a universal affirmative quantified statement: recognizing that the falsity of "All A are B" (∀x: A→B) is logically equivalent to "At least one A is not B" (∃x: A ∧ ¬B), and distinguishing this genuine contradictory from the too-strong contrary ("No A are B" / "All A are not B") and from irrelevant/converse distractors.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Quantifiers and Euler diagrams — negating a universal affirmative
questions.skill: Recognizing that the falsity of "All X are P" means ∃x(X ∧ ¬P), and selecting the Euler configurations consistent with a compound existential condition while rejecting the too-strong contrary
questions.stem: In a quality-control audit, each turbine blade is recorded on two properties: whether it is made of alloy-X (set X) and whether it passed inspection (set P). An inspector claims: "All alloy-X blades passed inspection." When the records are opened, TWO facts turn out to hold simultaneously: (1) the inspector's claim is FALSE, and (2) at least one alloy-X blade did pass inspection. The five Euler diagrams above show every possible way the sets X and P could relate. Exactly which of the diagrams are consistent with BOTH recorded facts?
questions.explanation: Two conditions must hold together. Fact (1) "All X are P" is false means ∃x(X ∧ ¬P): there must be an alloy-X blade OUTSIDE P — an X-only region. Fact (2) means ∃x(X ∧ P): the X and P circles must overlap. Testing each diagram: I (X⊂P) — every X is in P, so the claim is TRUE; violates (1). II (P⊂X) — the ring of X outside P satisfies (1), and the inner P region inside X satisfies (2); valid. III (partial overlap) — the left crescent gives X∧¬P for (1), the lens gives X∧P for (2); valid. IV (disjoint) — satisfies (1) but no blade is in both, so (2) fails. V (X=P) — every X is P, claim TRUE; violates (1). Only II and III satisfy both, so A. Trap B adds IV, the classic error of treating "claim is false" as the ONLY condition and forgetting fact (2) forces an overlap. Trap C reads "the claim is false" as the too-strong contrary "NO alloy-X blade passed," collapsing to the disjoint diagram. Trap D selects exactly the two diagrams where the claim is TRUE, inverting the truth value. Trap E accepts only symmetric two-sided overlap and overlooks II, failing to see that P nested inside X still leaves an X-only region of alloy-X blades that did not pass.

questions.competency: Combinatorial counting of unordered pairs — recognizing that a round-robin schedule yields C(n,2) = n(n-1)/2 matches and inverting that relation to solve for n (the "handshake"/complete-graph edge-count principle).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combinatorial counting of unordered pairs via incremental complete-graph edge counting (round-robin / handshake), and inverting the relation to solve for n
questions.stem: A regional volleyball league is run as a single round-robin: during the season every pair of teams plays each other exactly once. For the coming season the league admits 3 additional teams, and the season is again played as a single round-robin among all the teams. As a result, the total number of matches played in the season increases by 45 compared with this season. How many teams played in the league this season, before the expansion?
questions.explanation:
Let n be the current number of teams. Adding 3 teams creates exactly the new edges of the complete graph: each of the 3 new teams plays each of the n existing teams (3n matches), plus the 3 new teams play a round-robin among themselves (C(3,2) = 3 matches). So the increase is 3n + 3. Setting 3n + 3 = 45 gives n = 14. Check: C(17,2) − C(14,2) = 136 − 91 = 45. Correct answer D (14).

Distractor traps, each a distinct error:
- E) 15: forgot the matches among the 3 new teams, solving only 3n = 45 (misses the internal C(3,2) = 3 edges).
- C) 13: counted the new-vs-new games as ordered pairs, 3×2 = 6 instead of C(3,2) = 3, giving 3n + 6 = 45.
- B) 12: counted the new-vs-new games as 3×3 = 9 (using k² instead of k(k−1)/2), giving 3n + 9 = 45.
- A) 10: misread "increases by 45" as "the season has 45 matches in total" and solved the direct handshake equation C(n,2) = 45 → n(n−1) = 90 → n = 10, ignoring the incremental structure.

questions.competency: Recognizing logical equivalence of a conditional statement via its contrapositive and discriminating it from the non-equivalent converse and inverse.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Conditional statements: contrapositive equivalence vs converse/inverse, combined with hypothetical syllogism
questions.skill: Recognizing logical equivalence of a conditional statement via its contrapositive and discriminating it from the non-equivalent converse and inverse
questions.stem:
An avionics engineer models a satellite's telemetry chain as the directed implication network shown below. Each proposition is a node, and an arrow X → Y means "if X is true, then Y is true." Only the four implications that are actually drawn — together with whatever validly follows from them — may be assumed true.

Nodes: P = the primary transmitter is on; T = the backup transmitter is on; Q = the carrier signal is present; R = the downlink is locked; S = the ground station receives data.

Which one of the following statements is logically equivalent to an implication that the network guarantees, and is therefore itself guaranteed to be true?

options.A: If the ground station does not receive data, then the primary transmitter is not on.
options.B: If the ground station receives data, then the primary transmitter is on.
options.C: If the backup transmitter is not on, then the ground station does not receive data.
options.D: If the backup transmitter is not on, then the primary transmitter is not on.
options.E: If the primary transmitter is not on, then the downlink is not locked.

questions.explanation:
The network supplies four arrows: P⇒Q, Q⇒R, R⇒S, and T⇒Q. Chaining the first three by hypothetical syllogism gives a guaranteed implication P⇒S ("if the primary transmitter is on, the ground station receives data"). A conditional is logically equivalent ONLY to its contrapositive, so the guaranteed equivalent statement is ¬S⇒¬P — option A. It cannot be read off a single arrow; the student must trace the full P→Q→R→S path in the figure and then contrapose.

Each distractor encodes a distinct error, and every one requires the figure to reject:
- B is the converse (S⇒P): it assumes receiving data requires the primary, but the figure's T→Q→R→S branch lets the backup produce data on its own, so S does not imply P.
- C is the inverse of T⇒S (equivalently the converse S⇒T): it treats the backup as necessary, ignoring the parallel primary path P⇒S that also reaches S.
- D asserts P⇒T: it invents a connection between the two independent source nodes — no arrow or path links P and T in the figure.
- E asserts R⇒P (the converse of the derived P⇒R): a locked downlink does not force the primary on, because the backup can supply the carrier that locks the downlink.

Only A is the contrapositive of a genuinely guaranteed implication; B, C, D, and E are all converse/inverse-type statements that the one-directional arrow structure does not support.

questions.competency: Recognizing the logical equivalence of a conditional and its contrapositive, and rejecting converse/inverse fallacies.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Chaining conditionals (hypothetical syllogism) and identifying the logically equivalent contrapositive while rejecting converse/inverse and premature-stop traps
questions.stem: The diagram shows every if-then rule wired into an automated hydraulic controller (no other rules may be assumed). By following the arrows, the network entails exactly one conditional linking sensor A directly to channel C. Reading the arrow directions in the figure, which statement is LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT to that entailed A-to-C conditional?

options.A: If channel C does not fill, then sensor A did not trigger.
options.B: If channel C fills, then sensor A triggered.
options.C: If sensor A does not trigger, then channel C does not fill.
options.D: If pump B does not run, then sensor A did not trigger.
options.E: If drain D opens, then channel C fills.

questions.explanation: Reading the figure, the only path from A to C is A→B and B→C, so by hypothetical syllogism the network entails the composite conditional "if A then C" (if sensor A triggers, channel C fills). A conditional is logically equivalent to its contrapositive, so "if A then C" ≡ "if not C then not A." Option A states exactly this contrapositive — correct. Option B is the CONVERSE of the A→C rule (C→A): a classic converse fallacy. Option C is the INVERSE (¬A→¬C): negating both parts without reversing — the inverse fallacy. Option D is the trap of stopping the chain one link too early: ¬B→¬A is the contrapositive of the single arrow A→B, a true statement in the network but equivalent to A→B, NOT to the asked A-to-C conditional, so it is not the required equivalent. Option E misreads the negated arrow D→NOT C (it even reverses its meaning to D→C), contradicting the figure. Only A is the contrapositive of the specific composite conditional, so it is the unique logically equivalent statement.

questions.competency: Negating a universal affirmative categorical proposition — recognizing that the contradictory of "All S are P" is "Some S are not P" (square of opposition / logical negation of quantified statements)
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Negating a universal affirmative (A) proposition via the square of opposition; identifying its contradictory O-proposition and its forced Venn region
questions.stem: In the Venn diagram, the left circle S is the set of sensors that triggered the alarm during a plant test, and the right circle P is the set of sensors that a later inspection found to be faulty. The four regions created by the two circles are marked ①, ②, ③ and ④ as shown. An engineer had asserted: "Every sensor that triggered the alarm was faulty." The inspection report proves this assertion to be FALSE. Reading the region labels off the diagram, exactly one of the following statements is GUARANTEED to be true. Which one?

options.A: Region ① contains at least one sensor
options.C: Region ② contains at least one sensor
options.D: Region ③ contains at least one sensor
options.E: Region ④ contains at least one sensor

questions.explanation: The engineer's claim is the A-proposition "All S are P" (every alarm-sensor is faulty). Its contradictory — the ONLY thing guaranteed when an A-proposition is false — is the O-proposition "Some S are not P": at least one sensor that triggered the alarm is not faulty. Reading the diagram, "in S but not in P" is precisely the left crescent, region ①, so region ① must contain at least one sensor. Correct: A. Trap B ("Region ② is empty") is the contrary "No S are P" (S∩P empty); negating "all" only requires ONE exception, it does not force zero overlap — over-negation from the O to the E form. Trap C ("Region ② nonempty" = Some S are P) wrongly assumes the two sets must still overlap; but the falsity of "All S are P" is fully consistent with S and P being disjoint, so an overlapping sensor is not guaranteed. Trap D ("Region ③ nonempty" = Some P are not S) swaps the subject and predicate — it describes faulty sensors that did not alarm, which the claim says nothing about. Trap E ("Region ④ nonempty") concerns sensors outside both sets and is entirely irrelevant to the claim. Only region ①, the S-and-not-P region, is forced, which is why the figure is essential: the statements are stated purely as region labels.

questions.competency: Deductive symbol-mapping in an unknown code: isolating a word-to-token correspondence by cross-referencing (set-intersecting) the shared elements across multiple parallel encoded strings — i.e., constraint-satisfaction reasoning over an invented cipher/language.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Deductive symbol-to-word mapping by set-intersecting membership patterns across parallel encoded strings using a correspondence grid
questions.stem:
An epigrapher is decoding four short inscriptions written in the lost Vareen trade-script. She has already established what each inscription says in plain language. The four plain-word contents (each an UNORDERED set — the order the glyphs appear on the stone carries no meaning) are:

• Inscription I  →  STONE, GIFT, MOON
• Inscription II →  STONE, RIVER, MOON
• Inscription III → STONE, TRADE
• Inscription IV →  RIVER, GIFT, TRADE

In this script each plain word is written with exactly one glyph, and the same word is always written with the same glyph. The grid records which of the five Vareen glyphs (kesu, raki, domu, lami, toza) is present in each inscription — this glyph-by-inscription information appears ONLY in the grid.

Using the word-sets above together with the grid, which single glyph writes the word RIVER?
questions.explanation: Reason by set-intersection. From the plain-word lists, RIVER occurs in exactly inscriptions II and IV (and in no other). Since each word is one fixed glyph, RIVER's glyph must be present in exactly inscriptions II and IV — matching that pattern is impossible from the text alone; the glyph-by-inscription memberships live only in the grid. Reading the grid rows: kesu = {I,II,III}, raki = {II,IV}, domu = {I,IV}, lami = {I,II}, toza = {III,IV}. Only raki appears in exactly II and IV, so raki writes RIVER — answer B. Each distractor shares exactly ONE inscription with RIVER's {II,IV}, trapping a candidate who cross-references incompletely: A) kesu is the most-frequent glyph (3 inscriptions) and shares inscription II — the trap of equating 'most frequent glyph' with the target or grabbing any glyph seen alongside RIVER; kesu actually writes STONE ({I,II,III}). C) domu shares inscription IV but pairs it with I instead of II — the error of confirming one overlap (IV) and stopping; domu writes GIFT ({I,IV}). D) lami shares inscription II but pairs it with I instead of IV — the mirror error of stopping after the II overlap; lami writes MOON ({I,II}). E) toza shares inscription IV but pairs it with III instead of II — again a single-overlap match on IV; toza writes TRADE ({III,IV}). Only raki satisfies BOTH constraints simultaneously, so the item rewards full two-inscription cross-referencing over any single-overlap shortcut, and the frequency heuristic fails because the target glyph appears in only two inscriptions, not the most.

questions.competency: Counting unordered pairs with C(n,2)=n(n-1)/2 and inverting it to solve for n given the number of pairwise interactions.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Combinatorics: counting unordered pairs (complete graph edges)
questions.skill: Inverting the pairwise-count formula C(n,2)=n(n-1)/2 via its incremental difference and identifying the requested quantity
questions.stem: In a data centre, every pair of servers is joined by exactly one direct cable, and no other cables exist. When a single new server is installed and connected to the existing network in the same way, the total number of cables increases by 12. After this new server has been installed, how many cables are in the network?
questions.explanation:
With m servers the number of cables is C(m,2)=m(m-1)/2, since each cable is an unordered pair. Installing one server (m → m+1) creates one new cable to each existing server, so the increase equals m. The increase is given as 12, therefore m=12 before installation. After installation there are 13 servers, giving C(13,2)=13·12/2=78 cables (check: 78−66=12). Correct: D=78.

Trap analysis:
A) 12 — takes the stated increase itself as the answer, ignoring that 12 is the number of PRE-EXISTING servers, not a cable count.
B) 13 — reports the number of servers after installation instead of the number of cables (confuses vertices with edges).
C) 66 — computes C(12,2)=66, the cable count BEFORE the new server is added; an off-by-one that answers the wrong network state (also equals treating the 12 existing servers as the final count).
E) 156 — uses ordered pairs n(n−1)=13·12=156, double-counting every cable from both endpoints instead of using n(n−1)/2.

questions.competency: Worst-case counting via the pigeonhole principle: determining the minimum number of draws that GUARANTEES a multi-category target condition by exhausting every adversarial (unfavorable) draw before the condition is forced — i.e., summing the maximal counts of the categories that can be avoided and adding one.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Guaranteeing a multi-category target condition by exhausting all adversarial draws
questions.stem: A quality-control bin on an assembly line holds compression springs of five stiffness grades mixed together: 5 of grade A, 6 of grade B, 4 of grade C, 20 of grade D, and 15 of grade E. Assembling one calibrated actuator requires exactly one grade-A spring, one grade-B spring, and one grade-C spring; grades D and E are bulk stock not used in this actuator. A technician picks springs one at a time without looking and cannot put any back. What is the minimum number of springs that must be picked to be CERTAIN of ending up with at least one spring of each of grades A, B, and C?
questions.explanation:
Worst-case (adversarial) reasoning: to delay completing the target set {A, B, C} as long as possible, the unlucky technician draws every spring that is NOT of the target grade that is easiest to keep missing. Since the actuator needs one each of A, B and C, failure can persist only by never drawing one entire target grade — and to draw the most springs first, one should stay short of the SMALLEST target grade, which is C (4 springs). So the technician can draw all of A (5) + B (6) + D (20) + E (15) = 46 springs and still lack a grade-C spring. The very next (47th) pick must be a grade C, guaranteeing one of each. Formula: (total) − (smallest target-grade count) + 1 = 50 − 4 + 1 = 47.

Distractor traps:
A) 36 — blindly applies the familiar "one of each color" template (sum of the two largest groups + 1 = 20 + 15 + 1) to all five grades, ignoring that D and E are not part of the target and that A, B, C must each actually appear.
B) 45 — sets up the worst case but omits the LARGEST target grade (B = 6) instead of the smallest: 50 − 6 + 1 = 45; leaving out C, not B, is what lets the most springs be drawn first.
C) 46 — computes the correct exhaustion count (all 46 non-C springs) but forgets the single forcing draw, dropping the "+1".
E) 49 — correctly reaches 46 but then adds one forcing draw for EACH target grade (+3 = 49) instead of a single one, wrongly treating the three grades as needing separate guarantees.

questions.competency: Iterated squaring of a recurrence a(n)=a(n-1)^2 and recognizing that it produces double-exponential growth — the exponent itself doubles each step, so a(n)=2^(2^(n-1)). Tests fluency with nested/stacked exponents and the distinction between exponential and double-exponential growth, not mere multiplication.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Recognizing double-exponential growth from iterated squaring and expressing it with stacked exponents
questions.stem: A text-expansion routine starts with the two-character string "AB". In each pass, every character of the string is simultaneously replaced by a full copy of the string exactly as it was at the start of that pass. (For example, after the first pass "AB" becomes "ABAB".) If Lₙ denotes the number of characters in the string after n passes, which expression gives Lₙ for every n ≥ 0?
questions.explanation: Each pass replaces every one of the L current characters with a copy of the whole current string (length L), so the new length is L·L = L²: the length is SQUARED each pass. Starting from L₀ = 2 = 2^1, write Lₙ = 2^(eₙ). Squaring the string squares the number, which DOUBLES its exponent: eₙ = 2·eₙ₋₁ with e₀ = 1, so eₙ = 2ⁿ. Hence Lₙ = 2^(2ⁿ) — a double-exponential, because the exponent 2ⁿ is itself exponential. (Check: 2, 4, 16, 256, 65536.) A) Correct. B) 2^(2n) is the trap of confusing "the exponent doubles each step" (giving 2ⁿ) with "the exponent grows by a factor of 2 in total" (giving 2n); this is only ordinary exponential growth and is the core exponential-vs-double-exponential error. C) 2^(n+1) comes from mistaking squaring for mere doubling of the length (2 → 4 → 8 → …), treating L → 2L instead of L → L². D) 4^(2ⁿ) has the right doubling-exponent structure but uses the wrong base: it takes the post-first-pass length 4 as the base, i.e. squares one extra time, giving 2^(2^(n+1)) = Lₙ₊₁ (off by one squaring). E) 2^(n²) is the instinct that growth is "faster than exponential" so the exponent must be polynomial (n²); but a polynomial exponent is still only exponential growth, not the stacked exponent 2ⁿ required here.

questions.competency: Constructing the contrapositive of a conditional statement and recognizing its logical equivalence to the original (P→Q ≡ ¬Q→¬P), distinguishing it from converse and inverse.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Constructing the contrapositive of a chained conditional read from a directed implication diagram, and distinguishing it from converse and inverse
questions.stem: The directed diagram represents the guaranteed logical behaviour of a furnace controller. Each of the five boxes is a condition, and each arrow X → Y asserts the single implication "if X holds, then Y holds." The four arrows shown are the ONLY implications you may assume; no arrow may be read backwards, and no condition is claimed to have a unique cause. Reading the diagram, exactly one of the following statements is logically GUARANTEED to be true. Which one?

options.A: If the backup valve opens, then the fuel pressure is low.
options.B: If the fuel pressure is not low, then the backup valve does not open.
options.C: If the backup valve does not open, then the fuel pressure is not low.
options.D: If the warning lamp is not on, then the backup valve does not open.
options.E: If the fuel pressure is low, then the backup valve does not open.

questions.explanation: Tracing the diagram, the chain P → W → T → V is a directed path, so by transitivity the composite implication P → V ("if fuel pressure is low, the backup valve opens") holds. The contrapositive of P → V is ¬V → ¬P: "if the backup valve does not open, then the fuel pressure is not low." That is option C, and a conditional is always logically equivalent to its contrapositive, so C is guaranteed. Every distractor encodes one specific error. A is the CONVERSE V → P (affirming the consequent): the valve could in principle open by another route, and arrows may not be read backwards. B is the INVERSE ¬P → ¬V (negating without reversing): ¬P cannot be propagated forward along the arrows, so it guarantees nothing about V. D is the key figure trap — it is a correctly negated-and-swapped statement, but only for the implication V → L, and no directed path runs from V to L. From ¬L one may legitimately step BACK to ¬P (since P → L gives ¬L → ¬P), yet ¬P still cannot move forward to ¬V; the statement is therefore not guaranteed, and this can only be seen by reading the arrow directions in the figure. E negates just the consequent (P → ¬V), directly contradicting the derived chain P → V. Only C both matches the true directed path and applies the contrapositive correctly.

questions.competency: Counting ordered arrangements without repetition — direct application of the multiplication principle / permutations P(n,k), i.e. selecting k distinct items from n in order (here 9·8·7).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Ordered arrangements without repetition (multiplication principle / P(n,k))
questions.skill: Applying the multiplication principle to a constrained ordered selection: fill the restricted position first, then order the remaining distinct roles from the reduced pool
questions.stem: A robotics club must assign three distinct roles for a competition — Pilot, Navigator, and Mechanic — with each role given to a different member of its 8-person team. Because the Pilot operates certified equipment, only the 3 members who hold a pilot licence may serve as Pilot; any of the remaining team members may serve as Navigator or as Mechanic (a licensed member who is not chosen as Pilot is still eligible for the other two roles). In how many different ways can the three roles be filled?
questions.explanation:
Fill the restricted role first. Pilot must be one of the 3 licensed members: 3 choices. Once the Pilot is fixed, that person is removed, leaving 7 eligible members for the remaining two DISTINCT roles, which must be counted in order: Navigator has 7 choices and Mechanic has 6, giving 7·6 = 42. Total = 3·(7·6) = 126 (option A).

Distractor traps:
- B) 336 = 8·7·6: ignores the Pilot restriction entirely, treating all 8 members as eligible for every role.
- C) 168 = 3·8·7: applies the restriction (3 for Pilot) but fails to remove the chosen Pilot from the pool, wrongly drawing the next two roles from all 8 then 7.
- D) 63 = 3·C(7,2): correctly restricts the Pilot and reduces the pool to 7, but treats Navigator and Mechanic as interchangeable (unordered), using a combination instead of the ordered 7·6.
- E) 42 = 7·6: forgets to multiply by the 3 ways of choosing the Pilot, counting only the two supporting roles as if the Pilot were predetermined.

questions.competency: Deductive decoding of a constructed-language cipher: cross-referencing several parallel phrase/translation pairs to isolate the code token for a target word through systematic set intersection and elimination (matrix-style logical deduction over overlapping constraints).
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Matrix-style deductive set intersection and elimination over overlapping constraints
questions.stem:
In the invented trading language Korrûn, five words — red, silk, three, sails, ship — are each written as exactly one code token. Within a phrase the tokens are ALWAYS listed in a fixed alphabetical order of the tokens, so a token's column position tells you nothing about which word it represents. Four verified manifest entries and their unordered token sets are recorded in the grid below.

Using only the grid, determine the single code token that means "sails".
questions.explanation:
Chain the intersections, never relying on position. (1) "silk" occurs in rows 1 and 2: {tor,vun} ∩ {kel,mip,tor} = {tor}, so silk = tor. (2) "red" occurs in rows 1 and 3: {tor,vun} ∩ {daz,vun} = {vun}, so red = vun. (3) Row 2 = {kel,mip,tor} is three+sails+silk; removing silk (tor) leaves {kel,mip} = three+sails. (4) "three" occurs in rows 2 and 4: {kel,mip,tor} ∩ {daz,kel} = {kel}, so three = kel. (5) Therefore in row 2 the leftover token, mip, is "sails". Answer A (mip).

Distractor traps: B tor is "silk" — the solver stops after the very first intersection and mislabels it. C kel is "three" — confuses the two remaining tokens of row 2 without doing the rows 2∩4 step. D vun is "red" — takes the other token of row 1 instead of following the chain. E daz is "ship" — assumes the word paired with "ship" must be the target, but "sails" never appears in rows 3 or 4, so daz can be eliminated outright.

questions.competency: Logical equivalence of a conditional statement via its contrapositive — recognizing that P→Q is equivalent to ¬Q→¬P, and discriminating it from the converse (Q→P) and inverse (¬P→¬Q) fallacies.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Conditional statements: contrapositive vs. converse and inverse fallacies
questions.skill: Contrapositive equivalence of a composite conditional read from an implication graph
questions.stem: An engineer models a power plant's monitoring logic as the implication diagram below. Each arrow X → Y means the conditional "if X, then Y", and ONLY the arrows actually drawn are known to hold (no other implications may be assumed). Reading structure from the diagram alone, which statement is LOGICALLY FORCED to be true?

options.A: If the turbine is not powered, then the reactor is not online.
options.B: If the reactor is not online, then the turbine is not powered.
options.C: If the coolant flows, then the gauge reads normal.
options.D: If the turbine is powered, then the reactor is online.
options.E: If the coolant flows, then the reactor is online.

questions.explanation:
The diagram gives four edges: A→B (reactor online → coolant flows), A→C (reactor online → gauge normal), B→D (coolant flows → turbine powered), C→D (gauge normal → turbine powered). Composing a branch gives A→B→D, i.e. A→D (reactor online → turbine powered). The ONLY statement logically forced is the contrapositive of that composite implication: ¬D→¬A, "if the turbine is not powered, then the reactor is not online" — which requires reading the arrow directions and chaining them, then negating both ends and reversing. This is option A.

Trap analysis: B (¬A→¬D) is the INVERSE of the composite A→D — negating both parts without reversing direction; the reactor being offline does not force the turbine off (some other source could power it). D (D→A) is the CONVERSE of the composite chain — reading the whole chain backwards; D has no outgoing arrow, so it forces nothing. E (B→A) is the CONVERSE of the single edge A→B — reversing one arrow; B likewise has no path back to A. C (B→C) is the COMMON-CAUSE fallacy: B and C are both consequences of A (two arrows out of A), but sibling effects of a shared cause do not imply each other, and no path runs from B to C. Each distractor encodes a distinct structural error (inverse, converse-of-chain, converse-of-edge, common-cause), and none is actually forced by the drawn edges, so exactly one option — A — is correct. The item is unsolvable from the text alone because the edges and their directions live only in the figure.

questions.competency: computing uniform acceleration as rate of change of velocity (a = Δv/Δt), ideally reframed as reading slope on a velocity-time graph across motion phases
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Reading acceleration as the slope of a velocity–time graph across multiple motion phases
questions.stem: The velocity–time graph shows a test vehicle moving in a straight line through four successive phases (P1, P2, P3, P4). Each phase is a straight segment, so the acceleration within each phase is uniform. Using the coordinates shown on the graph, in which phase is the MAGNITUDE of the vehicle's acceleration the greatest?

options.A: Phase P1 (0 s to 4 s), because the vehicle is speeding up from rest — magnitude 4.0 m/s²
options.B: Phase P3 (10 s to 16 s), because the vehicle reaches its highest speed during this phase — magnitude 3.0 m/s²
options.C: Phase P4 (16 s to 21 s) — magnitude 6.0 m/s²
options.D: Phase P2 (4 s to 10 s), because the velocity line is horizontal and a steady velocity means the acceleration holds at its maximum value
options.E: Phases P1 and P4 are equal and both greatest, since both segments are the steepest lines on the graph

questions.explanation: Acceleration is the slope Δv/Δt of the velocity–time line, and "greatest magnitude" means the steepest segment regardless of sign. Reading the marked vertices: P1 = (16−0)/(4−0) = +4.0 m/s²; P2 = 0 (horizontal); P3 = (34−16)/(16−10) = +3.0 m/s²; P4 = (4−34)/(21−16) = −30/5 = −6.0 m/s², magnitude 6.0 m/s². The braking phase P4 is steepest, so C is correct. A (4.0 m/s²) is the true slope of P1 but is not the greatest — it traps students who assume the launch-from-rest phase must have the largest acceleration and never check the decreasing segment. B encodes the classic misconception that the phase reaching the highest velocity has the greatest acceleration, confusing large v with large Δv/Δt; 3.0 m/s² is P3's real slope. D encodes "constant velocity = maximum (or unchanging) acceleration," whereas a horizontal line means zero acceleration. E is the trap for students who eyeball rather than compute: both P1 and P4 look steep, but the exact slopes 4.0 and 6.0 are unequal, so they are neither equal nor jointly greatest. Only C survives an exact slope reading of the figure — the numeric values cannot be obtained from the text alone.

questions.competency: Uniform-motion kinematics: relating distance, constant speed, and elapsed time (d = v·t) with a time-unit conversion (minutes to hours). At Elite level this competency should be lifted to reading total distance/displacement as the area under a velocity–time graph across multiple phases (acceleration ramp + constant plateau + deceleration), where the student decomposes the graph into triangles/rectangles and sums signed areas rather than plugging into a single formula.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Reading total distance as the signed area under a multi-phase velocity–time graph by decomposing into triangles and a rectangle
questions.stem: The velocity–time graph shows the motion of a metro train along a straight track between two stations. The train accelerates uniformly, then travels at constant velocity, then decelerates uniformly to rest. Using the graph, determine the total distance the train travels between the two stations.
questions.explanation: Distance equals the area under the v–t graph. Decompose into three regions: acceleration triangle (0–40 s, 0→20 m/s) = ½·40·20 = 400 m; constant plateau rectangle (40–120 s at 20 m/s) = 80·20 = 1600 m; deceleration triangle (120–160 s, 20→0 m/s) = ½·40·20 = 400 m. Total = 400 + 1600 + 400 = 2400 m (D). Distractor traps: A (800 m) sums only the two ramp triangles and drops the plateau. B (1600 m) counts only the constant-velocity rectangle, treating the trip as pure uniform motion and ignoring both ramps. C (2000 m) includes the plateau and one ramp but forgets the deceleration triangle. E (3200 m) multiplies the maximum speed by the total time (20·160), treating the whole trip as a single rectangle at top speed and ignoring that the ramps are triangles (half-area).

questions.competency: Propagation and computation of relative (fractional/percentage) uncertainty — elite target: propagate uncertainty through a derived quantity (product/quotient/power) rather than a single Δx/x division.
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Propagation of uncertainty in derived quantities
questions.skill: Combining fractional uncertainties through products, quotients, and powers
questions.stem: A student determines the density of a solid cylinder from ρ = 4m / (πD²h), where m is the mass, D the diameter, and h the height. The measured relative uncertainties of the three directly measured quantities are: mass 1.0%, diameter 2.0%, and height 1.5%. Assuming the uncertainties combine in the way that gives the largest possible (worst-case) fractional uncertainty in the result, what is the percentage uncertainty in the computed density ρ?
