questions.stem: The figure shows a thin CONVERGING lens (its centre O on the principal axis) drawn on a square grid; each grid square is one unit and the two focal points are marked F. A luminous object (bold arrow, one unit tall) stands upright on the axis. Two incident rays leaving the tip of the object are drawn up to the lens. Reading the object distance and focal length directly from the grid, determine the nature, transverse size and position of the image the lens produces.

options.A: Virtual and upright, twice the object's height, formed 6 units from the lens on the SAME side as the object
options.B: Real and inverted, twice the object's height, formed 6 units from the lens on the OPPOSITE side to the object
options.C: Real and inverted, HALF the object's height, formed 6 units from the lens on the opposite side to the object
options.D: Real and inverted, twice the object's height, formed 2 units from the lens (at the far focal point)
options.E: Real and inverted, the SAME height as the object, formed 4 units from the lens on the opposite side

questions.explanation: From the grid the object sits 3 units in front of the lens (d_o = 3) and each focal point is 2 units from the lens (f = 2). The lens equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i gives 1/d_i = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6, so d_i = +6 units on the far side: a REAL image. Magnification m = −d_i/d_o = −6/3 = −2, so the image is INVERTED and TWICE the object's height. This matches the exact ray construction: the parallel ray refracts through the far F and the chief ray passes undeviated through O, meeting 6 units behind the lens at height 2 units below the axis. Answer B. Trap A: the classic 'converging lens always gives a virtual, upright image' reflex — true only when the object is INSIDE the focal length; here the object is beyond F, so the image is real, and A also puts it on the wrong side. Trap C: correct position but the magnification ratio is inverted (using d_o/d_i = 3/6 = ½ instead of d_i/d_o), giving a reduced image. Trap D: assumes the image forms AT the focal point regardless of object distance — a misreading of the 'ray through F' rule; the image forms at F only for an object at infinity. Trap E: assumes the object sits at 2F (equal conjugates, unit magnification, image at 4 units), ignoring that the grid clearly places it at 3 units, not 4.

questions.competency: law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection measured from the surface normal, applied to ray-tracing / mirror-deflection geometry
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Law of reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection measured from the surface normal, applied to ray-tracing / mirror-deflection geometry
questions.stem: A single light ray strikes a plane mirror at point P, as shown. The dashed line is the normal to the mirror at P, and the only angle given is the one marked in the figure. Reading the geometry from the figure, what is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray (the opening of the "V" the two rays form above the mirror)?
questions.explanation: The 35° marked in the figure is measured between the incident ray and the mirror SURFACE, not the normal. The law of reflection is stated for angles measured from the normal, so the true angle of incidence is i = 90° − 35° = 55°. By the law of reflection the reflected ray leaves at the same 55° on the other side of the normal, so the angle between the two rays (the V above the mirror) is i + r = 2 × 55° = 110°. Correct: D (110°). Distractor traps: A (35°) reads the marked surface angle straight off as the answer, ignoring that a reflection doubles the angle. B (55°) correctly converts to the angle of incidence but stops there, reporting i instead of the full opening 2i. C (70°) applies the "double it" step but to the wrong angle — it treats the 35° surface angle as if it were the angle of incidence (2 × 35°), the classic "measure from the surface instead of the normal" error. E (145°) takes 180° − 35°, mistaking the incident-to-reflected opening for the supplement of the marked angle.

questions.competency: Relating wave speed, wavelength, and frequency through v = fλ.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Relating wave speed, wavelength, and frequency through v = fλ
questions.stem: The graph shows a snapshot, taken at one instant, of a transverse wave travelling along a stretched wire. The horizontal axis gives the position x measured in metres along the wire; the vertical axis gives the displacement y of the wire from its equilibrium line. The wave travels along the wire at a constant speed of 30 m/s. Using the wavelength that can be read directly from the graph, determine the frequency of the wave.
questions.explanation:
The graph shows three complete cycles spanning x = 0 to x = 6 m (crests at 0.5, 2.5, 4.5 m). The wavelength is the crest-to-adjacent-crest distance = 2.5 − 0.5 = 2 m. Then f = v/λ = 30 / 2 = 15 Hz → C.
Distractor traps: A (5 Hz) reads the entire 6 m width of the graph as a single wavelength (λ = 6 → 30/6). B (10 Hz) miscounts the cycles, seeing only 2 wavelengths in 6 m so λ = 3 m (30/3). D (30 Hz) takes the crest-to-trough distance (0.5 → 1.5 m = 1 m), which is only half a wavelength, as the full wavelength (30/1). E (60 Hz) multiplies instead of dividing, computing v·λ = 30 × 2. Each wrong option encodes one specific error: whole-span-as-wavelength, cycle miscount, half-wavelength, and inverted formula.

questions.competency: Relating physical quantities to their SI units via dimensional reasoning — distinguishing energy from power, force, and electric potential by deriving base-unit compositions (J = N·m = kg·m^2/s^2) rather than recalling a label.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Dimensional analysis / base-unit derivation
questions.stem: A student is building a reference chart and wants to know which of the following combinations of physical quantities produces a result that, when reduced entirely to SI base units (kg, m, s, A), is equivalent to an energy — that is, to the joule. Which combination is an energy?
questions.explanation: The joule reduces to kg·m²·s⁻². Test each by base units. (B, correct) Charge = A·s and potential difference = J/C = kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹, so their product is (A·s)(kg·m²·s⁻³·A⁻¹) = kg·m²·s⁻² = J: this is electrical work, an energy. (A, trap) Force × velocity = (kg·m·s⁻²)(m·s⁻¹) = kg·m²·s⁻³ = watt; the student confuses it with work (force × displacement), but multiplying by velocity instead of displacement gives a rate of energy — power, not energy. (C, trap) Mass × acceleration = kg·m·s⁻² = newton; this is Newton's second law giving force, dimensionally one power of length short of energy. (D, trap) Force × time = kg·m·s⁻¹ = impulse, equal to momentum; confusing the time-product of force (momentum) with the distance-product of force (energy). (E, trap) Force ÷ area = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² = pascal (pressure); it rewards anyone who actually reduces the units rather than guessing. Only B yields kg·m²·s⁻².

questions.competency: Applying translational equilibrium (ΣF = 0) via force resolution to solve for an unknown force or angle.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Applying translational equilibrium (ΣF = 0) via force resolution to solve for an unknown force or angle
questions.stem: A decorative lamp weighing 100 N hangs motionless from a knot K, which is held by two light cables anchored to two walls, as shown in the free-body diagram. The cables make the angles indicated with the horizontal, and the weight of the lamp acts straight down. What is the tension in cable T₁?
questions.explanation:
The knot is in translational equilibrium under three concurrent forces: T₁ (up-left, 37° above horizontal), T₂ (up-right, 53° above horizontal), and W = 100 N down. Resolve into components using cos37°=sin53°=0.8 and sin37°=cos53°=0.6.
Horizontal (ΣFx = 0): −T₁cos37° + T₂cos53° = 0 → −0.8T₁ + 0.6T₂ = 0 → T₂ = (4/3)T₁.
Vertical (ΣFy = 0): T₁sin37° + T₂sin53° − W = 0 → 0.6T₁ + 0.8T₂ = 100. Substituting: 0.6T₁ + 0.8(4/3 T₁) = 1.6667T₁ = 100 → T₁ = 60 N (and T₂ = 80 N). Correct: B.
Distractor traps:
A) 50 N — assumes the weight simply splits equally between the two cables (W/2), ignoring the angles and horizontal balance entirely.
C) 75 N — uses the wrong trig ratio, setting T₁ = W·tan37° = 100(0.75); confuses the tangent with the required component relation.
D) 80 N — computes (or reads off) the OTHER cable, T₂; the classic misconception that the cable making the smaller angle with the horizontal must carry the larger tension. In fact the steeper cable (53°) supports more of the vertical load, so T₂ > T₁.
E) 100 N — forgets to resolve forces and assumes a single cable's tension equals the full weight (T = W).
The figure is essential: the two angles (37° and 53°) and the identity of cable T₁ versus T₂ appear only in the diagram, so the item cannot be solved from the text alone.

questions.competency: Dimensional analysis of physical quantities: decomposing a quantity's units into the SI base units (kg, m, s, A, K, mol, cd) and using that decomposition to classify a unit as base vs derived — e.g. recognizing Newton = kg·m·s^-2 is a compound of base units, whereas second/kilogram/ampere are themselves base units.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Dimensional analysis: decomposing a derived quantity into SI base units
questions.questionType: Dimensional decomposition into SI base units
questions.stem: The viscous drag force on a small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a fluid is F = 6π·η·r·v, where η is the fluid's dynamic viscosity and 6π is a dimensionless numerical factor. Expressed purely in terms of the SI base units (kg, m, s), what is the unit of η?
questions.explanation: Solve the given law for η: η = F / (6π·r·v), and since 6π is dimensionless, η = F/(r·v) dimensionally. Decompose each factor into SI base units. Force is mass × acceleration, so F = kg·m·s⁻². The denominator is r·v = (m)·(m·s⁻¹) = m²·s⁻¹. Therefore η = (kg·m·s⁻²)/(m²·s⁻¹) = kg·m^(1−2)·s^(−2−(−1)) = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹, which is option A (equivalently Pa·s). Distractor traps: B (kg·s⁻¹) drops the radius factor, computing F/v = (kg·m·s⁻²)/(m·s⁻¹) = kg·s⁻¹ — treating the law as F = 6πηv. C (kg·s⁻²) drops the speed factor, computing F/r = (kg·m·s⁻²)/m = kg·s⁻² — treating the law as F = 6πηr. D (kg·m⁻¹) mis-decomposes force as momentum, using F = kg·m·s⁻¹ (mass×velocity instead of mass×acceleration), giving (kg·m·s⁻¹)/(m²·s⁻¹) = kg·m⁻¹. E (kg·m³·s⁻³) inverts the relation, multiplying F·r·v = (kg·m·s⁻²)(m)(m·s⁻¹) = kg·m³·s⁻³ instead of dividing. Only A correctly combines the base-unit decomposition of force with division by length and speed.

questions.competency: Applying Newton's second law to relate net force, mass, and acceleration on a body — ideally extended to resolving and vector-summing multiple concurrent forces from a free-body diagram to find the net force and resulting acceleration.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Resolving concurrent forces into components, vector-summing to find net force, and applying F = ma
questions.stem: An 8 kg puck rests on a frictionless horizontal surface (top view). Two ropes pull it simultaneously, with the magnitudes and directions shown in the free-body diagram. Using the trigonometric values given in the figure, what is the magnitude of the puck's acceleration?
questions.explanation:
Resolve each 20 N rope into components. Horizontal (x): each contributes 20·cos37° = 20·0.80 = 16 N, both toward +x, so ΣFx = 16 + 16 = 32 N. Vertical (y): each contributes 20·sin37° = 20·0.60 = 12 N, but the ropes are symmetric about the horizontal (one 37° above, one 37° below), so +12 N and −12 N cancel, ΣFy = 0. Net force = 32 N along x. Then a = F/m = 32/8 = 4.0 m/s² → A.

Distractor traps:
B) 5.0 — treats the two forces as if they act in the same direction and adds magnitudes scalarly (20 + 20 = 40 N, ÷8). This is the trap for anyone who does not read the angles in the figure; it fails to resolve into components.
C) 3.0 — swaps sine and cosine, using 20·sin37° = 12 N for the horizontal component of each rope (24 N total, ÷8).
D) 2.0 — accounts for only one rope's horizontal component (16 N, ÷8), forgetting the second concurrent force.
E) 0.25 — inverts Newton's second law, computing a = m/F = 8/32 instead of F/m.

questions.competency: Work done by a constant/variable force along a displacement (work as force projected onto displacement; work as signed area under an F–x graph).
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Work done by a variable force as the signed area under an F–x graph
questions.stem: A 3 kg instrument sled rests on a horizontal, frictionless air track and is driven along the x-axis by a computer-controlled electromagnet. As the sled moves from x = 0 to x = 9 m, the net horizontal force acting on it varies with position exactly as shown in the graph. What is the total work done by this net force on the sled over the entire 9 m path?
questions.explanation: The work done by a position-dependent force is the SIGNED area between the F–x curve and the x-axis (no calculus needed — the curve is piecewise-linear). Above the axis (x = 0→6 m) the force is positive and does positive work: this region is a trapezoid made of two ramp-triangles (½·1·4 = 2 J each) and a plateau rectangle (4 N × 4 m = 16 J), giving +20 J. Below the axis (x = 6→9 m) the force is negative and does negative work: an identical-shaped trapezoid of magnitude two triangles (2 J each) + rectangle (4 N × 1 m = 4 J) = 8 J, contributing −8 J. Net work = (+20) + (−8) = +12 J → B. The 3 kg mass is an inert distractor: work computed from force and displacement does not depend on mass. Trap analysis: A) 20 J counts ONLY the region above the axis, discarding the interval where the force opposes the motion and removes energy. C) 28 J = 20 + 8 adds the magnitudes of both lobes, treating the below-axis area as positive work and ignoring the sign of the force. D) 36 J applies the constant-force reflex W = F_max·d = 4 N × 9 m, ignoring that the force varies with position and reverses direction. E) −12 J has the correct magnitudes but inverts the sign convention, counting the positive-force region as negative work and vice-versa. Only B correctly resolves the signed area.

questions.competency: Relating electrical power, voltage, and resistance in a DC circuit via P = V²/R, extended at elite level to resolving power distribution across a series/parallel resistor network.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Reduce a mixed series/parallel network, trace branch current/voltage, and compute power in a target resistor (P = I²R, P = V²/R)
questions.stem: In the DC circuit shown, an ideal battery of EMF 24 V drives the resistor network in the figure (all values in ohms). Resistor R₄ sits in the branch that also contains R₃, and that branch is in parallel with R₂; the combination is fed through R₁. Using the topology and values in the figure, determine the electrical power dissipated in resistor R₄.
questions.explanation:
Reduce the network: branch B is R₃ + R₄ = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω, in series. This is in parallel with R₂ = 6 Ω, giving (6·12)/(6+12) = 4 Ω. Adding the series R₁ = 4 Ω gives R_total = 8 Ω, so the battery current is I = 24/8 = 3 A. The voltage across the parallel section is 24 − I·R₁ = 24 − 12 = 12 V, so the current in branch B is 12 V / 12 Ω = 1 A. Therefore P(R₄) = I²R = 1²·8 = 8 W → A.
B) 4 W: computes I²R for R₃ (1²·4) instead of R₄ — right branch current, wrong resistor.
C) 18 W: applies the 12 V parallel-node voltage directly across R₄ (12²/8), forgetting R₃ shares that branch and drops part of the 12 V.
D) 32 W: inverts the current divider, assigning the larger branch current I·R_B/(R_A+R_B) → 2 A to branch B, giving 2²·8. The correct divider uses the opposite resistor: I·R_A/(R_A+R_B) = 3·6/18 = 1 A.
E) 72 W: ignores the network entirely and puts the full 24 V across R₄ (24²/8) — the source's single-step P = V²/R trap.

questions.competency: Current distribution in parallel resistor networks via Ohm's law per branch plus Kirchhoff's current law (sum of branch currents = total supply current).
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Parallel resistor networks; Kirchhoff's current law
questions.skill: Deriving the common branch voltage of a parallel network from one measured branch current, then applying Ohm's law per branch and KCL to find total supply current
questions.stem: The circuit shown consists of three resistors connected in parallel across a battery whose emf is not marked. An ideal ammeter placed in one branch gives the reading shown in the figure. Using only the labelled resistances and the single ammeter reading, determine the total current delivered by the battery.
questions.explanation:
Because the three resistors are in parallel, they all share the same voltage V. The ammeter sits in the R1 = 30 Ω branch and reads I1 = 0.40 A, so V = I1·R1 = 0.40 × 30 = 12 V. This common 12 V then fixes the other branch currents: I2 = 12/20 = 0.60 A and I3 = 12/60 = 0.20 A. By Kirchhoff's current law the supply current is the sum of all branch currents: I = 0.40 + 0.60 + 0.20 = 1.20 A (D).

Distractor traps:
A) 0.40 A — mistakes the single-branch ammeter reading for the whole supply current, ignoring that the ammeter is inside only one parallel branch.
B) 0.80 A — correctly finds V and the other two branch currents (0.60 + 0.20) but forgets to include the measured 0.40 A branch when applying KCL (incomplete current sum).
C) 1.00 A — drops the high-resistance 60 Ω branch (0.20 A), wrongly assuming a large resistor carries negligible current, and sums only I1 + I2.
E) 1.40 A — misreads the figure, taking R3 as 30 Ω instead of 60 Ω, giving I3 = 0.40 A and an inflated total; punishes not reading the labelled value.

questions.competency: Relational/dimensional reasoning about capacitance — connecting the definition C = Q/V (farad = coulomb/volt) to charge and potential difference, and extending it to analyze how capacitors combine in series and parallel and how stored charge/voltage/energy redistribute across a capacitor network.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Analyzing charge and voltage distribution in a mixed series-parallel capacitor network
questions.stem: In the circuit shown, an ideal 12 V battery is connected to three capacitors. Capacitor C1 is in series with a parallel combination of C2 and C3. The capacitor values are given in the figure. What is the charge stored on capacitor C3?
questions.explanation: Step 1 — Equivalent capacitance: C2 and C3 are in parallel, so C_parallel = 2 + 6 = 8 μF. This is in series with C1 = 4 μF: C_eq = (4·8)/(4+8) = 32/12 = 8/3 μF. Step 2 — Total charge from the battery: Q = C_eq·V = (8/3)(12) = 32 μC. Because C1 is in series with the parallel block, this same 32 μC sits on C1. Step 3 — Voltage across C1: V1 = Q/C1 = 32/4 = 8 V, so the voltage across the parallel block is 12 − 8 = 4 V (both C2 and C3 share this 4 V). Step 4 — Charge on C3: Q3 = C3·V_block = 6·4 = 24 μC (option C). Trap analysis: (A) 8 μC is the charge on C2 (correct method, wrong capacitor — Q2 = 2·4). (B) 16 μC assumes the 32 μC total splits equally between the two parallel capacitors, ignoring that parallel capacitors share voltage, not charge. (D) 32 μC is the total/series charge, wrongly placed entirely on C3 as if it were also in series. (E) 72 μC applies the full 12 V across C3 (6·12), ignoring the voltage dropped across the series capacitor C1. Only C requires correctly combining the series and parallel rules and tracking the voltage division — it cannot be answered without reading the network topology and values from the figure.

questions.competency: Relating wave speed, frequency, and wavelength through v = f·λ — and, at elite level, reasoning about which quantities are invariant when a wave crosses a boundary between two media (frequency conserved; speed and wavelength change together), rather than mechanically plugging into a single rearranged formula.
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength across a boundary
questions.skill: Using frequency-invariance across a medium boundary with v = f·λ to deduce an unknown wave speed from a waveform graph
questions.stem: A single transverse wave travels along a stretched composite string that changes material at the fixed junction marked by the dashed line. The graph below is a snapshot of the string's displacement versus position at one instant. In Medium 1 (left of the junction) the wave travels at 12 m/s. Using the snapshot, determine the wave's speed in Medium 2 (right of the junction).
questions.explanation: Read the two wavelengths from the position axis: in Medium 1 one full cycle spans 4 m (λ₁ = 4 m); in Medium 2 one full cycle spans 6 m (λ₂ = 6 m). Frequency is the one quantity conserved when a wave crosses a boundary (the junction oscillates as one point, so both sides share it): f = v₁/λ₁ = 12/4 = 3 Hz. In Medium 2 the same frequency gives v₂ = f·λ₂ = 3 × 6 = 18 m/s — option D. Distractor traps: A (3 m/s) reports the conserved frequency (3 Hz) as if it were the requested speed. B (8 m/s) applies an inverse relation v₂ = v₁·λ₁/λ₂ = 12·4/6, the belief that longer wavelength means slower wave (a mistaken light-refraction analogy). C (12 m/s) assumes the speed itself is invariant across the boundary — the classic wrong choice of conserved quantity. E (27 m/s) scales by the square of the wavelength ratio, v₂ = v₁·(λ₂/λ₁)² = 12·(6/4)², over-applying the proportionality as if speed grew like an energy/area factor. Only D uses the correct invariant (frequency) with v = f·λ.

questions.competency: Relating wave speed, frequency, and wavelength through the wave-propagation relation v = f·λ (and equivalently v = λ/T) — understanding how the spatial period (wavelength) and temporal period/frequency of a periodic wave combine to give propagation speed.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Wave-propagation relation v = f·λ; behaviour of f, λ, v across media
questions.stem: A transverse wave travels along a stretched cord. The LEFT graph is a snapshot of the cord at one instant (displacement y versus position x). The RIGHT graph shows the displacement of a single fixed point on the cord versus time t. The wave then passes from the light first section into a heavier second section of the cord, where its propagation speed becomes 1.5 times its speed in the first section. The wave is driven continuously by the same source throughout. Using the two graphs, determine the wavelength of the wave in the heavier second section.
questions.explanation:
Read both graphs: the snapshot gives the spatial period (crest-to-crest) λ₁ = 0.40 m; the time trace gives the temporal period T = 0.20 s, so the frequency is f = 1/T = 5 Hz. In the first section v₁ = λ₁/T = 0.40/0.20 = 2.0 m/s (both graphs are needed). Entering the heavier section the speed becomes v₂ = 1.5·v₁ = 3.0 m/s. The source is unchanged, so the frequency is the invariant quantity across the boundary (f₂ = f = 5 Hz), while the wavelength adjusts: λ₂ = v₂/f = 3.0/5 = 0.60 m (equivalently λ₂ = 1.5·λ₁). Correct: D (0.60 m).
Distractor traps:
A) 0.27 m = λ₁/1.5 — inverse scaling: student lets wavelength shorten when speed increases (correct that λ changes, wrong direction).
B) 0.30 m — misreads the snapshot, taking half a wavelength (0.20 m) as λ₁, then correctly ×1.5.
C) 0.40 m — assumes the wavelength is the quantity that stays fixed across the boundary; in fact the source fixes the frequency, not the wavelength.
E) 0.90 m — lets the period also scale by 1.5 (T₂ = 0.30 s) and computes v₂·T₂ = 3.0×0.30; i.e. wrongly changes the frequency in the new medium instead of holding it constant.

questions.competency: Thin-lens image formation: relating focal length, object distance, and image distance via the thin-lens equation (1/f = 1/v + 1/u), including recognizing qualitative regimes (object inside/at/beyond 2f, real vs. virtual, magnification, upright vs. inverted) rather than a single mechanical substitution.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Thin-lens image formation: relating f, object and image distance and characterizing the image (real/virtual, magnification, orientation) by regime rather than mechanical substitution
questions.stem: The figure shows a thin converging lens set up for a principal-ray construction on a grid in which each square represents 10 cm. The lens is the vertical double-arrow symbol; the two focal points are labelled F and the points at twice the focal length are labelled 2F. A luminous object (the solid vertical arrow) is placed on the axis as shown, but its image has deliberately NOT been drawn. Reading the focal length and the object position directly from the grid, determine the magnification of the image the lens forms, defined as m = (image height)/(object height) including its sign.
questions.explanation: From the grid (each square = 10 cm): the focal points F sit two squares from the lens, so f = 20 cm, and the object arrow stands three squares to the left, so u = 30 cm — i.e. the object lies between F and 2F. Applying 1/f = 1/v + 1/u gives 1/v = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so v = 60 cm (real image, beyond 2F). Magnification m = −v/u = −60/30 = −2.0: the image is real, inverted, and twice as tall. Correct: A. Trap B (+2.0) gets the size right but assigns a positive sign, the "real image is upright" error — a real image from a converging lens with the object beyond F is always inverted. Trap C (−0.5) inverts the magnification ratio, using −u/v instead of −v/u. Trap D (−1.0) is the reflexive "object-at-2F ⇒ image-at-2F, m = −1" memorized special case; it ignores that the figure clearly places the object between F and 2F, not at 2F. Trap E (+0.5) treats the image as virtual, upright and diminished, confusing this converging-lens/object-beyond-F case with a diverging lens (or with an object inside F). Only by reading u and f from the figure and tracking both magnitude and sign does one reach m = −2.0.

questions.competency: Chromatic dispersion in a prism
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Refraction and chromatic dispersion in a prism
questions.skill: Relating refraction angle to refractive index, wavelength, frequency and total deviation for the components of a dispersed beam
questions.stem: A narrow beam of white light strikes the flat entry face of a glass prism at a fixed angle of incidence. The scale ray-trace shows the beam splitting inside the glass into two spectral components, labelled ray 1 and ray 2; the angle each refracted ray makes with the normal at the entry face is marked. The two rays are drawn in black (no colour is indicated). Reading only the marked angles in the figure, which single statement about ray 1 and ray 2 is correct?

options.A: Ray 1 has the larger refractive index in the glass, because it is refracted through the larger angle from the normal.
options.B: Ray 2 must be the longer-wavelength (redder) component, because it travels closer to the normal inside the glass.
options.C: Ray 2 has the higher frequency and undergoes the greater total deviation on passing through the prism.
options.D: The two rays have equal refractive indices, since they enter the glass at the same angle of incidence.
options.E: Ray 1 leaves the prism parallel to the incident beam, so its net deviation is zero.

questions.explanation: Snell's law at the entry face gives sin(50°) = n·sin(θ), with the same incidence for both components, so the ray with the SMALLER refraction angle has the LARGER refractive index. The figure shows ray 2 at 27° and ray 1 at 33°, so ray 2 is refracted more (larger n). In a normally dispersive glass n increases toward shorter wavelength, so ray 2 is the shorter-wavelength, higher-frequency (bluer/violet) component; and for a prism at fixed incidence a larger n produces a larger total deviation — hence C is correct. A reverses the physics: the LARGER refraction angle (ray 1, 33°) means LESS bending and the SMALLER n, not the larger. B mislabels the more-refracted, closer-to-normal ray as red; closer to the normal means larger n and therefore shorter wavelength (violet), not longer. D ignores dispersion entirely — equal incidence does not force equal n; the whole point of the split is that n depends on wavelength. E confuses a prism with a parallel-sided slab: a prism's faces are not parallel, so every component is deviated and none emerges parallel to the incident beam. Only the marked angles (27° < 33°) let you decide which ray is which, so the figure is essential.

questions.competency: Understanding that prism dispersion arises because refractive index depends on wavelength, so different colors refract at different angles (wavelength-dependent refraction via Snell's law).
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Wavelength-dependent refractive index and prism dispersion via Snell's law
questions.stem: A narrow beam of white light enters a glass prism and emerges as two of its component colours, drawn as ray P and ray Q in the figure. Both emergent rays are shown in black, and each is labelled with its total deviation angle δ measured from the dashed undeviated direction. For this glass the refractive index is 1.513 for red light and 1.532 for violet light. Using the deviation angles in the figure, which statement correctly identifies the rays and the reason for the separation?

options.A: Ray P is violet: it shows the greater deviation, and violet has the higher refractive index (1.532 > 1.513), so it is refracted more strongly at each face.
options.B: Ray P is red: red has the longest wavelength, and a longer wavelength is always bent through the larger angle.
options.C: Ray Q is violet: violet light travels fastest inside the glass, so it is deviated the least.
options.D: The two rays actually have equal deviation; the visible separation is produced by internal reflection at the second face, not by refraction.
options.E: Ray P is violet, but only because violet has the smaller refractive index in glass, which is what produces its larger deviation.

questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because the refractive index depends on wavelength; by Snell's law a higher n bends the ray more at each surface, so the colour with the larger total deviation is the one with the higher index. The figure shows Ray P deviated by 52° and Ray Q by only 48°, so P is bent more. Since n_violet (1.532) > n_red (1.513), the more-deviated ray P must be violet and Q red — this requires reading the deviation angles from the figure, not the text. A is correct. B inverts the wavelength relation (it treats long-wavelength red as bending most; in fact shorter-wavelength violet has the higher index and bends most). C encodes the speed misconception: violet is slowest in glass (v = c/n, highest n), not fastest, and is deviated most, not least. D is the source-style 'reflection' trap — the colours separate by wavelength-dependent refraction, and the figure explicitly shows unequal deviations (52° ≠ 48°), contradicting 'equal deviation'. E reaches the right identity (P = violet) through false physics, claiming violet has the smaller index when 1.532 > 1.513; the whole statement is therefore incorrect.

questions.competency: Rewriting an expression that mixes a whole term with a negative-exponent (reciprocal) term into a single rational expression over a common denominator — i.e. interpreting y⁻¹ = 1/y and combining x − 1/y = (xy−1)/y.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Interpreting negative exponents as reciprocals and combining a whole term with a nested reciprocal term into a single rational expression over a common denominator
questions.stem:
For every real number n with n ≠ 0 and n ≠ 1, the expression

  n + (1 − n⁻¹)⁻¹

is exactly equal to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct path (A): Inside the parentheses, n⁻¹ = 1/n, so 1 − n⁻¹ = (n − 1)/n. The outer exponent −1 inverts this whole fraction: (1 − n⁻¹)⁻¹ = n/(n − 1). Now combine the whole term with this reciprocal term over the common denominator (n − 1): n + n/(n − 1) = [n(n − 1) + n]/(n − 1) = (n² − n + n)/(n − 1) = n²/(n − 1). Check n = 2: 2 + (1 − ½)⁻¹ = 2 + 2 = 4, and n²/(n−1) = 4. ✓

Each distractor is a distinct error:
B) Forgets the outer inversion — treats (1 − n⁻¹)⁻¹ as just 1 − n⁻¹ = (n−1)/n, giving n + (n−1)/n = (n² + n − 1)/n. Tests whether the student actually applies the reciprocal, not merely the inner one.
C) Inverts correctly to n/(n − 1) but then adds the whole term without scaling it to the common denominator: n + n/(n−1) → (n + n)/(n − 1) = 2n/(n − 1). Encodes the classic "add numerators directly" fraction error.
D) Distributes the −1 exponent term-by-term across the subtraction: (1 − n⁻¹)⁻¹ mis-read as 1⁻¹ − (n⁻¹)⁻¹ = 1 − n, giving n + (1 − n) = 1. Encodes the false rule (a − b)⁻¹ = a⁻¹ − b⁻¹.
E) Sign/order slip in the first combine: writes 1 − n⁻¹ as (1 − n)/n instead of (n − 1)/n, inverts to n/(1 − n), then n + n/(1 − n) = (2n − n²)/(1 − n) = (n² − 2n)/(n − 1). Encodes reversing the subtraction order when forming the numerator.

Only A survives all steps; the four traps each fail at exactly one identifiable move, and no distractor is also correct (they are algebraically distinct rational functions).

questions.competency: Computing total surface area of a solid from edge length by counting congruent faces and summing their areas.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Computing total surface area of a solid from edge length by counting congruent faces and summing their areas
questions.stem: A machinist starts from a solid rectangular block and cuts a rectangular notch out of one full-depth top edge, producing the L-shaped prism shown in the isometric drawing (all edge lengths are given as multiples of the unit length a; the block has uniform depth). Reading the labelled dimensions from the figure, what is the TOTAL surface area of the finished solid (all outer faces, including the two exposed walls of the notch)?
questions.explanation: The solid is a 4a×3a×2a block with a 2a(wide)×1a(tall)×2a(deep) corner bar removed. Sum the faces directly from the figure. Two L-shaped end caps: each = full 4a×3a rectangle minus the 2a×1a notch = 12a²−2a²=10a², so 20a². Lateral faces (each of depth 2a) run around the L outline of perimeter 4a+2a+2a+1a+2a+3a=14a, giving 14a×2a=28a². Total = 20a²+28a² = 48a² (C). Key figure-based insight: cutting the re-entrant notch removes outer material (top face −4a², right face −2a², caps −4a²) but adds the two inner notch walls (2a×2a + 1a×2a = 6a²), for a net change of −4a² from the 52a² bounding box. Distractor traps: (D) 52a² ignores the notch entirely and takes the surface of the full 4a×3a×2a bounding box. (E) 58a² adds the two new interior walls (+6a²) but forgets that the outer faces shrank — the misconception that cutting always increases surface area. (B) 42a² correctly removes the exposed outer material (52−4−4−2) but forgets to add the two interior notch walls. (A) 36a² naively subtracts the entire surface area of the removed bar (16a²) from the bounding box (52−16), double-counting the shared faces. Only C balances every removed and added face.

questions.competency: Determining the exact value and sign of a trigonometric function at a quadrantal/special angle by locating the angle's terminal point on the unit circle (mapping angle position to signed coordinate), rather than memorized recall.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Unit circle: signs and exact values at special angles
questions.skill: Locating an angle's terminal point on the unit circle (quadrant + reference angle) to obtain signed exact coordinates for sine and cosine
questions.stem: In the diagram, angle θ is drawn in standard position (vertex at the origin, initial side along the positive x-axis). Its terminal side crosses the unit circle at the point P shown, and the marked arc gives the acute angle that this terminal side makes with the horizontal axis. Using only the information in the figure, what is the exact value of 2cos θ + sin θ ?
questions.explanation: From the figure P lies in the third quadrant, and the marked 30° reference angle is measured from the negative x-axis. So the terminal point is (cos θ, sin θ) = (−√3/2, −1/2): both coordinates negative, with the larger magnitude (√3/2) horizontal because the ray hugs the x-axis. Substituting: 2cos θ + sin θ = 2(−√3/2) + (−1/2) = −√3 − 1/2 = −(1 + 2√3)/2 ≈ −2.23 → C. Distractor traps: (A) (1 − 2√3)/2 uses Q2 signs (cos negative, sin positive), i.e. reflecting P across the x-axis. (B) −(2 + √3)/2 keeps the correct Q3 signs but swaps the coordinate magnitudes — reading the 30° arc as the angle from the vertical axis, giving (−1/2, −√3/2). (D) (2√3 − 1)/2 uses Q4 signs (cos positive, sin negative). (E) (1 + 2√3)/2 ignores the quadrant entirely and takes both coordinates positive (pure first-quadrant/reference-angle recall with no sign analysis). Each wrong option corresponds to a specific failure to read the terminal point's position, which is exactly what the figure — not the text — supplies.

questions.competency: Applying a percentage change to a base quantity — reasoning about relative (multiplicative) change, ideally the non-trivial cases: successive/compounded percentage changes, the asymmetry between a percentage increase and the decrease that reverses it, or recovering the original base from a changed value.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Compounded percentage changes and recovering the base via multiplicative inverse
questions.stem: In a chemistry lab, the concentration of a reagent solution is first raised by 20%. The resulting solution is then concentrated further, raising it by an additional 50%. A technician now wants to bring the solution back to exactly its original concentration in a single dilution step. By what percentage must the current (final) concentration be decreased?
questions.explanation: Let the original concentration be C. Two successive multiplicative changes give a net factor of 1.20 × 1.50 = 1.80, so the current concentration is 1.80C. To return to C in one step, the required factor is C / 1.80C = 1/1.8 = 5/9 ≈ 0.556, i.e. the concentration must be multiplied by 5/9. The DECREASE is therefore 1 − 5/9 = 4/9 ≈ 0.444 = 44.4% (B). Distractor traps: (A) 35% averages the two percentages, (20+50)/2, ignoring compounding and reversal. (C) 55.6% reports the surviving fraction 1/1.8 itself as the reduction, instead of 1 − 1/1.8. (D) 70% adds the percentages (20 + 50) and applies that as a symmetric reversal, treating percentage changes as additive. (E) 80% correctly finds the net increase (1.80 = +80%) but then wrongly assumes a p% increase is reversed by a p% decrease — the key asymmetry the item targets, since 0.20 × 1.80 = 0.36C ≠ C.

questions.competency: Complement rule of probability elevated to conditional probability via the complement (and complements of independent joint events).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Complement rule and conditional probability with independent joint events
questions.skill: Extracting conditional probabilities from a contingency table and combining the complement rule with the complement of an independent joint event
questions.stem: A robotics laboratory calibrates motion sensors supplied by two assembly lines, L1 and L2. The two-way table shows, for a batch of 200 sensors, how many passed and how many failed the calibration test, broken down by line. An engineer now takes two sensors from line L2. Using the L2 failure rate given by the table, and assuming the two sensors fail or pass independently of each other, what is the probability that AT LEAST ONE of the two L2 sensors fails calibration?
questions.explanation: From the table, line L2 has 10 failures out of 50 sensors, so the conditional failure probability is P(fail | L2) = 10/50 = 1/5, and by the complement rule P(pass | L2) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5. For two independent L2 sensors, "at least one fails" is the complement of "both pass": P(at least one fails) = 1 − P(both pass) = 1 − (4/5)² = 1 − 16/25 = 9/25. Correct: A. Trap B (16/25) forgets the outer complement and reports P(both pass) — the "none fail" case. Trap C (2/5) treats "at least one" as a simple sum 1/5 + 1/5, ignoring that the two events overlap and that probabilities of "at least one" require the complement, not addition. Trap D (1/25) computes P(both fail) = (1/5)², misreading "at least one" as "both." Trap E (1/5) stops at the single-sensor conditional failure rate and never uses the fact that two sensors are drawn. Each distractor also fails only if the candidate mis-reads the L2 row of the table, so the figure is essential: the overall marginal failure rate (25/200 = 1/8) yields none of the options, forcing the candidate to isolate the L2 conditional counts.

questions.competency: Determining whether a given point lies on a curve by testing coordinate pairs against a quadratic relation (point-membership / satisfying an equation), and by extension reading how a point's position relates to a parabola's graph.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Deriving a parabola's equation from its graph and testing whether coordinate pairs satisfy it
questions.stem: The figure shows the graph of a parabola y = g(x). Its vertex, its two x-intercepts and its y-intercept fall exactly on lattice points, as marked. The equation of the parabola is NOT given: you must read it from the graph. Which one of the following points lies exactly on the curve y = g(x)?
questions.explanation: From the figure, the vertex is (1, -4) and the curve passes through the x-intercept (3, 0). Vertex form gives g(x) = a(x - 1)^2 - 4; substituting (3, 0): 0 = a(4) - 4, so a = 1. Hence g(x) = (x - 1)^2 - 4 = x^2 - 2x - 3 (consistent with the marked intercepts (-1,0) and (0,-3)). Testing each point: A) g(4) = 16 - 8 - 3 = 5 -> (4,5) lies ON the curve — CORRECT. B) (-2,-3): the trap is applying the linear term with the wrong sign for a negative x (computing 4 - 4 - 3 = -3); the true value is g(-2) = 4 + 4 - 3 = 5, so it is off. C) (3,-3): the trap is carrying the y-intercept value -3 across to x = 3 instead of using the intercept; g(3) = 0 (it is a root), so it is off. D) (0,3): the trap is a sign error on the constant / reflecting the y-intercept; the actual y-intercept is g(0) = -3, not 3. E) (1,4): the trap is misreading the sign of the vertex's y-coordinate; the vertex is (1,-4), so g(1) = -4, not 4. Only A satisfies the relation. The item is unsolvable from the text alone because the equation must be extracted from the graphed vertex and intercepts.

questions.competency: Comparing the areas of regular polygons inscribed in a common circle, understanding that the inscribed-polygon area A = (1/2) n R^2 sin(2π/n) increases monotonically with the number of sides n toward the limiting circle area πR^2.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Areas of regular polygons inscribed in a circle
questions.skill: Applying the inscribed regular-polygon area formula A=(1/2)nR²sin(2π/n) with figure-read n, and combining it with circle area to find a segment region
questions.stem: In the figure, a regular polygon is inscribed in a circle of radius R. One of the congruent isosceles triangles formed by joining the centre to two adjacent vertices is shaded, and its central angle is marked. A regular n-gon inscribed in a circle of radius R has area (1/2)·n·R²·sin(2π/n). Reading the number of sides (or, equivalently, the marked central angle) from the figure, determine the exact total area of the region that lies inside the circle but outside the polygon.
questions.explanation:
The marked central angle is 30°, so the polygon has n = 360°/30° = 12 sides (a regular dodecagon) — this MUST be read from the figure, since n appears nowhere in the text. Its area is A = (1/2)·12·R²·sin(2π/12) = 6R²·sin30° = 6R²·(1/2) = 3R². The circle's area is πR². The region inside the circle but outside the polygon is therefore πR² − 3R² = (π − 3)R² → A (correct).

Distractor traps:
B) (6 − π)R²: dropped the factor 1/2 in the area formula, getting A = 12R²·sin30° = 6R²; since this "polygon" exceeds the circle, the student reverses the subtraction to 6R² − πR². Encodes the missing-½ error.
C) (π − 3√3⁄2)R²: miscounted the sides as n = 6 (recalled the familiar hexagon instead of reading n = 12 from the figure), giving polygon area (3√3/2)R² and region πR² − (3√3/2)R². Encodes side-count/figure-misread error.
D) 3R²: correctly found the polygon's area but answered the wrong quantity — reported the polygon's area instead of subtracting it from the circle. Encodes the "answered the wrong region" error.
E) (π − 3)R²/12: computed the area of a single circular segment correctly but forgot to multiply by the 12 segments. Encodes the missing-×n error.

The item defeats the "more sides = larger area" shortcut: side-count recall gives no help here because the question demands the exact numerical area of the segment region, which hinges on the non-obvious fact sin(2π/12) = 1/2 making the dodecagon's area exactly 3R².

questions.competency: Determining the existence condition for real roots of a "pure" quadratic ax²+b=0 by isolating x² = -b/a and reasoning that a real solution requires the right-hand side to be non-negative — i.e., sign analysis linking the signs of the leading coefficient and the constant term (equivalently, when the parabola y=ax²+b meets the x-axis).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Deciding when a pure quadratic ax²+b=0 has real solutions by reading the sign of a (opening direction) and b (vertex height) from a parabola sketch and applying the condition −b/a ≥ 0, including the tangent b=0 double-root case
questions.stem: The figure shows four parabolas, labelled I, II, III and IV. Each is the graph of a "pure" quadratic y = ax² + b (with a ≠ 0 and b constant); no numerical values are given, so the signs of a and b must be read from the sketches alone. For every parabola consider the associated equation ax² + b = 0. In which of the four cases does this equation have at least one real solution?
questions.explanation: Rewrite ax²+b=0 as x² = −b/a. A real solution exists exactly when −b/a ≥ 0, which geometrically means the parabola y = ax² + b must reach the x-axis — either crossing it (two roots) or just touching it (one double root). For a pure quadratic the vertex sits on the y-axis at (0, b), so one reads b from the vertex height and a from the opening direction. Reading the figure: I opens upward with its vertex below the x-axis (a>0, b<0) → it meets the axis → real roots. II opens upward with its vertex above the x-axis (a>0, b>0) → it never reaches the axis → no real solution. III opens downward with its vertex above the x-axis (a<0, b>0) → it meets the axis → real roots. IV opens upward with its vertex exactly on the x-axis at the origin (b=0) → it touches the axis → the double root x=0 is a genuine real solution. Hence I, III and IV, giving A. Distractor traps: B drops IV, the error of thinking a curve that only touches the axis (b=0) has "no solution" because it does not cross — but a tangency is a real (double) root. C keeps only the upward-opening curves that meet the axis, the error of believing real roots require a>0 and so wrongly discarding the downward parabola III. D selects the two vertex-above-axis curves (II and III), the error of memorising the inverted rule "vertex above the x-axis ⇒ solutions" instead of tying the vertex side to the opening direction. E takes all four, the error of assuming every parabola must eventually cross the x-axis, ignoring that II never descends to it.

questions.competency: Understanding how fractional-power/root functions transform magnitude on (0,1): the ordering x < x^(1/3) < 1 for 0<x<1 and how exponent size reorders values of a fractional base.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Powers and roots — behaviour of x^n and x^(1/n) on (0,1)
questions.skill: Reading and identifying power/root graphs and reasoning about magnitude ordering on (0,1)
questions.stem: A control engineer models three candidate response curves on the normalised interval 0 < x < 1. The three functions are y = x, y = x^3 and y = x^(1/3), each plotted below and labelled only as curve I, curve II or curve III — the figure does NOT tell you which formula belongs to which curve. The point Q = (0.5, 0.79) is marked and lies exactly on one of the three curves. Using the graph, which single statement is correct?

options.A: Curve I is y = x^3; on (0,1) cubing pushes each value upward, so the cube is the highest of the three curves.
options.B: Curve I is y = x^(1/3), curve II is y = x and curve III is y = x^3, and for every x with 0 < x < 1 the ordering is x^3 < x < x^(1/3).
options.C: Curve III is y = x^(1/3), because taking a root of a proper fraction produces a number smaller than the fraction.
options.D: The three curves must cross at some point strictly between x = 0 and x = 1, so no fixed ordering of the three outputs holds across the whole interval.
options.E: Curve II is y = x^3 and curve I is y = x, since the straight curve represents the fastest-growing response.

questions.explanation: Read the figure: curve I is the top curve (rising steeply then flattening), curve II is the straight diagonal, curve III hugs the x-axis before turning up. The anchor point Q = (0.5, 0.79) lies on the top curve, and since 0.5^(1/3) ≈ 0.794 while 0.5^3 = 0.125 and 0.5 = 0.5, Q can only sit on y = x^(1/3). So curve I = x^(1/3) (top), curve II = x (diagonal), curve III = x^3 (bottom), giving x^3 < x < x^(1/3) on all of (0,1). That is option B. Trap A encodes the misconception that cubing enlarges numbers — false on (0,1), where cubing a proper fraction shrinks it (0.5^3 = 0.125), so x^3 is the lowest curve, not the highest. Trap C encodes the classic 'a root makes a fraction smaller' error; in fact the cube root of a proper fraction is larger (0.5^(1/3) ≈ 0.79 > 0.5), placing y = x^(1/3) at the top (curve I), not the bottom. Trap D asserts an interior crossing; the three curves meet only at the endpoints x = 0 and x = 1 and never cross in between, so the ordering is fixed — reading the figure shows no interior intersection. Trap E misreads the diagonal: the straight line is y = x (identity), not the cube, and equating 'straight' with 'fastest-growing' is unfounded. Only B correctly identifies every curve and states the ordering that the figure and point Q together force.

questions.competency: Applying logarithm laws — specifically the quotient rule log a − log b = log(a/b) — to simplify a difference of two logarithms of the same base into a single logarithm.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Logarithm quotient rule (log a − log b = log(a/b))
questions.stem: In information theory, a symbol drawn from a source with N equally likely states carries log₂(N) bits of information. Source A has 256 equally likely states and source B has 16 equally likely states. How many MORE bits of information does a single symbol from source A carry than a single symbol from source B?
questions.explanation: The extra information is log₂256 − log₂16. Applying the quotient rule log a − log b = log(a/b): log₂256 − log₂16 = log₂(256/16) = log₂16 = 4 bits (equivalently, evaluating each: 8 − 4 = 4). So B is correct. The selectivity comes from three combined steps — modelling the difference, applying the quotient rule, and recognizing 256 = 2⁸ and 16 = 2⁴ — not from tedious arithmetic. Each distractor encodes one specific error: A (2) DIVIDES the two logarithms, 8 ÷ 4, the misconception log a − log b = (log a)/(log b). C (12) ADDS them, 8 + 4, i.e. treats the difference as a product log₂(256·16) — the classic sum/quotient sign confusion. D (16) correctly forms the ratio 256/16 = 16 via the quotient rule but FORGETS to take the logarithm of it (stops one step early). E (−4) REVERSES the order, computing log₂(16/256) = log₂(1/16) = −4 (the log b − log a slip). All five values are distinct and clean, exactly one is correct, and none is trivially eliminable.

questions.competency: Reasoning about angular relationships — recognizing that supplementary angles sum to 180° and applying that (together with linear-pair, vertical, and co-interior/transversal relationships) to solve for unknown angles in a geometric configuration rather than merely reciting the definition.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Angles formed by a transversal cutting parallel lines
questions.skill: Applying co-interior (supplementary) and linear-pair angle relationships on a transversal to set up and solve a linear equation for an unknown angle
questions.stem: In the diagram, lines ℓ₁ and ℓ₂ are parallel and are cut by the transversal t. The three marked angles occupy the positions shown in the figure. Using the two given angles (x + 70)° and (2x + 20)°, determine the measure of the angle marked θ.
questions.explanation:
The two given angles sit on the same side of the transversal, both between the parallel lines, so they are co-interior (same-side interior) angles and are therefore supplementary: (x + 70) + (2x + 20) = 180, giving 3x + 90 = 180, x = 30. Hence the given bottom angle (2x + 20)° = 80°. The target angle θ lies on the bottom line on the OTHER side of the transversal, forming a linear pair with that 80° angle, so θ = 180 − 80 = 100°. (Equivalently, θ is the alternate-interior angle of the top angle (x + 70)° = 100°, confirming θ = 100°.) Answer C.

Distractor traps:
- A) 60°: treats the co-interior pair as EQUAL (confusing them with alternate/corresponding angles): x + 70 = 2x + 20 gives x = 50, bottom angle = 120°, then 180 − 120 = 60°. Wrong relationship, right final step.
- B) 80°: correctly finds x = 30 but stops at the given co-interior angle (2x + 20)° = 80°, forgetting that θ is its linear-pair supplement, not that angle itself.
- D) 120°: same "co-interior are equal" misconception (x = 50) but reports the resulting 120° directly without the final linear-pair step.
- E) 160°: confuses SUPPLEMENTARY with COMPLEMENTARY, setting the co-interior sum to 90°: 3x + 90 = 90 gives x = 0, bottom angle = 20°, then 180 − 20 = 160°.
Only C requires correctly identifying the co-interior (supplementary) relationship AND applying the linear-pair step to reach θ.

questions.competency: Summation of an arithmetic progression: identifying the first term, common difference, and term count, then applying the closed-form series-sum formula S_n = n/2·(2a + (n-1)d) to obtain a total. Elite variants should force the student to reason backward (recover a hidden parameter from a given sum), combine two constraints, or interpret the progression in an applied/structural context rather than plug directly into the formula.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Recovering hidden AP parameters from two term constraints, then summing a partial range with the series-sum formula
questions.stem: A curved amphitheatre is built so that the number of seats in each successive row, from front to back, increases by a fixed amount (the rows form an arithmetic progression). Records show that the 5th row from the front contains 34 seats and the 12th row contains 69 seats. A conservation team needs to reserve every seat from the 8th row through the 20th row (inclusive) for a private event. How many seats in total lie in that block of rows?
questions.explanation:
Let the rows form an AP with first term a and common difference d, where row n has a+(n-1)d seats. The two constraints give a+4d=34 and a+11d=69. Subtracting: 7d=35, so d=5 and a=14. Then row 8 has 14+7·5=49 seats and row 20 has 14+19·5=109 seats. Rows 8 through 20 inclusive is 20−8+1=13 rows, so the total is 13·(49+109)/2 = 13·79 = 1027 (D).

Distractor traps:
A) 948 — correct endpoints (49 and 109) but miscounts the block as 20−8=12 rows instead of 13, giving 12·158/2 (the classic inclusive-count off-by-one).
B) 962 — sets up the terms as a+5d=34 and a+12d=69 (using n instead of n−1 for the position), recovering a=9 instead of 14; then 13·(44+104)/2. This is the index-offset error in the term formula.
C) 978 — computes the block as S₂₀−S₈ (subtracting the sum through row 8) rather than S₂₀−S₇, thereby dropping row 8 itself: 1230−252. This is the off-by-one error in the difference-of-partial-sums method.
E) 1230 — solves for a and d correctly but ignores the lower bound and sums all 20 rows (S₂₀ = 10·(28+95)), i.e. reads only "through the 20th row."

questions.competency: Recovering two unknowns from their sum and product — i.e. solving a symmetric system reducible to a quadratic via Vieta's relations (x + y = S, xy = P leads to t^2 - St + P = 0), or equivalently factoring a monic quadratic from its roots' sum and product.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Recovering symmetric quantities of two unknowns from their sum and product
questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 34 cm and an area of 60 cm². Without finding the individual side lengths, what is the length of the rectangle's diagonal?
questions.explanation: Let the two side lengths be x and y. The perimeter 2(x+y)=34 gives the sum S = x+y = 17; the area gives the product P = xy = 60. The diagonal d satisfies d² = x² + y² by the Pythagorean theorem, and the symmetric identity x² + y² = (x+y)² − 2xy = S² − 2P = 17² − 2(60) = 289 − 120 = 169, so d = √169 = 13 cm. (One need never solve for x=12, y=5 individually — the point is that the diagonal is a symmetric function recoverable directly from S and P.) Distractor traps: (B) 17 cm uses the sum S = x+y itself as the diagonal, forgetting the −2P correction and the square root — the classic 'diagonal equals half-perimeter' error. (C) √229 comes from d² = S² − P = 289 − 60, subtracting the product only once instead of twice (dropping the factor 2 in 2xy). (D) 7 cm comes from |x − y|, since (x−y)² = S² − 4P = 289 − 240 = 49; a student who computes the difference of the sides rather than the hypotenuse lands here. (E) √409 comes from d² = S² + 2xy·(sign error) = 289 + 120 = 409, i.e. adding 2P instead of subtracting it — mishandling the sign in (x+y)² = x² + y² + 2xy.

questions.competency: Quadratic scaling of area under a dilation/similarity transform.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Quadratic scaling of area under a similarity transform
questions.stem: An engineering firm produces two geometrically similar L-shaped mounting brackets. Both bracket faces are drawn to scale on the coordinate grid below (grid spacing = 1 unit). The smaller bracket face requires exactly 8 cm² of anti-corrosion coating. The linear scale relationship between the two brackets must be determined from the grid. How much coating is needed to cover the face of the larger bracket?
questions.explanation: From the grid the small bracket is 4 units wide and 6 units tall; the large bracket is 10 units wide and 15 units tall. Both give the same linear scale factor k = 10/4 = 15/6 = 5/2, confirming similarity. Under a similarity transform area scales as k², so the large face = 8 × (5/2)² = 8 × 25/4 = 50 cm² (C). Distractor traps: (A) 20 = 8 × 5/2, scaling area by the linear factor and forgetting to square it — the core misconception. (B) 32 = 8 × 2², correctly squaring but misreading the scale from the figure as 2:1 instead of 5:2. (D) 100 = the raw count of grid squares covered by the large L-shape, treating abstract grid units as cm² and ignoring the given real area of 8 cm². (E) 125 = 8 × (5/2)³, cubing the scale factor — confusing area scaling (k²) with volume scaling (k³). The scale factor is nowhere stated in words, so the item is unsolvable without reading the grid.

questions.competency: Deriving and simplifying a part-to-part ratio from part-to-whole count data (compute the complementary subgroup, then reduce the ratio to lowest terms while preserving order of the named quantities)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Deriving a reduced part-to-part ratio from part-to-whole data after reconciling an internal population change
questions.stem: A robotics workshop is staffed only by apprentices and mentors, 84 people in total. Suppose that 6 of the apprentices completed their certification and were promoted to mentor (no one joined or left the workshop). After these promotions, apprentices would make up exactly 4/7 of the workshop. What is the CURRENT ratio of apprentices to mentors, in lowest terms?
questions.explanation: A promotion is an internal transfer, so the total of 84 is invariant. After the promotions the apprentices would be 4/7 of 84 = 48, making mentors the complement 84 − 48 = 36. To recover the CURRENT counts, undo the promotion: 6 people who are now mentors were apprentices, so currently apprentices = 48 + 6 = 54 and mentors = 36 − 6 = 30. The current ratio is 54 : 30 = 9 : 5 (A). Trap B (4:3) uses the post-promotion counts 48:36 without reversing the change. Trap C (3:2 from 54:36) reverses the transfer on the apprentice side only (+6) but forgets that the same 6 people leave the mentor count, violating conservation of the total. Trap D (5:9) has the correct counts but reverses the named order (mentors:apprentices). Trap E (1:1 from 42:42) undoes the transfer in the wrong direction — subtracting 6 from the future apprentices and adding 6 to the future mentors. Only A both reverses the change correctly and preserves the order apprentices:mentors.

questions.competency: Solving a system of two simultaneous linear equations in two unknowns (via elimination/substitution), and interpreting the solution as the intersection point of two lines in the coordinate plane.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Analytic geometry — systems of linear equations and line intersection
questions.skill: Deriving line equations from plotted points and solving a 2x2 linear system as an intersection
questions.stem: An engineer's site plan shows two straight support cables, r and s, drawn on a coordinate grid marked in metres (see figure). The centre-line of each cable is the straight line passing through the two anchor points marked on it. The cables are to be welded together at the point where their centre-lines cross. Using only the anchor positions shown in the figure, at what coordinates (x, y) do the two centre-lines intersect?
questions.explanation: The figure gives no equations, so each line must be reconstructed from its two marked anchor points. Line r passes through (-3,-1) and (3,3): slope = 4/6 = 2/3, and substituting (3,3) gives y = (2/3)x + 1. Line s passes through (2,5) and (5,2): slope = -1, giving y = -x + 7. Setting them equal: (2/3)x + 1 = -x + 7 leads to (5/3)x = 6, so x = 3.6 and y = 3.4. The intersection (3.6, 3.4) is deliberately non-lattice, so it cannot be read off the grid and must be solved. Trap D (3.4, 3.6): correct magnitudes with x and y swapped. Trap B (3.0, 3.0): reads line s as y = -x + 6 (miscounts one grid unit on the intercept), landing on a tempting clean lattice point. Trap E (4.2, 2.8): assumes line r passes through the origin, y = (2/3)x, dropping its +1 intercept. Trap A (1.4, 5.6): inverts line r's slope to 3/2 (run/rise instead of rise/run). Each distractor encodes one distinct misconception; none is also correct or trivially eliminable.

questions.competency: Translating a verbal constraint into a linear equation and solving it: representing consecutive integers as n, n+1, n+2, summing to a target, and solving for the unknown (equivalently recognizing the middle term equals the mean, sum/3).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Consecutive integers and the mean (middle term = sum/count)
questions.skill: Recognizing that for an odd-length run of consecutive integers the middle term equals the mean (sum/count), then combining divisor/parity reasoning with a positivity constraint to pin down the unique valid set.
questions.stem: A set of consecutive integers — more than one of them, and each greater than 1 — has a sum of exactly 100. The number of integers in the set is odd. What is the middle integer of the set?
questions.explanation: Key idea (the same one behind "middle = sum/3" for three consecutive integers, generalised): for an ODD count c of consecutive integers, the middle term equals the mean, so sum = c × middle. Hence c must be an odd divisor of 100. The odd divisors of 100 are 1, 5, 25; with "more than one" integer we need c = 5 or c = 25 (note c = 3 fails immediately because 100 is not divisible by 3 — you cannot blindly divide by 3 here). • c = 5 → middle = 100/5 = 20, giving the run 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, all greater than 1 ✓. • c = 25 → middle = 100/25 = 4, giving the run −8 … 16, which violates "each greater than 1" ✗. So the unique valid set has middle term 20. Distractor traps: (A) 4 is the middle of the rejected 25-term run — obtained by skipping the "each greater than 1" constraint check. (B) 5 reports the number of terms (the count c) instead of the middle term. (D) 50 comes from naively halving the sum (100/2), treating it like a pair/average of two numbers. (E) 18 is the smallest term of the correct run, an endpoint reported instead of the middle. Only 20 satisfies sum = count × middle with every integer greater than 1.

questions.competency: Solving a one-variable linear equation by isolating the unknown through inverse operations (add/subtract constant, then divide by coefficient).
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Isolating an unknown via inverse operations within a two-constraint linear model
questions.stem: A rental company charges a fixed booking fee plus a constant hourly rate. A 3-hour rental costs €47, and the company advertises that "each additional hour after the first always adds the same amount, and renting for the first hour alone costs exactly €23." Let the hourly rate be r euros and the fixed booking fee be b euros, so the cost of an h-hour rental is b + r·h. Using both stated facts, what is the hourly rate r?
questions.explanation: Set up two facts as equations in the linear cost model b + r·h. Fact 1 (3-hour rental): b + 3r = 47. Fact 2 (first hour alone, h = 1, costs €23): b + r = 23. Subtracting the second equation from the first isolates the change over two hours: (b + 3r) − (b + r) = 47 − 23, i.e. 2r = 24, so r = 12. This is the correct answer (C), reached by isolating the unknown through inverse operations (subtract to eliminate b, then divide by the coefficient 2). Distractor A (€8) comes from wrongly dividing the full 3-hour cost by 3 minus something, or treating 47 = 3r+ b with b guessed as 23 then (47−23)/3 = 8 — mistakenly using h = 3 instead of the difference, a coefficient-misuse error. Distractor B (€11) comes from computing b first incorrectly: assuming the "first hour alone" means r = 23 − b with b = 12, then averaging — an averaging misconception (47/? ). More directly, 11 arises from (47 − 3·? ) slips where a solver does 3r + something and rounds; it encodes solving 3r = 34 → r ≈ 11, i.e. subtracting 13 instead of using both equations. Distractor D (€15) comes from ignoring the fixed fee entirely and doing (47 − 23)/? incorrectly as 47 − 32, or from (47+23)/? ; specifically it is the trap of computing b = 47 − 32 and mislabeling. Most cleanly, 15 = 47 − 32 arises from a solver who finds b = 8 (from 3r = 39) and reports 15 by mixing r and b. Distractor E (€23) is the salient trap of reporting the first-hour total cost €23 as the hourly rate, forgetting that €23 already includes the fixed booking fee b, so it overstates r. Only C survives using both constraints correctly.

questions.competency: Dimensional analysis: deriving a physical quantity's dimensional formula (in M, L, T) from its defining relation, and using dimensional homogeneity to identify or check unknown quantities/exponents.
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Using dimensional homogeneity to solve for an unknown exponent in a composite relation
questions.questionType: Multi-step dimensional reasoning (solve for unknown power)
questions.stem:
In a fluid-mechanics experiment, the steady (terminal) speed v at which a small sphere sinks through a viscous liquid is modelled by the empirical relation

  v = k · rᵖ · g · ρ / η

where k is a dimensionless constant, r is the sphere's radius, g is the acceleration due to gravity, ρ is the density of the liquid, and η is the liquid's coefficient of viscosity, whose dimensional formula is [η] = M L⁻¹ T⁻¹. Assuming the relation is dimensionally homogeneous, the exponent p must equal:
questions.explanation:
Write each factor in M, L, T. v = L T⁻¹; rᵖ = Lᵖ; g = L T⁻²; ρ (mass ÷ volume) = M L⁻³; and 1/η = M⁻¹ L T. Multiplying the right-hand side: M-exponent = +1 (ρ) − 1 (η) = 0; T-exponent = −2 (g) + 1 (η) = −1; L-exponent = p + 1 (g) − 3 (ρ) + 1 (η) = p − 1. The M and T powers already match v automatically, so homogeneity is fixed by the length equation: p − 1 = 1 ⇒ p = 2, giving option C.

Distractor traps:
A) 0 — confuses the liquid's (volume) density ρ = M L⁻³ with a linear density M L⁻¹, giving p + 1 − 1 + 1 = 1 ⇒ p = 0.
B) 1 — forgets that v itself carries one power of length and sets the right-hand side's length exponent to 0: p − 1 = 0 ⇒ p = 1.
D) 3 — treats g as a pure T⁻² acceleration and drops its length dimension: p + 0 − 3 + 1 = 1 ⇒ p = 3.
E) 4 — fails to invert η's dimensions for the denominator (uses L⁻¹ instead of L⁺¹): p + 1 − 3 − 1 = 1 ⇒ p = 4.
Each wrong answer follows from one specific dimensional slip, and only p = 2 makes all three dimensions balance.

questions.competency: Propagation of measurement uncertainty through a power-law formula: combining fractional/percentage errors under multiplication and exponentiation, where each factor's relative error adds and a variable raised to power n contributes n times its relative error (here ΔKE% = Δm% + 2·Δv%).
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Propagation of maximum measurement uncertainty through a power-law formula; exponent-weighted error sensitivity and strategic error reduction
questions.stem: A technician determines the power dissipated in a resistive heating element from P = V²/R, where V is the measured voltage across the element and R its measured resistance. Her instruments give a maximum error of ±2% in V and ±3% in R. She has time to recalibrate exactly one instrument, which would halve that single measurement's percentage error (leaving the other unchanged). To obtain the smallest possible maximum percentage error in the calculated power P, which instrument should she improve, and what maximum percentage error in P then results?

options.A: Improve the voltmeter (V); the resulting maximum error in P is about 5%
options.B: Improve the ohmmeter (R); the resulting maximum error in P is about 5.5%
options.C: Improve the ohmmeter (R); the resulting maximum error in P is about 3.5%
options.D: Either instrument gives the same result; the maximum error in P is about 5% either way
options.E: Improve the voltmeter (V); the resulting maximum error in P is about 4%

questions.explanation: For P = V²/R the maximum fractional error adds each factor's contribution weighted by its exponent: ΔP% = 2·ΔV% + ΔR%. Initially ΔP% = 2(2) + 3 = 7%. The key insight is that V enters with exponent 2, so each point of error in V is worth twice as much as a point of error in R — halving V's error removes 2×(1%) = 2%, while halving R's error removes only 1×(1.5%) = 1.5%. Halving V: ΔP% = 2(1) + 3 = 5%. Halving R: ΔP% = 2(2) + 1.5 = 5.5%. So improving V wins even though R has the larger raw error → answer A (5%). Distractor traps: B does the arithmetic correctly but chooses R because its raw error (3%) is larger, ignoring the ×2 weighting on V — the central misconception. C drops the exponent entirely, treating P ∝ V/R so ΔP% = ΔV% + ½ΔR% = 2 + 1.5 = 3.5%, which makes R (the larger error) look like the better target. D assumes halving either measurement cuts the total error equally (symmetry), missing that the exponent breaks the symmetry. E correctly identifies V but forgets to re-apply the factor of 2 to the reduced value, computing 1% + 3% = 4%.

questions.competency: Interpreting instantaneous velocity as the derivative of a position function and locating the instant of momentary rest where velocity changes sign (v = dx/dt = 0)
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Kinematics — position–time graphs and instantaneous velocity
questions.skill: Reading instantaneous velocity as the slope of an x–t graph and locating momentary rest at the horizontal-tangent turning point where velocity changes sign
questions.stem: A magnetic test sled runs back and forth along a single straight horizontal rail. A position sensor records the sled's coordinate x along the rail as a function of time t, and the recorded data are plotted in the position–time (x–t) graph shown below. The sled is momentarily at rest at any instant when its velocity is zero and it is about to reverse its direction of travel. Reading the graph, determine the instant at which the sled is momentarily at rest.
questions.explanation:
On an x–t graph the velocity is the slope of the curve, so momentary rest occurs where the tangent is horizontal (slope = 0) and the velocity changes sign. The plotted curve falls from x = 5 m at t = 0, reaches its lowest point x = −4 m at t = 3 s, then rises again. Only at t = 3 s is the tangent horizontal: the slope is negative just before (sled moving in −x) and positive just after (sled moving in +x), so the velocity passes through zero and reverses. Hence C is correct.

A (t = 0 s): assumes the motion "starts from rest." But at t = 0 the curve is steep (large negative slope), so the sled is already moving fastest, not at rest — this confuses the beginning of the record with zero velocity.

B (t = 1 s): the curve crosses x = 0 here. This trap mistakes zero position (passing the origin of the rail) for zero velocity; the slope at t = 1 s is clearly nonzero, so the sled is moving quickly through the origin.

D (t = 5 s): the curve crosses x = 0 a second time on the way back. Same position-vs-velocity confusion as B, offered symmetrically to lure students who match the two axis crossings; the slope there is nonzero (positive).

E (t = 6 s): picks the point of greatest x (a "peak"), expecting the turning point to be a maximum as in a projectile height–time graph. This parabola opens upward, so its turning point is the minimum at t = 3 s; at t = 6 s the slope is steep and positive, not zero.

questions.competency: Evaluating a trigonometric ratio at a special angle by interpreting it geometrically (the tangent as the ratio of opposite to adjacent legs / slope of the terminal ray on the unit circle), rather than reciting a memorized table value.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Trigonometric ratios on the unit circle
questions.skill: Interpreting the tangent geometrically as the signed slope (y/x) of the terminal ray
questions.stem: In the coordinate plane shown, the terminal side of angle θ (measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis) passes through the point P. A right triangle is inscribed with its legs parallel to the axes, and the two leg lengths are marked on the figure. Using the geometric meaning of the tangent — the ratio of the terminal ray's vertical displacement to its horizontal displacement — determine the exact value of tan θ. (Read the leg lengths and the quadrant directly from the figure.)
questions.explanation: From the figure, P lies in the second quadrant: its horizontal displacement is −3 (the ray runs left of the y-axis) and its vertical displacement is +3√3. The tangent is the slope of the terminal ray, tan θ = (vertical)/(horizontal) = (3√3)/(−3) = −√3, so B is correct (this is the 120° ray, but the value is read from the figure, not recalled). Each distractor is a specific error path: A = √3/2 comes from computing sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse using r = √(3² + (3√3)²) = 6, i.e. 3√3/6 — using the hypotenuse instead of the adjacent leg. C = √3 has the correct magnitude but drops the sign, ignoring that x < 0 in the second quadrant (treating both legs as positive). D = −√3/3 = −1/√3 inverts the ratio, computing horizontal/vertical (adjacent/opposite) instead of opposite/adjacent. E = −1/2 comes from computing cos θ = x/r = −3/6 — the wrong ratio entirely. All five differ in sign and form, so none can be eliminated by inspection, and only B is the correctly signed slope.

questions.competency: Solving a logarithmic equation via the definition of a logarithm (log-to-exponential conversion) with domain validation; reading the zero/x-intercept of a transformed logarithmic function.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Log-to-exponential conversion with domain validation; reading a transformed logarithmic graph
questions.stem:
The curve in the figure is the graph of a function f. The graph never states its formula: you must determine f from its vertical asymptote and the three marked points, all of which have integer coordinates. Using that function, find every real number x that satisfies

f(x) + f(x − 2) = 3.
questions.explanation:
Read the figure first. The vertical asymptote is at x = 1, so f has the form f(x) = log_b(x − 1). The marked point (3, 1) gives log_b(2) = 1, so b = 2; the point (5, 2) confirms log_2(4) = 2, and (2, 0) is the x-intercept log_2(1) = 0. Hence f(x) = log_2(x − 1) — this cannot be known from the text alone.

Now f(x) + f(x − 2) = log_2(x − 1) + log_2(x − 3) = log_2[(x − 1)(x − 3)] = 3. Converting to exponential form (the definition of a logarithm): (x − 1)(x − 3) = 2^3 = 8, so x^2 − 4x − 5 = 0, giving (x − 5)(x + 1) = 0 and x = 5 or x = −1. Domain validation: both logs require x − 1 > 0 AND x − 3 > 0, i.e. x > 3. Only x = 5 survives; x = −1 is extraneous. Correct answer: C.

Distractor traps: (A) x = 4 comes from dropping the exponential step — setting the product equal to 3 instead of 2^3 = 8: (x−1)(x−3) = 3 gives x^2 − 4x = 0, x = 4 after domain. (B) x = 6 encodes the log-of-a-sum error, treating f(x)+f(x−2) as log_2[(x−1)+(x−3)] = log_2(2x−4) = 3, so 2x − 4 = 8, x = 6. (D) x = 5 and x = −1 solves the quadratic correctly but skips domain validation entirely, keeping the extraneous root. (E) x = −1 inverts the domain test — writing the condition as x < 3 (a flipped inequality), which accepts −1 and rejects the true root 5.

questions.competency: recognizing a perfect-square quadratic and its repeated root, linking factorization to a parabola tangent to the x-axis
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Quadratic functions: discriminant, repeated roots, and parabola–axis tangency
questions.skill: Reading a perfect-square (tangent-to-x-axis) parabola from its graph and converting geometric features into the coefficients of y = x² + bx + c via the zero-discriminant condition
questions.stem: The figure shows the parabola y = x² + bx + c, where b and c are real constants. The parabola is tangent to the x-axis. Using only the information shown in the figure, determine the value of c − b.
questions.explanation: See explanation field.

questions.competency: Solving a single-variable linear equation by isolating the unknown through inverse operations (add/subtract a constant, then divide by the coefficient)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Setting up and solving a single-variable linear equation with the unknown on both sides by combining like terms and dividing by the coefficient
questions.stem: A laboratory has two water tanks. Tank A currently holds 40 litres and is draining steadily at 3 litres per minute. Tank B currently holds 28 litres and is being filled steadily at 1 litre per minute. Assuming both rates stay constant, after how many minutes will the two tanks hold exactly the same volume of water?
questions.explanation:
