Model each volume as a linear function of time t (minutes): Tank A = 40 − 3t, Tank B = 28 + t. Set them equal (the single linear equation to solve): 40 − 3t = 28 + t. Isolate t by inverse operations: add 3t to both sides → 40 = 28 + 4t; subtract 28 → 12 = 4t; divide by the coefficient 4 → t = 3. Check: A = 40 − 9 = 31 L, B = 28 + 3 = 31 L. Correct answer B.

Distractor traps:
• A) t = 6: used the DIFFERENCE of the rates (3 − 1 = 2) as the closing rate, computing 12 ÷ 2. This ignores that draining and filling both shrink the gap, so the correct combined rate is the sum, not the difference.
• C) t = 12: divided the 12-litre gap by only Tank B's fill rate (1), i.e. 12 ÷ 1, crediting only one tank with closing the gap.
• D) t = 4: divided the 12-litre gap by only Tank A's drain rate (3), i.e. 12 ÷ 3, the mirror-image single-rate error.
• E) t = 17: added the initial volumes (40 + 28 = 68) instead of subtracting to find the gap, then divided by the correct combined rate 4, giving 68 ÷ 4. This confuses "difference to be closed" with "total volume."

questions.competency: Evaluating and combining integer powers of small bases (applying exponent definitions and order of operations to compute a product of powers)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Combining integer powers of a common base using the power-of-a-power and product rules
questions.stem: A memory buffer has a capacity of exactly 4⁵ × 8² × 16³ bytes. Written as a single power of 2, this capacity equals:
questions.explanation: Rewrite each factor as a power of 2, using the power-of-a-power rule (multiply the exponents), then the product rule (add the exponents). 4⁵ = (2²)⁵ = 2¹⁰; 8² = (2³)² = 2⁶; 16³ = (2⁴)³ = 2¹². Product = 2^(10+6+12) = 2²⁸ (E). The number is far too large to brute-force, so the exponent laws must be applied — this is why the item is selective. Distractor traps: (A) 2¹⁰ ignores the base conversion entirely and simply adds the visible exponents 5+2+3, treating 4⁵ as 2⁵, 8² as 2², 16³ as 2³. (B) 2¹⁹ applies the power-of-a-power rule as ADDITION instead of multiplication within each factor: (2+5)+(3+2)+(4+3) = 7+5+7. (C) 2²⁰ correctly handles 4⁵ and 8² but drops the exponent on the last factor, reading 16³ as just 16 = 2⁴: 10+6+4. (D) 2²⁵ mis-identifies 16 as a power of 2, using 16 = 2³ (confusing it with 8) so 16³ = 2⁹: 10+6+9. Each distractor encodes one specific, distinct error and none is also correct.

questions.competency: Geometric/exponential decay through repeated percentage multiplication: recognizing that a constant annual depreciation rate compounds multiplicatively, so value after n periods is V0·(1−r)^n rather than V0·(1−n·r) (linear) — and correctly resisting the linear-subtraction trap.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Recognizing multiplicative percentage decay and extrapolating a geometric sequence from a graph while rejecting linear-subtraction reasoning
questions.stem:
The solid curve in the graph shows the resale value of an industrial 3D printer that loses the SAME percentage of its remaining value every year; the marked dots give its actual value at the end of years 0, 1 and 2. The dashed line shows an alternative model in which the printer instead loses a fixed number of dollars each year. Reading the required figures only from the graph, what is the printer's actual resale value at the end of year 3?

(No numerical values are given in the text — you must read them from the marked points.)
questions.explanation:
From the marked dots: year 0 = €20,000, year 1 = €14,000, year 2 = €9,800. The ratio 14,000/20,000 = 0.7, and 9,800/14,000 = 0.7 confirm a constant multiplicative factor of 0.7 (a 30% loss of the REMAINING value each year), so value follows V0·(0.7)^n. Year 3 = 9,800 × 0.7 = 20,000 × 0.7^3 = €6,860 (C). 

Distractor traps: (A) €2,000 = the linear-subtraction fallacy 'n×r': 3 years × 30% = 90% lost, leaving 10% of €20,000; this is exactly where the DASHED (fixed-dollar) line lands at year 3, the trap the figure is built to expose. (B) €5,600 extends the last visible straight segment linearly (9,800 − 4,200, the year 1→2 drop) instead of applying the ratio — extrapolating the graph as a straight line. (D) €9,800 is an off-by-one read: reporting the year-2 dot without advancing one more period. (E) €4,802 over-compounds by one year (0.7^4, the year-4 value), reading one period too far along the curve. Only C applies the correct geometric factor to the correct period.

questions.competency: Part-whole proportional reasoning: expressing a complementary subset as a percentage of a total (total minus the known part, then converting the resulting fraction to a percentage).
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Percentages and complementary subsets from contingency tables
questions.skill: Part-whole proportional reasoning: expressing a complementary subset as a percentage of the total after deriving a hidden count from a two-way table
questions.stem: A polytechnic surveyed all of its engineering students, classifying each student by faculty (Mechanical or Electrical) and by whether they passed the national certification exam. The complete results are summarised in the two-way table below, in which one interior value has been deliberately left blank. Using the table, what percentage of the surveyed students are NOT Electrical-engineering students who passed the certification exam?
questions.explanation:
First derive the blank cell. Electrical students who passed = (Passed column total) − (Mechanical ∩ Passed) = 260 − 150 = 110, which is confirmed by the Electrical row: 180 − 70 = 110. The group asked for is the COMPLEMENT of that single intersection over the grand total: (400 − 110)/400 = 290/400 = 72.5% → E (correct).

Distractor traps:
A) 27.5% = 110/400 — computes the target subgroup itself but ignores the word "NOT," failing to take the complement.
B) 35% = (400 − 260)/400 — takes the complement of the Passed column margin (260) instead of the derived Electrical∩Passed cell, complementing the wrong quantity.
C) 55% = (400 − 180)/400 — uses the entire Electrical row total (180) as "Electrical who passed," never isolating the passed sub-cell, then complements.
D) 62.5% = (400 − 150)/400 — grabs the visible Mechanical∩Passed cell (150) rather than deriving the missing Electrical∩Passed value, then complements.
Each distractor corresponds to a specific misstep in reading the table, deriving the hidden cell, or applying the complement, and none is also correct.

questions.competency: Reversing a percentage change: recovering an original quantity from its post-discount value by inverting a multiplicative decrease (original = final / (1 - rate)).
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Reversing successive percentage decreases to recover an original quantity
questions.stem: During a two-phase clearance, the price of a cordless drill was first cut by 25%. The following week the already-reduced price was cut by a further 20%. A customer who buys the drill in the second week pays 360 euro. What was the drill's original list price, before any reduction?
questions.explanation: The two discounts act multiplicatively because the second is applied to the already-reduced price: final = original x 0.75 x 0.80 = original x 0.60. Reversing requires dividing by the combined multiplier: original = 360 / 0.60 = 600 euro (check: 600 -> 450 -> 360). (E) is correct. Distractor traps: (A) 450 = 360/0.80, reversing only the second (20%) markdown and forgetting the first. (B) 480 = 360/0.75, reversing only the first (25%) markdown and forgetting the second. (C) 522 = 360 x 1.45, collapsing the two cuts into a single additive 45% and then 'adding it back' instead of dividing (double error: additive combination plus inverse-as-addition). (D) 540 = 360 x 1.25 x 1.20, keeping the correct multiplicative structure but multiplying the factors back instead of dividing by them — the classic 'add the percentage back' misconception. Every option exceeds the paid price of 360, so none is eliminable by the trivial 'original must be larger' check; the discriminating insight is that sequential discounts compound (0.75 x 0.80 = 0.60, not 1 - 0.45 = 0.55) and that reversal is division, not re-inflation.

questions.competency: Solving a system of two simultaneous linear equations in two unknowns (elimination/substitution) and, geometrically, interpreting the solution as the intersection point of two lines in the coordinate plane.
questions.subject: logic
questions.topic: Mathematics / Logic — Algebra and Coordinate Geometry
questions.subtopic: Systems of two linear equations in two unknowns; intersection of two lines
questions.skill: Extract each line's equation from a labeled graph, solve the 2×2 system by elimination, and interpret the solution as the intersection point
questions.questionType: Essential-figure / graph interpretation with misconception distractors
questions.stem: The figure shows two straight lines, r and s, on a coordinate grid. Several points with integer coordinates that lie on each line are marked, but the point where the lines cross is NOT labelled. Taken together, lines r and s represent a system of two linear equations in x and y. Reading the data you need from the graph, determine the ordered pair (x, y) that is the simultaneous solution of the system — that is, the coordinates of the point where the two lines intersect. Which of the following is that point?
questions.explanation:
From the marked points, line r passes through (0, 5) and (5, 0), so its slope is (0-5)/(5-0) = -1 and its equation is y = -x + 5, i.e. x + y = 5. Line s passes through (0, -1) and (1, 1), so its slope is (1-(-1))/(1-0) = 2 and its equation is y = 2x - 1, i.e. 2x - y = 1. Adding the two equations eliminates y: (x + y) + (2x - y) = 5 + 1, giving 3x = 6, so x = 2 and y = 3. The intersection — the only point satisfying BOTH equations — is (2, 3), option A.

Distractor traps:
- B (3, 2): the correct pair with its coordinates transposed, reported as (y, x). It even lies on line r (3 + 2 = 5), which makes it visually tempting, but it fails s (2·3 - 2 = 4 ≠ 1).
- C (4, 1): reads line s's slope as the reciprocal 1/2 instead of 2 (run-over-rise inverted), giving y = ½x - 1; solving -x + 5 = ½x - 1 yields x = 4, y = 1. This point sits on line r, not at the true crossing.
- D (5, -1): mistakes the two y-intercepts (5 from r and -1 from s) for the intersection point — confusing 'intercepts' with 'intersection'. It satisfies neither equation (5 + (-1) = 4 ≠ 5).
- E (2, 2): finds x = 2 correctly but fails to substitute back, reusing the x-value for y instead of computing y = 3.
Only A satisfies both x + y = 5 and 2x - y = 1, so exactly one option is correct.

questions.competency: Proportional reasoning via ratio scaling: mapping a known quantity onto its share of a part-to-part ratio to recover the unit value, then rescaling to find the corresponding other part. At elite level this competency should require multi-constraint proportional reasoning — e.g. combining two ratios sharing a common term, handling a part-to-whole vs part-to-part distinction, or inferring an unknown before the ratio can be applied — rather than a single divide-and-multiply.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Reconciling two ratios that share a common term, then scaling a part-to-part sum to recover an unknown part
questions.stem: At a robotics competition the entrants are split into three divisions: Junior, Senior, and Open. The number of Junior teams to Senior teams is in the ratio 4 : 5, and the number of Senior teams to Open teams is in the ratio 3 : 2. Counting only the Junior and Open divisions, there are 66 teams altogether. How many Senior teams are there?
questions.explanation: The two ratios share the Senior term, so they cannot be chained directly — the shared term must first be made consistent. Junior:Senior = 4:5 and Senior:Open = 3:2; scaling each so Senior matches its LCM (15) gives Junior:Senior = 12:15 and Senior:Open = 15:10, i.e. Junior:Senior:Open = 12:15:10. The 66 teams are the Junior + Open divisions only (a part-to-part, non-adjacent sum, not a whole): 12 + 10 = 22 parts = 66, so 1 part = 3. Senior = 15 parts = 45 (D). Trap analysis: (E) 55 is the central error — chaining the ratios as 4:5:2 without reconciling the common Senior term, giving Junior+Open = 6 parts = 66, 1 part = 11, Senior = 5×11 = 55; it is the tempting answer for a fast solver because it is the right division computed by the wrong method, and it happens to be a clean integer. (C) 44 also fails to reconcile the shared term (4:5:2) but then reports the Junior division (4 parts × 11) instead of Senior; 44 sits right next to 45 to punish the reconciliation slip. (B) 36 reconciles correctly (12:15:10, 1 part = 3) but answers the wrong division, reporting Junior = 12 × 3. (A) 30 likewise reconciles correctly but reports Open = 10 × 3. Only D combines the correct reconciliation of the shared term with the correct target division.

questions.competency: Recovering a square's side length from its perimeter and using it to compute area — relating the linear (perimeter) and quadratic (area) measures of a plane figure through the shared side dimension. Generalizable to reasoning about how perimeter and area scale non-linearly, or deriving the area of a composite/constrained figure from perimeter information.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: area of a composite/trapezoidal figure recovered from perimeter
questions.skill: reconstructing an unknown linear dimension from a stated perimeter (with a Pythagorean coupling for the slant), then relating it to the quadratic area measure of a composite/constrained figure
questions.stem: The figure shows the flat metal face-plate of a support bracket. Its outline is a four-sided polygon: the two vertical edges (left and right) and the horizontal base meet at right angles, while the top edge is a single straight slanted cut. Only the two vertical edges are dimensioned in the figure; the length of the base (marked "?") is not given. The total perimeter of the plate is 36 cm. What is the area of the plate?
questions.explanation: The two vertical sides (12 cm and 6 cm) are the parallel sides of a right trapezoid; the base b and the slanted top s are both unknown. Because the base meets both verticals at right angles, the slant's vertical drop is 12 − 6 = 6, so s = √(b² + 6²) = √(b² + 36). Perimeter: 12 + 6 + b + s = 36, so b + √(b²+36) = 18 → √(b²+36) = 18 − b → b² + 36 = 324 − 36b + b² → 36b = 288 → b = 8 (and s = 10). Area = ½(12 + 6)(8) = 72 cm² → B. This REQUIRES the figure: the text alone never states which edges are parallel, where the right angles are, or which side is the unknown base, and the base cannot be read off — it must be recovered from the perimeter via the Pythagorean coupling with the slant. Distractor traps: A) 48 = 8 × 6 — correct base but treats the plate as a rectangle of height equal to the shorter vertical. C) 81 = 9 × 9 — splits the leftover perimeter 18 evenly between base and slant (b = s = 9), skipping the Pythagorean relation, then averages the verticals. D) 96 = 8 × 12 — correct base but treats it as a rectangle of height equal to the taller vertical, ignoring the trapezoid averaging. E) 108 = 12 × 9 — mistakes the slant's vertical drop (6) for the slant's length, giving base = 36 − 12 − 6 − 6 = 12, then averages correctly. Only B uses both the correct base (Pythagoras + perimeter) and the correct trapezoid-area rule.

questions.competency: Computing a component quantity as a percentage of a known total (part = percent × whole), the core of proportional/percentage reasoning applied to mixtures and concentrations.
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Proportional/percentage reasoning: computing a component quantity as part = percent × whole, tracking it through a drain-and-replace operation
questions.stem: A 500 mL radiator is filled with a coolant that is 20% antifreeze by volume, the rest being water. A mechanic drains off exactly 100 mL of this coolant (fully mixed, so the drained liquid has the same composition as the rest) and then tops the radiator back up to 500 mL using pure antifreeze. What is the antifreeze concentration of the coolant now in the radiator?
questions.explanation: Start with the antifreeze inventory: 20% of 500 mL = 100 mL antifreeze (and 400 mL water). Because the drained 100 mL has the SAME 20% composition, it carries off 0.20 × 100 = 20 mL of antifreeze (and 80 mL water), leaving 80 mL antifreeze in 400 mL of coolant. Topping up to 500 mL adds 100 mL of PURE antifreeze, giving 80 + 100 = 180 mL antifreeze in a 500 mL total. Concentration = 180 / 500 = 36% (option C). Trap C-checks each distractor: (A) 16% comes from treating the top-up as water instead of antifreeze — 80 mL / 500 mL — i.e. forgetting to add the pure antifreeze back. (B) 20% is the 'equal-volume swap leaves it unchanged' misconception (or stopping after the drain: 80 mL / 400 mL) — it ignores that the refill is pure, not same-strength. (D) 40% assumes the drained 100 mL was all water, so the antifreeze is conserved at 100 mL and 100 mL more is added → 200 / 500; this forgets the drained mixture also carried antifreeze. (E) 45% correctly finds 180 mL of antifreeze but divides by the post-drain volume of 400 mL instead of the refilled 500 mL — a wrong-denominator error (and physically impossible, since the antifreeze can never exceed 200 mL / 500 mL = 40%). Only C uses the correct inventory and the correct final volume.

questions.competency: Translating a verbal constraint into a linear equation over consecutive integers: representing three consecutive numbers as n-1, n, n+1 (or 3n+3), recognizing that their sum equals three times the middle term, and solving for the sequence.
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Consecutive integers under a linear constraint
questions.skill: Translating a verbal constraint into a linear equation over a run of consecutive integers, partitioning the run, solving, and mapping the variable to the requested term
questions.stem: Five consecutive integers are written down in increasing order. It turns out that the sum of the three smallest of them is exactly equal to the sum of the two largest of them. What is the value of the LARGEST of the five integers?
questions.explanation:
Represent the five consecutive integers as n, n+1, n+2, n+3, n+4. The three smallest sum to (n)+(n+1)+(n+2) = 3n+3; the two largest sum to (n+3)+(n+4) = 2n+7. The condition gives 3n+3 = 2n+7, so n = 4. The integers are 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and the largest is 8 (check: 4+5+6 = 15 = 7+8). Correct: D (8).

Distractor traps, each a distinct error path:
- A) 4 — the value of n itself. The student sets up and solves the equation correctly but reports the variable (the smallest term) instead of mapping it to the requested largest term (n+4).
- B) 6 — the middle integer. This is the "sum ÷ 3 = the middle number" reflex carried over from the trivial three-consecutive-integers version; that shortcut does not apply to this five-term partition problem, so the reflex actively misleads.
- C) 7 — the fourth integer (n+3). An off-by-one miscount of which term counts as "largest" among the five, reporting the second-largest.
- E) 11 — comes from dropping the internal +1 and +2 offsets when summing the three smallest, i.e. writing 3n instead of 3n+3. That gives 3n = 2n+7, n = 7, and largest n+4 = 11. It encodes the failure to represent the increments of consecutive integers within a group.

Why it is selective: the sum-of-consecutive-integers "divide by 3" habit that trivializes the source item produces distractor B here, and back-solving from the options requires constructing five consecutive integers and comparing two partial sums for each candidate, so no option is eliminable by inspection.

questions.competency: Computing average speed as total distance divided by total time — and, at Elite level, distinguishing true average speed from the naive arithmetic mean of segment speeds (harmonic-mean reasoning when a trip is split into legs at different rates).
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Computing overall average speed as total distance over total elapsed time from a multi-segment position–time graph, distinguishing it from the arithmetic mean of segment speeds and from moving-time-only speed
questions.stem: A bicycle courier's delivery run is recorded on the position–time graph below, which plots the courier's distance from the depot against elapsed time. The trip has three legs: an initial ride, a stop, and a final ride. Reading every value directly from the graph, what is the courier's average speed for the ENTIRE trip (from departure to arrival)?
questions.explanation: Average speed for the whole trip = total distance ÷ total elapsed time. From the graph the courier reaches 110 km from the depot at t = 5 h, having started at (0 h, 0 km), so avg = 110 km ÷ 5 h = 22 km/h → B. Each distractor is a specific misconception. A (20 km/h): reading only the slope of the final, longest leg (from (2 h, 50 km) to (5 h, 110 km): 60 km / 3 h = 20), mistaking the ending steady rate for the trip average. C (27.5 km/h): dividing total distance by MOVING time only (110 km ÷ 4 h), forgetting that the 1-hour rest (the flat segment from t = 1 h to t = 2 h) still counts as elapsed time. D (35 km/h): taking the arithmetic mean of the two moving-leg speeds, (50 + 20)/2 — the harmonic-mean fallacy of averaging rates instead of weighting them by their distances/times. E (50 km/h): reading only the steepest first leg (0→50 km in 1 h), mistaking peak speed for average speed. The figure is essential: none of the coordinates (50 km at 1 h, rest to 2 h, 110 km at 5 h) appear in the text, so the values and the presence of the rest interval must be read from the graph.

questions.competency: Recognizing a right triangle from a Pythagorean triple and computing area as half the product of the legs
questions.subject: logic
questions.subtopic: Right triangles, Pythagorean triples, and area on a coordinate grid
questions.skill: Recognizing a right triangle from a Pythagorean triple and computing area as half the product of the legs
questions.questionType: coordinate-geometry / area of a right triangle
questions.stem: A land surveyor records three boundary stakes of a triangular plot as the points A, B and C on a coordinate grid marked in metres, as shown. The length of each boundary segment is indicated on the figure. No angle is marked as a right angle. What is the area of the plot?
questions.explanation:
Step 1 — recognise the right triangle from the triple. The marked sides are 15, 20 and 25 m, i.e. 5×(3,4,5). Since 15² + 20² = 225 + 400 = 625 = 25², the triangle is right-angled, and the right angle sits opposite the longest side (BC = 25), namely at vertex A. The grid confirms this: A→B has slope 12/9 = 4/3 and A→C has slope −12/16 = −3/4, whose product is −1, so AB ⊥ AC. The two legs are therefore AB = 15 and AC = 20; the 25-side is the hypotenuse. Area = ½·(leg)·(leg) = ½·15·20 = 150 m² (B).

Distractor traps:
- A) 192 = ½·16·24: reads the coordinate bounding-box dimensions (x-range 0→16, y-range 0→24) and mistakes those grid spans for the legs, instead of using the true side lengths.
- C) 187.5 = ½·15·25: mislocates the right angle at B, pairing a leg (15) with the hypotenuse (25) — fails to identify which side is the hypotenuse.
- D) 250 = ½·20·25: mislocates the right angle at C, pairing the other leg (20) with the hypotenuse (25).
- E) 300 = 15·20: identifies the legs correctly but forgets the factor ½, using product-of-legs as the area.

The figure is essential: the stem states no lengths and marks no right angle, so the solver must read the side lengths off the figure, deduce from the Pythagorean triple which vertex holds the right angle, and pair the correct two legs — none of which is available from the text alone.

questions.competency: Applying the first law of thermodynamics to a constant-volume process: recognizing that zero volume change means zero work, so all heat supplied goes to internal energy (Q = ΔU)
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Applying Q = ΔU on a constant-volume leg identified from a P-V cycle
questions.stem: A fixed amount of monatomic ideal gas is taken around the cycle A → B → C → A shown on the pressure–volume diagram (arrows give the direction of travel). Consider ONLY the single leg of this cycle during which the gas volume does not change. For that leg, how much heat is exchanged with the surroundings? (Use the sign convention: + means heat absorbed by the gas, − means heat released by the gas. Recall that for a monatomic ideal gas the internal energy is U = (3/2)pV.)

options.A: 0 J — no volume change means no work, so no heat is exchanged on that leg

questions.explanation: First the figure must be read to find the constant-volume (vertical) leg: only A→B is vertical, at V = 2 L with pressure rising from p_A = 100 kPa to p_B = 400 kPa. On a constant-volume leg the area under the path is zero, so W = 0, and the first law gives Q = ΔU. For a monatomic gas ΔU = (3/2)Δ(pV) = (3/2)·V·(p_B − p_A) = (3/2)·(2 L)·(300 kPa) = (3/2)(600 J) = +900 J. Because pressure (hence temperature) rises, ΔU > 0, so heat is absorbed: Q = +900 J (C). Trap A conflates W = 0 with Q = 0 — the defining error this competency targets; in fact zero work means all the heat becomes internal energy, not zero heat. Trap B computes Δ(pV) = 600 J but forgets the 3/2 factor linking pV to the internal energy of a monatomic gas. Trap D has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign, from assuming the gas releases heat (as it would if compressed) rather than reading that pressure and temperature increase. Trap E uses the final-state value (3/2)p_B V = 1200 J instead of the change (3/2)(p_B − p_A)V, forgetting that only the difference in internal energy matters. Note the other two legs are deliberately non-isochoric (B→C is diagonal, C→A is isobaric), so the figure — not the text — is required to locate the correct leg and read its two pressures.

questions.competency: Applying Newton's law of universal gravitation: F = G·m₁·m₂/r², recognizing the inverse-square dependence on separation and direct product dependence on the two masses
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Newton's law of universal gravitation; inverse-square and mass-product dependence
questions.stem: A space probe hovers at the midpoint between a planet and its moon, whose centres are a fixed distance apart. At this midpoint the gravitational pull of the planet on the probe is exactly 9 times the gravitational pull of the moon on the probe. Engineers now move the probe along the straight line joining the two bodies to a new hover point where the planet's pull and the moon's pull are equal in magnitude (so the net gravitational force is zero). Measuring distances from the planet's centre, at what fraction of the total planet–moon separation is this balance point located?

options.A: 3/4 of the way from the planet to the moon
options.C: 1/4 of the way from the planet to the moon
options.D: 9/10 of the way from the planet to the moon
options.E: 1/10 of the way from the planet to the moon

questions.explanation: At the midpoint both bodies are the same distance from the probe, so the inverse-square term is identical for each; the 9:1 force ratio must therefore come entirely from the masses. Hence M_planet / M_moon = 9. At the balance point, let the distance from the planet be d and the total separation be L, so the distance from the moon is (L − d). Equal forces require G·M_planet/d² = G·M_moon/(L − d)². Substituting M_planet = 9·M_moon gives 9/d² = 1/(L − d)², so 3/d = 1/(L − d), giving 3(L − d) = d, hence d = (3/4)L. The balance point is three-quarters of the way from the planet to the moon — closer to the weaker moon, as expected. Correct: A. Distractor B assumes the balance point is the midpoint, wrongly equating equal DISTANCE with equal FORCE and ignoring the mass difference entirely. Distractor C is the mirror error: taking d = L/(1+3) = L/4, placing the balance point near the planet — it inverts which body the probe must sit closer to (a student who reasons the probe should be nearer the more massive body). Distractor D comes from using the mass ratio directly instead of its square root: setting 9/d² = 1/(L−d)² but solving as 9(L−d) = d, giving d = (9/10)L. Distractor E is the same square-root omission mirrored, d = L/10, placing it near the planet. Only A correctly takes the square root of the mass ratio (√9 = 3) demanded by the inverse-square law.

questions.competency: recognizing that an even power is non-negative to determine the solution set of a polynomial inequality with no real solutions
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: quadratic inequalities and the geometry of the parabola vertex
questions.skill: recognizing that a squared (even-power) term is non-negative, so a strict inequality demanding a value below a parabola's minimum has an empty real solution set
questions.stem: The figure shows the graph of a quadratic function y = f(x) (solid curve) together with the dashed horizontal line y = 4. Reading the necessary information from the graph, determine the complete solution set, over the real numbers, of the strict inequality f(x) < 4.

options.C: There is no real value of x that satisfies the inequality

questions.explanation: From the graph the parabola opens upward with its vertex (lowest point) exactly on the dashed line, at (3, 4). So the minimum value of f is 4, meaning f(x) = 4 only at x = 3 and f(x) > 4 everywhere else — equivalently f(x) − 4 = a(x − 3)² with a > 0, a square that is never negative. The strict inequality f(x) < 4 asks where the curve lies strictly BELOW the line; the curve only touches the line and never dips below it, so the solution set is empty. Correct: C. A (x = 3) is the tangency point, where f equals 4, not less than 4 — the trap of confusing < with ≤. B (1 < x < 5) treats the single tangency as if the curve crossed the line at two points, inventing phantom roots and an interval below the line. D (x < 3) mistakes the left, decreasing branch for the part lying below the line, though that branch is still above y = 4. E (all x except 3) reverses the inequality: it correctly sees f(x) ≥ 4 with equality only at x = 3 but reports where f(x) > 4 instead of where f(x) < 4.

questions.competency: Applying the Remainder Theorem: the remainder of P(x) divided by (x − a) equals P(a), via evaluation at the root of the linear divisor
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Polynomial division and the Remainder Theorem
questions.skill: Applying the Remainder Theorem: the remainder of P(x) divided by (x − a) equals P(a)
questions.stem: A polynomial P(x) with real coefficients satisfies two conditions: the sum of all its coefficients equals 7, and P(x) leaves a remainder of −5 when divided by x. A new polynomial is defined by R(x) = P(x) + 3x − 1. What is the remainder when R(x) is divided by (x − 1)?
questions.explanation: The key insight is that evaluating a polynomial at x = 1 gives the sum of its coefficients, so the "sum of coefficients = 7" condition means P(1) = 7. By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder of R(x) ÷ (x − 1) equals R(1) = P(1) + 3(1) − 1 = 7 + 3 − 1 = 9 (C). The second condition — remainder −5 on division by x, i.e. P(0) = −5 (the constant term) — is a deliberate lure that is irrelevant to the answer. Distractor traps: A (7) applies the Remainder Theorem correctly but forgets to add the +3x − 1 transformation, reporting P(1) itself. B (11) mishandles the sign of the constant, computing 7 + 3 + 1. D (−3) makes the classic error of thinking the "remainder" is the constant term, using P(0) = −5 in place of P(1): −5 + 3 − 1 = −3. E (−5) assumes the remainder is unchanged by the divisor and just reuses the remainder of P on division by x. Each distractor encodes a distinct, specific misconception, and only C follows the correct multi-step path.

questions.competency: evaluating and summing cosines of the known angles of a standard special triangle (45-45-90)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: special right triangles and trigonometric values of standard angles
questions.skill: deducing the special angles of a 45-45-90 triangle from coordinate data and summing their cosines
questions.stem: A steel gusset plate is modelled as triangle ABC on a coordinate grid (units in cm), exactly as shown in the figure. The vertex positions and the marked interior angle are given only in the figure. Using this information, evaluate the sum cos A + cos B + cos C of the cosines of the plate's three interior angles.
questions.explanation: Read the vertices from the figure: A(2,1), B(4,2), C(1,3). The leg vectors from the marked right-angle vertex are AB = (2,1) and AC = (−1,2). Their dot product is 2·(−1) + 1·2 = 0, confirming the right angle at A, and |AB| = |AC| = √5, so the triangle is isosceles and right-angled — a 45-45-90 triangle. Hence A = 90°, B = C = 45°, giving cos A + cos B + cos C = 0 + √2/2 + √2/2 = √2 (option C). Distractor traps: (A) 1 comes from misjudging the tilted, scalene-looking triangle as near-equilateral and taking the base angles as 60° → 2cos60° + cos90° = 1; the coordinates must be used to see the legs are equal, not eyeballed. (B) √2/2 collapses the two equal base angles into a single term because of the symmetry, counting cos45° only once plus cos90° = 0. (D) 1 + √2 uses cos90° = 1 (confusing the cosine of the right angle with sin90°), giving 1 + √2/2 + √2/2. (E) 3√2/2 ignores the marked right angle and treats all three interior angles as 45°, giving 3·√2/2. Each wrong path fails a different required step — reading the coordinates, identifying which angle is the right angle, or evaluating cos90° — so the figure is essential and no distractor is also correct.

questions.competency: applying exponent product/quotient laws to combine same-base powers with symbolic exponents
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: applying exponent product/quotient laws to combine same-base powers with symbolic exponents
questions.questionType: multi-step algebraic simplification with divisibility condition
questions.stem:
For an integer n, define P = (2^(n+3) · 2^(2n−1)) / (2^(n+2) · 2^(n−4)).

First rewrite P as a single power of 2, then determine for which integers n the resulting exponent is a multiple of 4. Which statement is correct?

options.A: P = 2^(n+4), and its exponent is a multiple of 4 exactly when n ≡ 0 (mod 4)
options.B: P = 2^(n+4), and its exponent is a multiple of 4 exactly when n is even
options.C: P = 2^(n+4), and its exponent is a multiple of 4 only when n = 0
options.D: P = 2^n, and its exponent is a multiple of 4 exactly when n ≡ 0 (mod 4)
options.E: P = 2^(5n), and its exponent is a multiple of 4 exactly when n is even

questions.explanation:
Combine the numerator with the product law: exponent = (n+3)+(2n−1) = 3n+2. Combine the denominator: (n+2)+(n−4) = 2n−2. Apply the quotient law: P = 2^((3n+2)−(2n−2)) = 2^(n+4). The exponent n+4 is a multiple of 4 ⇔ n+4 ≡ 0 (mod 4) ⇔ n ≡ 0 (mod 4). This is A.

Trap B: correct power 2^(n+4), but the solver relaxes "multiple of 4" to merely "even" (n+4 even ⇔ n even), a divisibility misconception. Trap C: correct power, but the solver demands the exponent itself equal 4 rather than be any multiple of 4, forcing n+4 = 4, i.e. n = 0. Trap D: sign-distribution error on the quotient — writing −(2n−2) as −2n−2 gives exponent 3n+2−2n−2 = n, so 2^n. Trap E: adds the denominator exponents instead of subtracting them (treating division like multiplication), giving (3n+2)+(2n−2) = 5n, then also mis-states the divisibility condition as "n even."

questions.competency: Using the tangent-perpendicular-to-radius property to model the tangent kite as two congruent right triangles, then applying Pythagoras to relate the external point's distance, radius, and tangent length via an area constraint.
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Plane geometry — circles, tangents and the tangent kite
questions.skill: Modelling two tangents from an external point as congruent right triangles and combining an area constraint with Pythagoras and the perpendicular-diagonals property of a kite
questions.stem: A circular fountain with centre O sits in a plaza. From a gate at point P, two straight walkways run tangent to the fountain's rim, touching it at A and B (see figure, where the small squares mark OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB). Gardeners will plant a flower strip along the straight segment AB that joins the two contact points. The four-sided region PAOB, enclosed by the walkways PA and PB together with the radii OA and OB, has area 300 m². Using the radius shown in the figure, find the length of the flower strip AB.
questions.explanation: The figure supplies the radius r = OA = 20 m (the text alone does not). Because PA and PB are tangents, OA ⟂ PA and OB ⟂ PB, so triangles OAP and OBP are congruent right triangles with legs r and t = PA = PB. Hence the kite PAOB has area r·t: 20·t = 300 gives t = 15 m. Pythagoras in right triangle OAP gives OP = √(20² + 15²) = √625 = 25 m. The diagonals of the kite, OP and AB, are perpendicular, so its area also equals ½·OP·AB; thus 300 = ½·25·AB, giving AB = 24 m → C. Distractor traps: A) 12 m drops the factor 2 (it is the half-chord area/OP = 300/25, i.e. AH, not the full chord AB = 2·AH). B) 15 m is the tangent length t, the intermediate result, reported instead of the requested chord. D) 25 m is OP, the distance to the centre, mistaking the diagonal for the chord (stopping at the Pythagoras step). E) 40 m assumes AB equals the diameter 2r, wrongly treating the two contact points as diametrically opposite.

questions.competency: Applying logarithm laws (product and power rules) to rewrite a transformed argument in terms of the original log value
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Applying logarithm laws (product and power rules) to rewrite a transformed argument in terms of the original log value
questions.stem: The figure shows the graph of f(x) = log₁₀x (blue) together with the graph of a related function h(x) (red) obtained by transforming f. Four points are marked with their coordinates. Reading the transformation from the graph, which single expression is equal to h(x) for all x > 0?
questions.explanation: From the figure, h passes through (1, 2) and (10, −1), while f passes through (1, 0) and (10, 1). Writing h(x) = a·log₁₀x + b: at x = 1, log₁₀1 = 0 so b = 2; at x = 10, log₁₀10 = 1 so a + 2 = −1, giving a = −3. Thus h(x) = −3·log₁₀x + 2. Converting to a single logarithm using the power rule (−3·log₁₀x = log₁₀x⁻³) and the fact that the additive constant 2 = log₁₀10² = log₁₀100, plus the product rule: h(x) = log₁₀(100·x⁻³) = log₁₀(100/x³) → A. Trap B keeps +3 (ignores that the red curve is DECREASING, i.e. reflected — reads the slope-in-log as +3 instead of −3). Trap C turns the additive +2 into a literal factor of 2 inside the log instead of 10² = 100 (forgets that a vertical shift of b becomes multiplication by 10ᵇ). Trap D reads the vertical stretch as ×2 instead of ×3 (the "classic" factor-of-2 value, e.g. from misreading the marked point), giving log₁₀(100/x²). Trap E inverts the power rule, writing −3·log₁₀x as log₁₀(x^(−1/3)) = log₁₀(1/∛x) instead of log₁₀(x⁻³). Only A applies reflection, stretch, and shift correctly.

questions.competency: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of a segment via midpoint plus negative-reciprocal slope in coordinate geometry
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Lines in the Cartesian plane: perpendicular bisector and equidistant locus
questions.skill: Constructing the perpendicular bisector of a segment via midpoint plus negative-reciprocal slope in coordinate geometry
questions.stem: In the coordinate plane shown, A and B are the endpoints of a segment (filled dots). The three open circles each mark a point that is equidistant from A and from B. Read all coordinates from the grid. Which equation represents the line containing every point equidistant from A and B (i.e. the perpendicular bisector of AB)?
questions.explanation:
From the grid, A(-2,1) and B(4,5). The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint M = ((-2+4)/2,(1+5)/2) = (1,3) with slope equal to the negative reciprocal of slope(AB). slope(AB) = (5-1)/(4-(-2)) = 4/6 = 2/3, so the bisector slope is -3/2. Then y - 3 = -3/2(x - 1) gives y = -3/2·x + 9/2. This line also fits the three equidistant open points (1,3), (3,0), (-1,6), confirming answer A.

Distractor traps:
B) y = 2/3·x + 7/3 — used slope(AB) = 2/3 itself through M, forgetting to take the negative reciprocal (perpendicularity missed entirely).
C) y = 3/2·x + 3/2 — took a reciprocal but dropped the sign (used +3/2 instead of -3/2); it still passes through M, so it looks tempting.
D) y = -3/2·x - 2 — correct perpendicular slope -3/2 but anchored the line at endpoint A(-2,1) instead of the midpoint, so it fails the equidistant points.
E) y = -2/3·x + 11/3 — negated slope(AB) to -2/3 instead of forming the true negative reciprocal -3/2 (confusing "opposite slope" with "perpendicular slope").

questions.competency: simplifying nested radical/rational-exponent expressions by applying index laws and rationalizing to match an equivalent form
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Simplifying nested radicals via index laws and rationalizing to an equivalent form
questions.stem:
Simplify the nested expression

E = √( (3/2) · √(2/3) )

and write the result with a rational (radical-free) denominator. Which of the following equals E?

(Here √ denotes a square root and ∜ denotes a fourth root.)
questions.explanation:
Correct path (A): Track the primes 2 and 3 separately. The inner radical √(2/3) = 2^(1/2)·3^(-1/2). Multiplying by 3/2 = 3^1·2^(-1): the product is 3^(1-1/2)·2^(-1+1/2) = 3^(1/2)·2^(-1/2) = (3/2)^(1/2). The OUTER square root halves that exponent: E = (3/2)^(1/4). Rationalize the fourth root by making the denominator a perfect 4th power: (3/2)^(1/4) = (3·2^3 / 2^4)^(1/4) = (24/16)^(1/4) = ∜24 / ∜16 = ∜24 / 2.

Trap in B (√6/2): the student treats the two stacked square roots as a single square root, stopping at (3/2)^(1/2) = √(3/2) = √6/2 — i.e. they forget that nesting a square root inside a square root produces a FOURTH-root (exponent 1/4), not 1/2.

Trap in C (∜6/2): correct value (3/2)^(1/4) = ∜3/∜2, but rationalized wrongly by multiplying top and bottom by ∜2 and claiming ∜2·∜2 = 2. In fact ∜2·∜2 = √2, so ∜3·∜2/(∜2·∜2) = ∜6/√2, not ∜6/2. This encodes the classic "multiply by the same radical clears it to an integer" error carried over from square roots.

Trap in D (∜54/3): the student subtracts the prime exponents in the wrong order (or inverts the fraction), getting (2/3)^(1/4) instead of (3/2)^(1/4). Rationalizing that inverted value: (2/3)^(1/4) = (2·3^3/3^4)^(1/4) = ∜54/3. The rationalization is done correctly, but on the reciprocal — a pure order-of-subtraction slip.

Trap in E (∜24/4): the rationalization set-up (24/16)^(1/4) is right, but the student evaluates ∜16 = 4 (confusing the fourth root with the square root √16 = 4). The true ∜16 = 2, so the denominator should be 2, not 4.

questions.competency: Decomposing a figure using the medial-triangle property (midpoint segments) to compute an area as a fraction of the whole via area-ratio scaling
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Plane geometry — triangles and the midpoint (medial) triangle
questions.skill: Iterated medial-triangle decomposition and area-ratio scaling to find a region's area as a fraction of the whole
questions.stem: The figure shows equilateral triangle ABC with area 48 cm². The midpoints of the sides of ABC are joined to form triangle DEF, and then the midpoints of the sides of DEF are joined to form triangle GHI. Using the shading in the figure, find the total area of the shaded region.
questions.explanation: Joining the midpoints of any triangle creates a medial triangle whose linear scale factor is 1/2, so its area is (1/2)² = 1/4 of the original — the shape being equilateral is irrelevant, only the scaling matters. Level 1: area(DEF) = (1/4)(48) = 12 cm². Level 2: area(GHI) = (1/4)(12) = 3 cm². The figure shades the RING inside DEF but outside GHI (the three corner sub-triangles of DEF), so shaded = area(DEF) − area(GHI) = 12 − 3 = 9 cm² → C. Distractor traps: A) 3 cm² takes only the innermost triangle GHI (misreads the shading as the center rather than the ring). B) 6 cm² uses the linear ratio 1/2 instead of the area ratio 1/4 for the second construction (GHI wrongly = 6, ring = 12−6 = 6), the classic linear-vs-area scaling error. D) 12 cm² stops at the first medial triangle and shades all of DEF, forgetting the inner triangle is cut out. E) 15 cm² adds the inner triangle instead of subtracting it (12 + 3), i.e. treats the shading as DEF together with GHI. Each distractor is a single, distinct reasoning slip, and none is independently correct.

questions.competency: successive percentage reduction on a changing base — applying a second percentage to the remaining fraction rather than the original total (multiplicative complement chaining)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Successive percentage change on a changing base (multiplicative complement chaining)
questions.stem: An industrial cooling system starts a maintenance cycle completely full of coolant. During the first phase, 20% of the coolant is drained off. During the second phase, a further 25% of the coolant still present in the system (i.e. of the amount left after the first phase) is drained off. In the third phase, technicians pump in fresh coolant to bring the level back up to exactly 90% of the original full amount. In the third phase, the volume of fresh coolant added is what percentage of the volume present in the system at the start of that phase?
questions.explanation:
Take the full system as 100 units. Phase 1 removes 20% → 80 units remain. Phase 2 removes 25% of what remains (base change), i.e. 25% of 80 = 20 units → 60 units remain. The target is 90% of the original = 90 units, so the volume added in phase 3 is 90 − 60 = 30 units. The question asks for this as a percentage of the volume present at the START of phase 3, which is 60 units: 30/60 = 50%. Correct = A.
B) 30%: expresses the 30 units added as a percentage of the ORIGINAL total (100) instead of the current base (60) — the classic 'wrong base' error the item targets.
C) 45%: naively 'adds back what was lost' by summing the two loss percentages (20% + 25%), ignoring that the second base differs and that only 90% must be restored.
D) 33%: uses the TARGET volume (90) as the base — 30/90 ≈ 33% — instead of the volume actually present when the addition begins.
E) 67%: restores to 100% of the original instead of 90% — (100 − 60)/60 = 66.7% ≈ 67% — correct base but wrong target level.

questions.competency: counting arrangements under position-parity constraints (multiplication principle: independent factorial choices for two disjoint slot sets)
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: multiplication principle over two disjoint slot sets (independent factorial arrangements)
questions.stem: A gallery displays 7 distinct statues on a row of 7 pedestals. The pedestals come in two sizes, arranged exactly as shown below (L = large pedestal, S = small pedestal). Five of the statues are large and each one can only stand on a large pedestal; the remaining two statues are small and each one can only stand on a small pedestal. In how many different ways can the curator place all seven statues on the seven pedestals?
questions.explanation: The figure must be read to determine the two slot sets: it shows 5 large pedestals (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 7) and 2 small pedestals (positions 2, 5). The 5 large statues can only occupy the 5 large pedestals and the 2 small statues only the 2 small pedestals, so the placements split into two disjoint, independent slot sets. By the multiplication principle the total is 5! x 2! = 120 x 2 = 240 (A). Distractor traps: B) 480 = 2 x 5! x 2! wrongly multiplies by 2, treating the assignment of a statue-group to a pedestal-size as a free choice, but the size match is forced (large statues cannot swap onto small pedestals). C) 122 = 5! + 2! adds the two independent factorial counts instead of multiplying them. D) 5040 = 7! ignores the size constraint entirely and permutes all statues freely. E) 21 = C(7,2) counts only WHICH pedestals hold the small statues (a mere selection) and forgets to order the distinct statues within each size group. Only A follows the multiplication principle correctly.

questions.competency: Understanding that buoyant force depends only on the volume of displaced fluid (Archimedes' principle), independent of the body's mass or density; recognizing mass as an irrelevant distractor.
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Fluid statics (Archimedes' principle) and Newton's second law
questions.skill: Buoyant force depends only on displaced-fluid volume, not on the body's mass; combining Archimedes' principle with F = ma
questions.stem: Two solid bodies P and Q have identical volume and are fully immersed in the same liquid. They are held at rest and then released simultaneously. The free-body diagram shows the forces acting on each body at the instant of release; the arrows are drawn to scale (blue = buoyant force B, red = weight W, with the numerical values indicated). Taking g = 10 m/s^2, what is the ratio of the magnitude of P's initial acceleration to the magnitude of Q's initial acceleration, a_P : a_Q?

options.E: Cannot be determined without knowing the density of the liquid

questions.explanation: Because P and Q have the same volume, they displace the same volume of liquid, so Archimedes' principle gives them equal buoyant forces — the figure shows both as B = 15 N (mass/weight is the irrelevant distractor for buoyancy). The weights differ: W_P = 5 N so m_P = W_P/g = 0.5 kg, and W_Q = 25 N so m_Q = 2.5 kg. Net forces: P has 15 - 5 = 10 N upward, Q has 25 - 15 = 10 N downward. Applying F = ma: a_P = 10/0.5 = 20 m/s^2, a_Q = 10/2.5 = 4 m/s^2, giving a_P : a_Q = 5 : 1 (option C). Distractor traps: A (1:1) equates the equal net-force magnitudes (10 N each) with equal acceleration, forgetting to divide by the unequal masses (it is also the answer of someone who thinks equal buoyancy implies equal motion). B (5:2) comes from adding buoyancy and weight instead of subtracting (net 20 N and 40 N, then /mass = 40:16 = 5:2), a sign error. D (1:5) takes the mass/weight ratio 1:5 directly as the acceleration ratio — the 'heavier accelerates more' misconception, the exact inverse of the truth. E encodes the misconception that the liquid's density is needed, when the to-scale figure already supplies every force, so the problem is fully determined.

questions.competency: Deriving kinetic energy of a freely falling body over time by combining v=gt with KE=½mv² and converting weight to mass (m=P/g)
questions.subject: physics
questions.subtopic: Kinematics and energy of free fall
questions.skill: Deriving kinetic energy of a freely falling body by reading g from a v-t graph slope, converting weight to mass (m=P/g), and applying KE=1/2 mv^2
questions.stem: On a distant planet, a small survey crate of weight P = 60 N is released from rest and falls freely toward the ground; air resistance is negligible. A sensor records the crate's motion, producing the velocity–time graph shown. The local gravitational acceleration is NOT given numerically — it must be obtained from the graph. Using the graph, determine the kinetic energy of the crate at the instant t = 2 s.
questions.explanation: The graph is a straight line through (0,0), (2,20) and (4,40), so its slope gives the local gravitational acceleration g = Δv/Δt = 40/4 = 10 m/s². Since weight P = mg, the mass is m = P/g = 60/10 = 6 kg. Reading the velocity at t = 2 s from the line gives v = 20 m/s. Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv² = ½(6)(20²) = ½(6)(400) = 1200 J → A. Traps: B = 2400 J drops the factor ½ (computes mv²). C = 12000 J uses the weight itself as the mass (m = P = 60, skipping the m = P/g conversion): ½(60)(400). D = 300 J misreads the graph, taking the velocity at t = 1 s (v = 10 m/s) instead of t = 2 s: ½(6)(100). E = 60 J forgets to square the velocity, computing ½mv = ½(6)(20). Only A applies all three required steps: extract g from the slope, convert weight to mass, and square the graph-read velocity.

questions.competency: Applying the thermodynamic efficiency definition (η = W/Q_absorbed) to recover absorbed heat from work output
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Applying the thermodynamic efficiency definition (η = W/Q_absorbed) to recover absorbed heat from work output
questions.stem: A stationary electric generator is driven by a heat engine that operates in cycles. In each cycle the engine takes in heat from burning fuel, delivers useful work, and rejects 1800 J of heat to the surrounding air. The engine runs at 4 cycles per second and delivers a steady mechanical power output of 2400 W. Assuming all of the mechanical work is produced by the engine's cycles, what is the thermodynamic efficiency of the engine?
questions.explanation:
Correct path (A): Work per cycle = power / cycle-rate = 2400 W / 4 s⁻¹ = 600 J. Heat absorbed per cycle = work + heat rejected = 600 + 1800 = 2400 J (first law over a cycle, ΔU = 0). Efficiency η = W/Q_absorbed = 600/2400 = 0.25 = 25%.
Distractor B (75%): computes the ratio of rejected heat to absorbed heat (1800/2400 = 0.75) and reports it as efficiency — confusing the rejected fraction with the useful fraction (η = 1 − Q_rejected/Q_absorbed is the correct relation, giving 25%).
Distractor C (40%): forgets to divide power by cycle rate and instead treats the rejected heat as if per second, or mismatches per-cycle and per-second quantities — e.g. takes W=2400 and Q_abs = 2400+1800·(fractional mix) leading to 2400/6000 = 40%; a units/rate-mixing error.
Distractor D (33%): uses η = W/Q_rejected = 600/1800 = 1/3, dividing work by the rejected heat instead of the absorbed heat (wrong denominator).
Distractor E (60%): computes Q_absorbed correctly as 2400 J but then takes η = Q_rejected... no — takes the complement of D or uses W/(Q_abs−W)·something; specifically 1 − 600/1800·... reflects mixing the two heats: 1800/(1800+1200) = 60%, an invented split. Each distractor corresponds to a distinct wrong denominator or a rate-mixing mistake, and none is also correct.

questions.competency: recognizing that sound is a mechanical/elastic wave requiring a material medium, with propagation speed set by the medium's properties (not a fixed universal constant, not able to travel through vacuum)
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Recognizing sound as a mechanical wave whose speed is determined by the medium and which cannot propagate through vacuum
questions.stem: An engineer designs a demonstration in which a small buzzer emits a steady tone. The buzzer is placed in turn inside three sealed identical chambers, and in each case the time for the sound to travel a fixed 3.0 m path to a microphone is measured. Chamber 1 is filled with air; Chamber 2 is filled with helium; Chamber 3 is evacuated to a near-perfect vacuum. A colleague predicts: "Since the buzzer, path length, and tone are identical, the travel time will be the same in all three chambers, because the speed of sound is a fixed property of the buzzer that produces it." Which single statement correctly evaluates this prediction?

options.A: The prediction fails on every chamber: the travel time differs between air and helium because sound speed is set by the medium, and in the vacuum no sound reaches the microphone at all because a mechanical wave needs a material medium to propagate.
options.B: The prediction is correct for the two gas-filled chambers but fails only for the vacuum, since sound travels at one universal speed through any gas but cannot cross a vacuum.
options.C: The prediction is correct: the tone's frequency is fixed by the buzzer, so the travel time is identical in all three chambers, including the vacuum, where the wave simply propagates more weakly.
options.D: The prediction fails only for the helium chamber; sound travels through air and vacuum at the same speed set by the source, but helium's different composition changes the speed.
options.E: The prediction fails on every chamber, but for a different reason: sound speed depends on the tone's frequency, so a single buzzer would give three different times, and in the vacuum the wave is simply slowest of all.

questions.explanation: The competency: sound is a mechanical/elastic wave that requires a material medium and whose speed is set by the medium's properties, not by the source and not by a universal constant. Correct answer A: helium and air are different media, so the sound speed (and thus travel time) differs between Chambers 1 and 2; in the vacuum there is no medium, so the mechanical wave cannot propagate and the microphone detects nothing — the prediction fails everywhere. Distractor B encodes the misconception that all gases carry sound at one common speed (e.g., "340 m/s in any gas"); in fact helium's low density/high sound speed makes it faster than air, so the two gas times differ. Distractor C is the source-owned-speed misconception plus the false belief that sound merely "weakens" in vacuum rather than being unable to propagate at all. Distractor D encodes the belief that vacuum behaves like air (sound crosses it) while only singling out helium — it wrongly lets sound cross the vacuum and wrongly ties speed to the source for air. Distractor E confuses wave speed with frequency (in a given medium, sound speed is independent of frequency) and repeats the false claim that sound is merely "slowest" in vacuum rather than absent. Only A correctly combines medium-dependent speed with the impossibility of propagation through vacuum.

questions.competency: thermal equilibrium via mass-weighted average temperature (calorimetry, conservation of heat with equal specific heats)
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Set up heat-conservation balance with equal specific heats and solve for an unknown mass given the equilibrium temperature
questions.stem: In a food-processing plant, an insulated tank holds 4.0 kg of water at 20 °C. A technician pours in an additional mass m of water at 80 °C. The added water is the same liquid (identical specific heat), the tank loses no heat to its surroundings, and no water evaporates. When thermal equilibrium is reached, the temperature is 32 °C. What is the added mass m?
questions.explanation: Heat is conserved: the heat released by the hot water equals the heat absorbed by the cold water. With equal specific heats, c cancels: m·(80 − 32) = 4.0·(32 − 20), i.e. m·48 = 4.0·12 = 48, so m = 1.0 kg (B). Each distractor is a specific error path. A) 0.8 kg: takes the hot-water fraction f = (32 − 20)/(80 − 20) = 0.2 and multiplies it by the known cold mass (0.2 × 4.0), forgetting that the unknown hot mass also enters the total mass, so this under-counts. C) 1.6 kg: uses absolute temperatures instead of temperature changes (m·80 = 4.0·32), i.e. treats "heat" as mass × temperature rather than mass × temperature change. D) 4.0 kg: assumes equal masses produce the mixture — but equal masses of 20 °C and 80 °C water would equilibrate at the midpoint 50 °C, not 32 °C, so this ignores that the final temperature is far from midway. E) 16 kg: swaps the two temperature drops, writing m·(32 − 20) = 4.0·(80 − 32); assigning the small drop to the hot water and the large drop to the cold water inverts the mass ratio. Only B balances the correct heat exchange.

questions.competency: recognizing the scalar projection of one vector onto another as (a·b)/|b|, distinguishing dot vs cross product roles
questions.subject: physics
questions.skill: Scalar projection of a vector; distinguishing dot vs cross product
questions.stem: A linear actuator applies a force, drawn as vector a from the point O, while a rigid guide rail extends from O along the direction of vector b. Both vectors are shown on the grid below (each square = 1 length unit), together with the perpendicular dropped from the tip of a onto the line of the rail. Reading the components of a and b directly from the grid, determine the scalar projection of a onto b — that is, the length of the shadow that a casts along the rail's line (the segment marked in bold from O to the foot of the perpendicular).
questions.explanation: From the grid, a = (6, 8) and b = (4, 3), so |b| = 5, |a| = 10, the dot product a·b = 6·4 + 8·3 = 48, and the cross-product magnitude |a×b| = |6·3 − 8·4| = 14. The scalar projection of a onto b is (a·b)/|b| = 48/5 = 9.6 (D). Each distractor is a specific error: (A) 0.96 = (a·b)/(|a||b|) computes cosθ, confusing the projection with the direction cosine and forgetting to multiply by |a|; (B) 2.8 = |a×b|/|b| uses the CROSS product instead of the dot product, which yields the perpendicular (rejection) distance from a's tip to the rail — the length of the dashed segment, not the bold one; (C) 4.8 = (a·b)/|a| normalizes by the wrong vector, dividing by the magnitude of a instead of the vector b that is being projected onto; (E) 1.4 = |a×b|/|a| compounds both mistakes (cross product plus wrong normalization). Only (a·b)/|b| gives the projection along b.

questions.competency: Translating a natural-language "not-P if not-Q" prohibition into a necessary-condition relation, and distinguishing necessary from sufficient conditions
questions.subject: logic
questions.skill: Translating negated conditionals and chaining necessary conditions
questions.stem: At a scientific congress two rules govern the Rossi Prize. Rule 1: "A paper is not eligible for the Rossi Prize if it does not have at least one undergraduate co-author." Rule 2: "Only papers that are eligible for the Rossi Prize are read aloud at the closing ceremony." If both rules are always applied, which of the following must be true?

options.A: Every paper read aloud at the closing ceremony has at least one undergraduate co-author.
options.B: Any paper that has at least one undergraduate co-author is eligible for the Rossi Prize.
options.C: Every paper eligible for the Rossi Prize is read aloud at the closing ceremony.
options.D: A paper that is not read aloud at the closing ceremony has no undergraduate co-author.
options.E: A paper is eligible for the Rossi Prize only if it both has an undergraduate co-author and is read aloud at the closing ceremony.

questions.explanation: Translate each rule into its conditional form. Rule 1, "not eligible if no undergraduate co-author," is "eligible → has an undergraduate co-author," i.e. having an undergraduate co-author is a NECESSARY condition for eligibility. Rule 2, "only eligible papers are read aloud," is "read aloud → eligible," i.e. eligibility is necessary for being read aloud. Chaining the two necessary conditions gives: read aloud → eligible → has an undergraduate co-author. Hence every paper read aloud must have an undergraduate co-author, so A is forced. Each distractor encodes a specific error: B is the converse of Rule 1 — it treats the necessary condition (co-author) as SUFFICIENT for eligibility, which the rules never state. C is the converse of Rule 2 — it treats eligibility (only necessary for being read aloud) as sufficient for being read aloud; many eligible papers may never be read. D is the inverse/denied-antecedent error on the chain — not being read aloud tells us nothing about co-authorship. E reverses the direction of Rule 2 by making "read aloud" a necessary condition for eligibility; in fact eligibility does not require being read aloud. Only A is a valid consequence of chaining the two genuine necessary conditions.

questions.competency: translating a percentage-complete statement into the whole via the complementary fraction (25% = 10 → find 100%)
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Percentages and fractions of a whole
questions.skill: Recovering the whole from a fractional/percentage change via the complementary fraction
questions.stem: A crew is laying a straight drainage pipeline of unknown total length. At the start of a work shift, the portion still to be laid is 5/8 of the whole pipeline. During the shift the crew lays another 1500 m of pipe, after which the portion still to be laid has dropped to 1/4 of the whole pipeline. What is the total length of the pipeline?
questions.explanation: Let T be the total length. The 1500 m laid during the shift is exactly the pipe that moved from "still to be laid" to "laid," so it corresponds to the DROP in the remaining fraction: 5/8 − 1/4 = 5/8 − 2/8 = 3/8 of T. Thus (3/8)·T = 1500 → T = 1500·8/3 = 4000 m (C). Distractor traps: (D) 6000 m equates the 1500 m with the FINAL remaining fraction 1/4 (1500 = T/4), confusing pipe just laid with pipe still left. (B) 2400 m equates 1500 m with the INITIAL remaining fraction 5/8 (1500 = 5T/8), the same confusion at the start of the shift. (A) 2000 m equates 1500 m with the total DONE fraction after the shift, 3/4 (1500 = 3T/4), forgetting that some pipe was already laid before the shift. (E) 12000 m comes from mis-computing the fractional drop as 1/8 instead of 3/8 (e.g., mis-subtracting 5/8 − 1/4) and solving 1500 = T/8. Only the complementary-fraction difference 3/8 correctly maps the measured 1500 m to the whole.

questions.competency: Recognizing the symmetry of an absolute-value (V-shaped) function about its vertex, so that f(a)=f(b) when a and b are equidistant from the vertex abscissa
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Recognizing the symmetry of an absolute-value (V-shaped) function about its vertex, so that f(a)=f(b) when a and b are equidistant from the vertex abscissa
questions.stem: The diagram shows part of the graph of a function y = |ax + b| (with a and b real constants). Point P lies on the left-hand branch. Two other points on the graph are joined by a dashed horizontal segment because they sit at the same height. Reading only the values shown on the graph, find the x-coordinate of the point on the right-hand branch that lies at the same height as P.
questions.explanation: A V-shaped graph y = |ax + b| is symmetric about the vertical line through its vertex, so two points have equal height exactly when they are equidistant from the vertex abscissa. The figure gives no formula, so the vertex must be located from the two equal-height points, which sit at x = 0 and x = 7; the axis of symmetry is their midpoint, x = (0 + 7)/2 = 3.5. Point P is at x = −2, and its mirror image across x = 3.5 is x = 2(3.5) − (−2) = 9 (correct, A). Distractor B (16) uses the marked point x = 7 as the axis of symmetry instead of the true vertex: 2(7) − (−2) = 16. Distractor C (5) drops the sign of P and reflects x = +2 about 3.5: 2(3.5) − 2 = 5. Distractor D (2) assumes symmetry about the y-axis, giving −(−2) = 2. Distractor E (5.5) adds P's distance-from-origin |−2| = 2 to the vertex (3.5 + 2) instead of P's true distance 5.5 from the vertex. Only x = 9 is equidistant from x = 3.5 as P.

questions.competency: Inverting a linear-fractional (Möbius) relation: solving a rational equation for the other variable by cross-multiplying and isolating
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.subtopic: Rational equations / solving for a variable
questions.skill: Inverting a linear-fractional (Möbius) relation by cross-multiplying and collecting the target variable
questions.stem:
In a negative-feedback amplifier the measured closed-loop gain G is related to the internal open-loop gain A and a fixed feedback fraction β by the relation

  G = A / (1 + βA).

An engineer knows G and β and wants to recover the open-loop gain A. Solving the relation for A gives A =
questions.explanation:
Cross-multiply: G(1 + βA) = A, so G + βGA = A. The target variable A now appears on BOTH sides — that collection step is what makes the item selective. Gather A: G = A − βGA = A(1 − βG), hence A = G/(1 − βG). Option A is correct.

Distractor traps:
B) G/(1 + βG): keeps the +βGA on the wrong side, writing G = A(1 + βG) — a sign slip in collecting the shared A term (the classic error absent from a one-sided invert).
C) G/(βG − 1): factors as A(βG − 1) = G, negating the whole denominator (sign reversal of the isolated group).
D) G(1 − βG): correctly finds the factor (1 − βG) but multiplies instead of dividing by it — failure to isolate.
E) (1 − βG)/G: inverts the final fraction (reciprocal error), a rote symmetry guess.
Each distractor is a distinct, plausible rational form; none is also correct and none is trivially eliminable.

questions.competency: Rearranging a simple proportional linear equation to express one variable in terms of another via the ratio of coefficients
questions.subject: mathematics
questions.skill: Rearranging and chaining proportional linear equations (variable elimination + coefficient-ratio inversion)
questions.questionType: Algebraic manipulation — eliminating a variable from a linear proportional system and expressing one unknown in terms of another via the ratio of coefficients
questions.stem:
In a gearbox, three shafts rotate at steady angular speeds a, b and c (in rad/s). The mechanical couplings between the shafts impose the two exact relations

  3a = 8b   and   6b = 5c.

Express c in terms of a.
questions.explanation:
The middle variable b must be eliminated. From 3a = 8b, correctly rearranged, b = (3/8)a. From 6b = 5c, correctly rearranged, c = (6/5)b. Substituting: c = (6/5)(3/8)a = 18/40 a = (9/20)a. So A is correct.

Each distractor is a distinct rearrangement error:
- B (3/5)a: the student assumes b simply "cancels," treating the two equations as 3a = 5c (dropping the 8 and 6 coefficients that belong to b), giving c = (3/5)a.
- C (5/16)a: the second relation is inverted — writing c = (5/6)b instead of c = (6/5)b — so (5/6)(3/8) = 5/16.
- D (16/5)a: the first relation is inverted — writing b = (8/3)a instead of (3/8)a — so (6/5)(8/3) = 16/5.
- E (20/9)a: both relations are inverted (b = (8/3)a and c = (5/6)b), compounding both mistakes into (5/6)(8/3) = 20/9.

Only A applies the ratio of coefficients correctly to both stages. The distractors have magnitudes both below and above 1, so none can be eliminated by a quick sanity check — the item is decided purely by correct rearrangement and elimination.
